In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will come to know.﴾.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will come to know.﴾.

Know that His saying ﴿These﴾ refers to the verses contained in the surah. By "the Book" and "the clear Qur'an" is meant the Book that Allah, exalted is He, promised to Muhammad (ﷺ). The indefinite form of "Qur'an" is for magnification. The meaning is: these verses are verses of that Book which is complete in being a Book and in being a Qur'an that conveys clarity.

As for His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: Nafi' and Asim read ﴿rubama﴾ with a light (unshaddahed) ba', while the others read it with a shaddah. Abu Hatim said: the people of the Hijaz pronounce ﴿rubama﴾ lightly, while Qays and Bakr pronounce it heavily. I say: this word has several dialectal forms, because the ra' of rubba may be vowelled with a damma or with a fatha. When it is vowelled with a damma, the ba' has come with a shaddah, with a light pronunciation, and with a sukun (vowelless), and in all these cases it occurs sometimes with the particle ma and sometimes without it. Also it occurs sometimes with the ta' and sometimes without it. They quoted in verse:

"Osamayya, what will tell you that many a young woman
I have enjoyed her delights with a dark, full cup?"

And rub with the ba' sukun, and they quoted the verse of the Hudhali:

"Uzuhayr, if the temples turn grey, then indeed
many a troop of armed men have I repelled with a troop."

Al-Haydal means an armed company. Also this word may come in both states of shaddah and lightness of the ba' with the particle "ma", as you say: rubama and rubbama; and sometimes with the ta', and with the particle "ma", as you say: rubatama and rubbatama. All of this is when the ra' of rubba is with a damma. It may also be with a fatha, so it is said: rabba, rabbama and rabbatama, as related by Qutrub. Abu Ali said: among the particles are those to which the feminine particle is attached, such as thamma and thammat, rubba and rubbat, and la and lat. All these dialects were related by al-Wahidi in al-Basit.

The second issue: rubba is a particle of jarr (governing the genitive) according to Sibawayh, and the particle ma is attached to it in two ways.

One of them: that it be indefinite, in the sense of "a thing", as in his saying:

"Many a thing that souls dislike of the matter
has a relief like the loosening of a tether."

So ma in this verse is a noun, and the evidence for this is that a pronoun refers back to it from the attribute, for the meaning is: many a thing that souls dislike. When the pronoun refers back to it, it is a noun and not a particle, just as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they reckon that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55]; when the pronoun refers back to it, we know thereby that it is a noun. And among what shows that ma may be a noun when it comes after rubba is the occurrence of "man" after it in the poet's saying:

"O many a one who diminishes our camels,
they departed, and they were lamenting their loss and going out."

Just as rubba entered upon the word "man" and it was indefinite, so it enters upon the word ma. This is one kind. The other kind is that ma enters as a restrictive particle, as in this verse. The grammarians call this ma "the restrictive ma," meaning that by its entry it restrains the particle from the work it used to do; and when this restraint takes place, then it becomes ready to enter upon what it did not enter upon before. Do you not see that rubba only enters upon a singular noun, as in "rubba man says that"; and it does not enter upon a verb? So when ma entered upon it, it prepared it to enter upon a verb, as in this verse. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: they agreed that rubba is placed to express paucity, and in paucity it is the counterpart of kam in abundance. So when a man says "rubama zara-na fulan" (perhaps so-and-so visited us), rubama indicates his visiting rarely. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever says that rubba is meant to express abundance has contradicted what the people of the language know. On this view, there is a question here: the disbeliever's wish to be a Muslim is certain, while the word rubba indicates conjecture; and also that wish occurs repeatedly and continually, so the word "rubama", which indicates paucity, is not fitting for it.

The answer to this has several aspects.

The first aspect: it is a custom of the Arabs that when they want to express abundance they mention a word that was set for paucity, and when they want to express certainty they mention a word that was set for doubt, and the purpose of that is to show expectation and to dispense with stating the matter plainly. So they say: "Perhaps you will regret what you have done," and "Perhaps you will regret your action," even though the knowledge that regret is abundant and occurs without doubt is already present. From this is the saying of the speaker:

"I may leave the opponent with his fingertips yellowed..."

The second aspect of the answer: this paucity is more forceful in threat, and its meaning is that a little regret suffices to deter you from this action, so how much more so a great deal of it?

The third aspect of the answer: that the punishment will occupy them from wishing for that except in a few cases.

The fourth issue: they agreed that the word rubba is specific to entering upon the past tense, as one says "rubama qasadani Abdullah" (perhaps Abdullah visited me), and the future tense is scarcely used after it. Some said: the matter is not so, and the evidence for this is the poet's saying:

"Perhaps souls dislike of the matter..."

This argument is weak, because we have shown that the word rubba in this verse enters upon a noun, whereas our discussion concerns when it enters upon a verb, in which case that verb must be past. How can one be connected to the other? However, I say what these men of letters say: that it is not permissible for this word to enter upon a future verb is a matter that cannot be established by rational proof; rather the reference in it is to transmission and usage. Had they found a verse containing this usage, they would have said that it is permissible and sound; and the speech of Allah is stronger, more majestic and more noble, so why do they not hold to its occurrence in this verse as evidence of its permissibility and soundness? Then we say: the men of letters answered this question in two ways.

The first: they said that what is expected in the reports of Allah, exalted is He, is like the past whose realization is certain, so it is as if it were said: "Perhaps they wished."

The second: that the word "ma" in His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾ is a noun, and ﴿yawaddu﴾ is an attribute of it, and the sense is: "many a thing those who disbelieved wish for." Al-Zajjaj said: whoever claims that the verse contains an implied "kana" (was), so that the sense is "perhaps those who disbelieved wished," has departed from the saying of Sibawayh, for do you not see that kana is not elided in his view? He did not permit "Abdullah al-maqbul" to mean "kana Abdullah al-maqbul" (Abdullah was the accepted one).

The fifth issue: concerning the interpretation of the verse, there are several views according to the exegetes, for each one took His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾ in a different sense. The most correct is what al-Zajjaj said, for he said: whenever the disbeliever sees one of the states of punishment, and sees one of the states of the Muslim, he wishes that he were a Muslim; and this view is the most correct. As for the earlier exegetes, they mentioned several views. Al-Dahhak said: it refers to what happens at death, for when the disbeliever witnesses the signs of punishment he wishes he were a Muslim. It was said: this state occurs when their faces turn black. It was said: rather, it occurs when they enter the Fire and the punishment descends, for then they say: ﴿Defer us to a near term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Abu Musa reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes and the people of the Fire gather in the Fire, and with them are whoever Allah wills from the People of the Qibla, the disbelievers will say to them: 'Were you not Muslims?' They will say: 'Yes.' They will say: 'Then what did your Islam avail you, since you have come to be with us in the Fire?' Then Allah, exalted is He, will show His bounty by the abundance of His mercy, and He will command that everyone who was of the People of the Qibla be brought out of the Fire, and they will come out of it. Then ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse. Most of the exegetes hold this view.

Mujahid related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah does not cease to show mercy to the believers and to bring them out of the Fire and admit them to Paradise through the intercession of the prophets and the angels, until at the end of the matter He says: "Whoever was among the Muslims, let him enter Paradise." He said: "Then ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾." The Qadi said: these narrations are based on the premise that He brings out the people of major sins from the Fire, and on the premise that the intercession of the Messenger is accepted in removing punishment; and these two principles are rejected by him. Therefore this report was interpreted in a way that agrees with his view and conforms to his doctrine: that He, exalted is He, delays the entry of a group of the believers into Paradise to such an extent that it dominates the assumption of these disbelievers that He will not admit them to Paradise; then He admits them to Paradise, and the grief and regret of the disbelievers increase, and there they wish that they had been Muslims. He said: by this path these reports are made sound. And Allah knows best.

If it is said: if the people of the Resurrection wish for such states, then it must be that the believer whose reward is small wishes for the rank of the believer whose reward is great; and the one who wishes, when he does not attain it, will be in grief and pain of heart; and this requires that most believers be in grief and pain of heart.

We say: the conditions of the people of the Hereafter are not to be measured by the conditions of the people of this world. Allah, glorified is He, has made everyone content with what he has, and has removed from their hearts the desire for more, as He said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will come to know﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: the meaning is: leave the disbelievers to take their portions of their worldly life, for that is their character, and they have no share in the Hereafter. His saying ﴿and let hope distract them﴾: it is said "lahiytu 'an al-shay' alha luhiyyan" (I was distracted from the thing). It is related in a report that Ibn al-Zubayr, whenever he heard the sound of thunder, was distracted from his speech. Al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i said: every thing you have abandoned, you have been distracted from it, and they quoted:

"She has cut your ties, so forget her, Zaynab;
indeed you have prolonged your rebuke of her, if only you would blame."

So His saying "fala-hi 'anha" means: leave her and turn away from her. The exegetes said: hope occupied them when taking their share, away from faith and obedience, so they will come to know.

The second issue: our companions used this verse as evidence that Allah, exalted is He, may turn a person away from faith and do to the accountable person what is a corruption for his religion. The proof of this is that He, exalted is He, said to His Messenger: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them﴾; so He judged that their absorption in enjoyment and their immersion in long hope distracts them from faith and obedience; then He permitted them to do so, and this indicates the intended point. The Mu'tazilites said: this is not permission and allowance; rather it is a threat and a warning.

We say: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿leave them﴾ is permission; at the very least, what is in the matter is that He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that their absorption in these deeds harms them in their religion. This is exactly what we mentioned: that He permitted something while stating explicitly that this thing is a corruption for them in religion.

The third issue: the verse indicates that preferring pleasure and luxury, and what long hope leads to, is not among the characters of the believers. It was reported from some of them: wallowing in this world is among the characters of the perishing. And the reports condemning hope are numerous. Among them is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The son of Adam grows old, and two things remain young in him: greed for wealth and long hope." And from him (ﷺ) that he drew three dots and said: "This is the son of Adam, this is hope, and this is the term; and beyond hope are ninety-nine deaths; if one of them seizes him, well and good; otherwise old age is behind him." And from Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: "I only fear two things for you: long hope and following desire; for long hope makes one forget the Hereafter, and following desire turns one away from the truth." And Allah knows best.

All of this is when the ra' of rubba is with a damma. It may also be with a fatha, so it is said: rabba, rabbama and rabbatama, as related by Qutrub. Abu Ali said: among the particles are those to which the feminine particle is attached, such as thamma and thammat, rubba and rubbat, and la and lat. All these dialects were related by al-Wahidi in al-Basit.

The second issue: rubba is a particle of jarr (governing the genitive) according to Sibawayh, and the particle ma is attached to it in two ways.

One of them: that it be indefinite, in the sense of "a thing", as in his saying:

"Many a thing that souls dislike of the matter
has a relief like the loosening of a tether."

So ma in this verse is a noun, and the evidence for this is that a pronoun refers back to it from the attribute, for the meaning is: many a thing that souls dislike. When the pronoun refers back to it, it is a noun and not a particle, just as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they reckon that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55]; when the pronoun refers back to it, we know thereby that it is a noun. And among what shows that ma may be a noun when it comes after rubba is the occurrence of "man" after it in the poet's saying:

"O many a one who diminishes our camels,
they departed, and they were lamenting their loss and going out."

Just as rubba entered upon the word "man" and it was indefinite, so it enters upon the word ma. This is one kind. The other kind is that ma enters as a restrictive particle, as in this verse. The grammarians call this ma "the restrictive ma," meaning that by its entry it restrains the particle from the work it used to do; and when this restraint takes place, then it becomes ready to enter upon what it did not enter upon before. Do you not see that rubba only enters upon a singular noun, as in "rubba man says that"; and it does not enter upon a verb? So when ma entered upon it, it prepared it to enter upon a verb, as in this verse. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: they agreed that rubba is placed to express paucity, and in paucity it is the counterpart of kam in abundance. So when a man says "rubama zara-na fulan" (perhaps so-and-so visited us), rubama indicates his visiting rarely. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever says that rubba is meant to express abundance has contradicted what the people of the language know. On this view, there is a question here: the disbeliever's wish to be a Muslim is certain, while the word rubba indicates conjecture; and also that wish occurs repeatedly and continually, so the word "rubama", which indicates paucity, is not fitting for it.

The answer to this has several aspects.

The first aspect: it is a custom of the Arabs that when they want to express abundance they mention a word that was set for paucity, and when they want to express certainty they mention a word that was set for doubt, and the purpose of that is to show expectation and to dispense with stating the matter plainly. So they say: "Perhaps you will regret what you have done," and "Perhaps you will regret your action," even though the knowledge that regret is abundant and occurs without doubt is already present. From this is the saying of the speaker:

"I may leave the opponent with his fingertips yellowed..."

The second aspect of the answer: this paucity is more forceful in threat, and its meaning is that a little regret suffices to deter you from this action, so how much more so a great deal of it?

The third aspect of the answer: that the punishment will occupy them from wishing for that except in a few cases.

The fourth issue: they agreed that the word rubba is specific to entering upon the past tense, as one says "rubama qasadani Abdullah" (perhaps Abdullah visited me), and the future tense is scarcely used after it. Some said: the matter is not so, and the evidence for this is the poet's saying:

"Perhaps souls dislike of the matter..."

This argument is weak, because we have shown that the word rubba in this verse enters upon a noun, whereas our discussion concerns when it enters upon a verb, in which case that verb must be past. How can one be connected to the other? However, I say what these men of letters say: that it is not permissible for this word to enter upon a future verb is a matter that cannot be established by rational proof; rather the reference in it is to transmission and usage. Had they found a verse containing this usage, they would have said that it is permissible and sound; and the speech of Allah is stronger, more majestic and more noble, so why do they not hold to its occurrence in this verse as evidence of its permissibility and soundness? Then we say: the men of letters answered this question in two ways.

The first: they said that what is expected in the reports of Allah, exalted is He, is like the past whose realization is certain, so it is as if it were said: "Perhaps they wished."

The second: that the word "ma" in His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾ is a noun, and ﴿yawaddu﴾ is an attribute of it, and the sense is: "many a thing those who disbelieved wish for." Al-Zajjaj said: whoever claims that the verse contains an implied "kana" (was), so that the sense is "perhaps those who disbelieved wished," has departed from the saying of Sibawayh, for do you not see that kana is not elided in his view? He did not permit "Abdullah al-maqbul" to mean "kana Abdullah al-maqbul" (Abdullah was the accepted one).

The fifth issue: concerning the interpretation of the verse, there are several views according to the exegetes, for each one took His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾ in a different sense. The most correct is what al-Zajjaj said, for he said: whenever the disbeliever sees one of the states of punishment, and sees one of the states of the Muslim, he wishes that he were a Muslim; and this view is the most correct. As for the earlier exegetes, they mentioned several views. Al-Dahhak said: it refers to what happens at death, for when the disbeliever witnesses the signs of punishment he wishes he were a Muslim. It was said: this state occurs when their faces turn black. It was said: rather, it occurs when they enter the Fire and the punishment descends, for then they say: ﴿Defer us to a near term; we will answer Your call and follow the messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 44]. Abu Musa reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes and the people of the Fire gather in the Fire, and with them are whoever Allah wills from the People of the Qibla, the disbelievers will say to them: 'Were you not Muslims?' They will say: 'Yes.' They will say: 'Then what did your Islam avail you, since you have come to be with us in the Fire?' Then Allah, exalted is He, will show His bounty by the abundance of His mercy, and He will command that everyone who was of the People of the Qibla be brought out of the Fire, and they will come out of it. Then ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse. Most of the exegetes hold this view.

Mujahid related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: Allah does not cease to show mercy to the believers and to bring them out of the Fire and admit them to Paradise through the intercession of the prophets and the angels, until at the end of the matter He says: "Whoever was among the Muslims, let him enter Paradise." He said: "Then ﴿those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾." The Qadi said: these narrations are based on the premise that He brings out the people of major sins from the Fire, and on the premise that the intercession of the Messenger is accepted in removing punishment; and these two principles are rejected by him. Therefore this report was interpreted in a way that agrees with his view and conforms to his doctrine: that He, exalted is He, delays the entry of a group of the believers into Paradise to such an extent that it dominates the assumption of these disbelievers that He will not admit them to Paradise; then He admits them to Paradise, and the grief and regret of the disbelievers increase, and there they wish that they had been Muslims. He said: by this path these reports are made sound. And Allah knows best.

If it is said: if the people of the Resurrection wish for such states, then it must be that the believer whose reward is small wishes for the rank of the believer whose reward is great; and the one who wishes, when he does not attain it, will be in grief and pain of heart; and this requires that most believers be in grief and pain of heart.

We say: the conditions of the people of the Hereafter are not to be measured by the conditions of the people of this world. Allah, glorified is He, has made everyone content with what he has, and has removed from their hearts the desire for more, as He said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will come to know﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: the meaning is: leave the disbelievers to take their portions of their worldly life, for that is their character, and they have no share in the Hereafter. His saying ﴿and let hope distract them﴾: it is said "lahiytu 'an al-shay' alha luhiyyan" (I was distracted from the thing). It is related in a report that Ibn al-Zubayr, whenever he heard the sound of thunder, was distracted from his speech. Al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i said: every thing you have abandoned, you have been distracted from it, and they quoted:

"She has cut your ties, so forget her, Zaynab;
indeed you have prolonged your rebuke of her, if only you would blame."

So His saying "fala-hi 'anha" means: leave her and turn away from her. The exegetes said: hope occupied them when taking their share, away from faith and obedience, so they will come to know.

The second issue: our companions used this verse as evidence that Allah, exalted is He, may turn a person away from faith and do to the accountable person what is a corruption for his religion. The proof of this is that He, exalted is He, said to His Messenger: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them﴾; so He judged that their absorption in enjoyment and their immersion in long hope distracts them from faith and obedience; then He permitted them to do so, and this indicates the intended point. The Mu'tazilites said: this is not permission and allowance; rather it is a threat and a warning.

We say: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿leave them﴾ is permission; at the very least, what is in the matter is that He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that their absorption in these deeds harms them in their religion. This is exactly what we mentioned: that He permitted something while stating explicitly that this thing is a corruption for them in religion.

The third issue: the verse indicates that preferring pleasure and luxury, and what long hope leads to, is not among the characters of the believers. It was reported from some of them: wallowing in this world is among the characters of the perishing. And the reports condemning hope are numerous. Among them is what is related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The son of Adam grows old, and two things remain young in him: greed for wealth and long hope." And from him (ﷺ) that he drew three dots and said: "This is the son of Adam, this is hope, and this is the term; and beyond hope are ninety-nine deaths; if one of them seizes him, well and good; otherwise old age is behind him." And from Ali, peace be upon him, that he said: "I only fear two things for you: long hope and following desire; for long hope makes one forget the Hereafter, and following desire turns one away from the truth." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 4–5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Never did We destroy a city but it had a decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can they delay it.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

Page 124

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, had earlier threatened those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ) with His saying, ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know,﴾ He followed it with what reinforces the warning, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Never did We destroy a city but it had a decreed term,﴾ concerning destruction and punishment. Advancement and delay occur within this: those who came before had the time of their destruction recorded in the Book as earlier, and those who came later had the time of their destruction recorded as later. This is the utmost in warning and admonition.

The second issue: Some said that the intended destruction is the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾsal) which God used to send down upon the obstinate deniers, as He explained concerning the people of Noah, the people of Hud, and others. Others said that the intended destruction is death. The judge (al-Qadi) said: The closer view is the first, because it is more forceful in warning. Thus God explained that this respite should not deceive the sensible person, because the punishment is stored up; for every nation there is a specific time for the descent of punishment that neither advances nor delays. Still others said that the intended destruction is the combination of both matters: the descent of the punishment of annihilation and the occurrence of death, since each of them shares with the other in being a destruction; therefore the wording must be understood as the common measure that includes both kinds together.

The third issue: al-Farra' said: If the wa' were not mentioned in His saying, ﴿and it had a decreed term,﴾ it would be correct, as in another verse: ﴿Never did We destroy a city but it had warners,﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 208]. This is like your saying: "I did not see anyone except that he had garments on him," and if you wish you may say: "except he had garments on him."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can they delay it,﴾ there are issues concerning it:

The first issue: al-Wahidi said: "min" in His saying ﴿from a nation﴾ is an emphatic extra particle, like your saying: "No one came to me." Others said that it is not extra, because it conveys partitiveness, meaning this ruling did not occur in any part of this reality, so that it is more emphatic in conveying the generality of negation.

The second issue: The author of al-Nazm said: The meaning of sabaqa, when it is applied to a person, is that he passed beyond and left behind, as in your saying: "Zayd outstripped ʿAmr," i.e., he passed him and left him behind him; and it means that he fell short of him and did not reach him. When it is applied to a time, it is the reverse in that respect, as in your saying: "So-and-so preceded the year such-and-such," meaning he passed before its arrival and did not reach it. So His saying ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can they delay it﴾ means that this term does not occur before that time nor after it, but occurs exactly at that very time. The reason is that the specification of each event to its determined time rather than the time before or after it is not by mere chance, nor without a preponderant cause or a specifier. For the preponderance of one of the two possible sides over the other without a preponderant cause is impossible. Its occurrence was specified to that determined time because the God of the world specified it to exactly that time. Given that, the power and will of God necessitated that specification, and His knowledge and wisdom related to that very specification. Since the change of God's attributes, namely power, will, knowledge and wisdom, is impossible, the change of that specification is impossible.

Having understood this, we say: this very argument applies to the actions of servants, namely that what proceeds from Zayd is faith and obedience, and from ʿAmr is disbelief and disobedience; therefore the entry of change into these two must be impossible.

If they say: This would follow only if the cause of the occurrence of disbelief and faith from Zayd and ʿAmr were the power and will of God. But if we say the cause of that is the power and will of Zayd and ʿAmr, the objection falls.

Page 125

We say: If the power and will of Zayd and ʿAmr are necessitating for that particular act, then the creator of that power and will which necessitate that act is the one who decreed that very act, and the objection returns. If they are not necessitating for that act, but are capable of it and of its opposite, then the preponderance of one of the two sides over the other would have no preponderant cause, and the matter returns to the specification occurring without a specifier, which is void. If there is a specifier, then that specifier, if it is the servant himself, the inquiry returns and an infinite regress follows; and if it is God, exalted is He, then the inquiry returns to the point that the servant's act is determined and decreed only by God's specification, and then the objection does not return.

The third issue: The verse indicates that whoever dies or is killed, he died only by his term, and that whoever says it is possible for him to die before his term is mistaken.

If they say: This argument is complete only if we take His saying ﴿Never did We destroy﴾ to refer to death. But if we take it to refer to the punishment of annihilation, how does it follow?

We say: His saying ﴿Never did We destroy﴾ either includes death under it or does not. If it includes it, the argument is clear and binding. If it does not include it, we say: what necessitated that the punishment of annihilation not advance or delay from its determined time exists also in death, so the ruling here must be likewise. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 15, verses 6–9:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?"﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted had gone to great lengths in threatening the disbelievers, He then mentioned their doubts about denying his prophethood.

The first doubt: they used to judge him to be mad, and this has several possible meanings.

The first: when revelation descended upon him, (peace be upon him) would experience a state resembling a swoon, and they thought that this was madness. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And they say, "Indeed he is mad!" But it is nothing except a reminder to the worlds﴾ [al-Qalam 68:51–52], and also His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾ [al-A'raf 7:184].

The second: they found it hard to accept that he was truly a messenger from Allah the Exalted. When a man hears a statement from another that he finds unlikely, he may say to him, "This is madness, and you are mad," because of how far what he says is from the path of reason. His saying: ﴿Indeed you are surely mad﴾ in this verse may carry two meanings.

As for His saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad!"﴾, there are two meanings to it:

The first: they said it in mockery, as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:27], and as the people of Shu'ayb said: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ [Hud 11:87], and as He the Exalted said: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21], because giving good news of punishment is impossible.

[p. 126]

The second: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad" is said by them according to their own claim and belief, and according to his companions and followers. Then He related that they said, in stating their doubts: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?﴾ and there are two issues here:

The first issue: the meaning is, "If you were truthful in claiming prophethood, you would bring us angels who would testify before us to the truth of what you claim regarding the message." This is because a wise sender, when he seeks to achieve an aim, has one path that certainly leads to achieving that aim, and another path that may or may not lead to it and that lies in the realm of doubts and suspicions. If that wise one wants to achieve that aim, he will seek to achieve it by the first path, not the second. Sending down angels who confirm you and affirm your words is a path that certainly leads to the achievement of this aim, whereas the path by which you establish the validity of your prophethood is a path lying in the realm of doubts and suspicions. So if you were truthful in claiming prophethood, then by the wisdom of Allah the Exalted it would be necessary to send down angels who explicitly testify to your truthfulness. Since you did not do that, we know that you have no part in prophethood at all. This is the explanation of this doubt. A parallel to it is His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And they said, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾ [al-An'am 6:8].

There is another possible meaning: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to warn them of the descent of punishment if they did not believe in him. So the people demanded from him the descent of punishment and said to him: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ meaning, the angels who descend upon you should descend upon us with that promised punishment. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, and were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come to them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:53].

Then Allah the Exalted answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite.﴾ So we say: if what is meant by their saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ is the first meaning, then the explanation of this answer is that the descent of angels occurs only with truth and when there is a benefit in it. Allah the Exalted knew from the condition of these disbelievers that if He had sent down angels to them, they would have persisted in their disbelief. According to this explanation, their descent would be pointless and vain, and would not be a truth. For this reason Allah the Exalted did not send them down. The exegetes said: the meaning of "truth" here is death, and the sense is that they do not descend except with death, or with the punishment of annihilation, and after their descent there is no respite or reprieve. We do not want the punishment of annihilation for this community, so for this reason We did not send down the angels.

As for if what is meant by His saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ is their urging the descent of the punishment with which the Messenger (peace be upon him) was threatening them, then the explanation of the answer is that the angels do not descend except with the punishment of annihilation, and our judgment regarding the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is that We should not do that to them, and that We should give them respite because of what We know of the faith of some of them and of the faith of the offspring of the rest.

The second issue: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "lawla" and "lawma" are two dialectal forms; their meaning is "hallа" (why not), and they are used in statements and in questions. The statement form is like your saying: "Lawla you, I would have done such-and-such," and from it is His saying: ﴿Had it not been for you, we would have been believers﴾ [Saba' 34:31]. The question form is like their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am 6:8] and like this verse. Al-Farra' said: in "lawma," the "m" is a substitute for the "l" in "lawla," and similar to it are "istawla 'ala al-shay'" and "istawma 'alayhi" (he overcame it), and al-Asma'i related: "khalaltuhu" and "khalamtuhu" when you befriend him, and he is "khilli" and "khilmi," i.e., my friend.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ was recited by Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim as: ﴿ma nunazzilu﴾ with the "n" and with a kasra on the "z" and a shadda, and "al-mala'ikata" in the accusative because the descent falls upon them. The one who sends down is Allah the Exalted. Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited: "ma tunazzalu," with the passive form whose subject is not named, and "al-mala'ikatu" in the nominative. The rest recited: "ma tunazzilu al-mala'ikatu," attributing the verb of descent to the angels. And Allah knows best.

[p. 127]

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿and they would not then be given respite﴾ means: if the angels had descended, they would not have been given respite, i.e., they would not have been granted delay, for obligation ceases when the angels descend. The author of "al-Nazm" said: the word "idhan" is composed of two words: "idh," which is a noun equivalent to "hina" (when), do you not see that you say: "I came to you idh you came to me," i.e., "when you came to me." Ibn al-Anbari strengthened this opinion, saying: when Allah mentioned the sending down and the one sent down, that indicated the one upon whom it was sent down, so the pronoun referring to him was fitting, because he was a known matter, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr 97:1], where this pronoun refers to the Qur'an even though its mention had not preceded, and the pronoun was fitting because of the known cause. So it is the same here. However, the first opinion is the stronger of the two opinions and the most similar to the apparent sense of the revelation. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: if we say that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, they differed about how Allah the Exalted preserves the Qur'an. Some said: He preserved it by making it miraculous and distinct from human speech, so that creation was unable to add to it or subtract from it, for if they added to it or subtracted from it, its arrangement would change, and it would become evident to all intelligent people that this is not from the Qur'an. Thus its being miraculous became like the surrounding of a city with walls, since it fortifies and protects it. Others said: He the Exalted safeguarded it and preserved it from any created being being able to oppose it. Others said: He made creation unable to nullify or corrupt it by appointing a group who would memorize it, study it, and make it known among people until the end of the period of obligation. Others said: the meaning of preservation is that if anyone attempted to change it by a letter or a dot, the people of the world would say to him: "This is a lie and an alteration of the speech of Allah the Exalted." Even if an esteemed elderly shaykh happened to commit a grammatical error or a slip in a letter of the Book of Allah the Exalted, every child would say to him: "You are wrong, O shaykh, and its correct form is such-and-such." This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and indeed We are its guardians.﴾

Know that no other book has achieved this kind of preservation. For there is no book that has not been affected by scribal error, distortion, and alteration, either in much of it or in little of it. The preservation of this Book free from all aspects of distortion, while the motives of the atheists, the Jews, and the Christians are strongly directed at nullifying and corrupting it, is among the greatest miracles. Also, Allah the Exalted reported its remaining preserved from alteration and distortion, and roughly six hundred years have now passed, so this was a report of the unseen, and that too is a miracle that overpowers.

The fourth issue: al-Qadi argued with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians﴾ against the corruption of the view of some of the Imamiyya (the Twelver Shi'a) that the Qur'an has been subjected to alteration, addition, and omission. He said: because if the matter were so, the Qur'an would not have remained preserved. This argument is weak, because it amounts to proving a thing by itself. The Imamiyya who say that the Qur'an has been subjected to alteration, addition, and omission may well say that this verse is among the additions that were attached to the Qur'an. Thus it is established that proving this claim by this verse amounts to proving a thing by itself, and that this is invalid. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 15, verses 6–9:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?"﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted had gone to great lengths in threatening the disbelievers, He then mentioned their doubts about denying his prophethood.

The first doubt: they used to judge him to be mad, and this has several possible meanings.

The first: when revelation descended upon him, (peace be upon him) would experience a state resembling a swoon, and they thought that this was madness. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And they say, "Indeed he is mad!" But it is nothing except a reminder to the worlds﴾ [al-Qalam 68:51–52], and also His saying: ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾ [al-A'raf 7:184].

The second: they found it hard to accept that he was truly a messenger from Allah the Exalted. When a man hears a statement from another that he finds unlikely, he may say to him, "This is madness, and you are mad," because of how far what he says is from the path of reason. His saying: ﴿Indeed you are surely mad﴾ in this verse may carry two meanings.

As for His saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad!"﴾, there are two meanings to it:

The first: they said it in mockery, as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:27], and as the people of Shu'ayb said: ﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ [Hud 11:87], and as He the Exalted said: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:21], because giving good news of punishment is impossible.

[p. 126]

The second: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are surely mad" is said by them according to their own claim and belief, and according to his companions and followers. Then He related that they said, in stating their doubts: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?﴾ and there are two issues here:

The first issue: the meaning is, "If you were truthful in claiming prophethood, you would bring us angels who would testify before us to the truth of what you claim regarding the message." This is because a wise sender, when he seeks to achieve an aim, has one path that certainly leads to achieving that aim, and another path that may or may not lead to it and that lies in the realm of doubts and suspicions. If that wise one wants to achieve that aim, he will seek to achieve it by the first path, not the second. Sending down angels who confirm you and affirm your words is a path that certainly leads to the achievement of this aim, whereas the path by which you establish the validity of your prophethood is a path lying in the realm of doubts and suspicions. So if you were truthful in claiming prophethood, then by the wisdom of Allah the Exalted it would be necessary to send down angels who explicitly testify to your truthfulness. Since you did not do that, we know that you have no part in prophethood at all. This is the explanation of this doubt. A parallel to it is His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And they said, "Why has an angel not been sent down to him?" And if We had sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided﴾ [al-An'am 6:8].

There is another possible meaning: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to warn them of the descent of punishment if they did not believe in him. So the people demanded from him the descent of punishment and said to him: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ meaning, the angels who descend upon you should descend upon us with that promised punishment. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, and were it not for a specified term, the punishment would have come to them﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:53].

Then Allah the Exalted answered this doubt with His saying: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and they would not then be given respite.﴾ So we say: if what is meant by their saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ is the first meaning, then the explanation of this answer is that the descent of angels occurs only with truth and when there is a benefit in it. Allah the Exalted knew from the condition of these disbelievers that if He had sent down angels to them, they would have persisted in their disbelief. According to this explanation, their descent would be pointless and vain, and would not be a truth. For this reason Allah the Exalted did not send them down. The exegetes said: the meaning of "truth" here is death, and the sense is that they do not descend except with death, or with the punishment of annihilation, and after their descent there is no respite or reprieve. We do not want the punishment of annihilation for this community, so for this reason We did not send down the angels.

As for if what is meant by His saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ is their urging the descent of the punishment with which the Messenger (peace be upon him) was threatening them, then the explanation of the answer is that the angels do not descend except with the punishment of annihilation, and our judgment regarding the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is that We should not do that to them, and that We should give them respite because of what We know of the faith of some of them and of the faith of the offspring of the rest.

The second issue: al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "lawla" and "lawma" are two dialectal forms; their meaning is "hallа" (why not), and they are used in statements and in questions. The statement form is like your saying: "Lawla you, I would have done such-and-such," and from it is His saying: ﴿Had it not been for you, we would have been believers﴾ [Saba' 34:31]. The question form is like their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ [al-An'am 6:8] and like this verse. Al-Farra' said: in "lawma," the "m" is a substitute for the "l" in "lawla," and similar to it are "istawla 'ala al-shay'" and "istawma 'alayhi" (he overcame it), and al-Asma'i related: "khalaltuhu" and "khalamtuhu" when you befriend him, and he is "khilli" and "khilmi," i.e., my friend.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾ was recited by Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim as: ﴿ma nunazzilu﴾ with the "n" and with a kasra on the "z" and a shadda, and "al-mala'ikata" in the accusative because the descent falls upon them. The one who sends down is Allah the Exalted. Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited: "ma tunazzalu," with the passive form whose subject is not named, and "al-mala'ikatu" in the nominative. The rest recited: "ma tunazzilu al-mala'ikatu," attributing the verb of descent to the angels. And Allah knows best.

[p. 127]

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿and they would not then be given respite﴾ means: if the angels had descended, they would not have been given respite, i.e., they would not have been granted delay, for obligation ceases when the angels descend. The author of "al-Nazm" said: the word "idhan" is composed of two words: "idh," which is a noun equivalent to "hina" (when), do you not see that you say: "I came to you idh you came to me," i.e., "when you came to me." Then "an" was added to it, so it became "idh an." Then they found the hamza heavy and dropped it, so it became "idhan." The coming of the word "idhan" is evidence that a verb is implied after it, and the implied meaning is: "and they would not have been given respite, since what they asked for [would have occurred]," and this is a good interpretation.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾ In it there are several issues:

The first issue: the people said: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ [al-Hijr 15:6] only because they had heard the Prophet (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed Allah the Exalted sent down the Reminder upon me." Then Allah the Exalted confirmed his statement in this verse, saying: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder﴾, although this form is plural, this is the speech of kings when displaying majesty: when one of them does an action or says a statement, he says, "We have done such-and-such, and We have said such-and-such." So it is the same here.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 10–12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We sent [messengers] before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿And there came not to them a messenger but that they used to ridicule him.﴾ ﴿Thus do We insert it into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, and the precedent of the former peoples has passed.﴾

Know that when the people behaved disrespectfully and addressed him with foolishness, saying, "Indeed, you are a madman," God, exalted is He, mentioned that the custom of these ignorant ones with all the prophets was thus, and that for you there is an example in patience regarding their foolishness and ignorance, [shown] by all the prophets, peace be upon them. This is the discourse on the arrangement of the verse. And in it there are issues:

The first issue: In the verse there is an omission, and the implied meaning is: "And indeed We sent before you messengers," except that the mention of the messengers was omitted because the sending (irsal) indicates them.

His saying: ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ means among the nations of the former peoples and their followers. Al-Farra' said: al-Shiya' (the sects) are the followers, whose singular is shi'ah. The shi'ah of a man are his followers, and the shi'ah is a nation; they were so named because some of them supported (shayya'a) others and resembled them. We discussed this word at His saying ﴿or confuse you with sects﴾ [al-An'am: 65]. Al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ is an idafa of the attribute to the thing it describes, like His saying ﴿the truth of certainty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95], and His saying ﴿from the western side﴾ [al-Qasas: 44], and His saying ﴿and that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5].

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And there came not to them a messenger but that they used to ridicule him.﴾ That is, the custom of these ignorant ones with all the prophets and messengers was that same mockery of them, just as they did to you. He mentioned it as consolation for the Prophet ﷺ.
Know that the causes that drive these ignorant ones to this wicked custom are several:

First: They find it burdensome to commit to acts of obedience and worship and to abstain from good things and pleasures.

Second: The Messenger calls them to abandon what they have become accustomed to of their wicked religions and false doctrines, and this is extremely difficult for natures.

Third: The Messenger is one who is followed and served, and peoples are obliged to obey and serve him, and this too is in extreme hardship.

Fourth: The Messenger ﷺ may be poor, without helpers or supporters, and without wealth or status, so the affluent and the leaders find it burdensome to serve one who has this attribute.

Fifth: God's abandonment of them, and His casting the motives of disbelief and ignorance into their hearts. This is the principal cause. So due to these causes and what resembles them, the ignorant and the misguided fall into these ugly deeds and reprehensible actions with the greatest of the prophets, peace be upon them.

﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ [Thus do We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals.] In this there are two issues:

The first issue: *al-salk* (threading, causing something to enter into something) is like inserting a thread into a needle or a spear into the one who is stabbed. It was said that it is used in His saying ﴿ما سَلَكَكم في سَقَرَ﴾ [What led you into Saqar?] (al-Muddathir 74:42), meaning: what made you enter Hell. Abu 'Ubayda and Abu 'Ubayd said: *salaktuhu* and *aslaktuhu* have the same meaning.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from this verse that God creates falsehood in the hearts of the disbelievers. They said: His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ means: thus do We cause falsehood and misguidance to enter the hearts of the criminals. The Mu'tazilites said: there has been no mention of misguidance or disbelief before this expression, so the pronoun cannot refer to it. It cannot be said that He said: ﴿وما يَأْتِيهِمْ مِن رَسُولٍ إلّا كانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ [No messenger comes to them but they mock him] and His saying ﴿يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ [they mock] indicates mockery, so the pronoun in ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ refers to it, and mockery of the prophets is disbelief and misguidance. Thus our statement is established: the meaning of ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ is that thus do We cause disbelief, misguidance, and mockery of God's prophets and messengers to enter the hearts of the criminals.

We reply: if the pronoun in ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ refers to mockery, then the pronoun in ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ [they do not believe in it] must also refer to mockery, because they are two pronouns that follow one another and are adjacent, so they must refer to one thing. Then it would be necessary that they do not believe in that mockery, which entails a contradiction, because the disbeliever must necessarily believe in his disbelief. The one who does not do so is the Muslim who knows the falsehood of disbelief and therefore does not affirm it. Furthermore, if God were the one who threads disbelief into the heart of the disbeliever and creates it in him, then no one would be more deserving of excuse than these disbelievers, and on this assumption it would be impossible for Him to blame them in this world or to punish them for it in the Hereafter. Thus it is established that this verse cannot be read in this way. We say: the correct interpretation (*ta'wil*, the deeper sense given to a text) is that the pronoun in His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ refers to the Reminder, which is the Qur'an, for He said before this verse: ﴿إنّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا الذِّكْرَ﴾ [Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder], and He said after it: ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾, meaning: thus do We cause the Qur'an to enter the hearts of the criminals. The intended meaning of this threading is that He makes them hear this Qur'an and creates in their hearts the memorization of this Qur'an and creates in them knowledge of its meanings. He explains that, due to their ignorance and persistence, they do not believe in it despite these conditions, out of obstinacy and ignorance, and so this necessitates severe blame befalling them. Two things indicate the soundness of this interpretation:

The first: the pronoun in His saying ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ refers to the Qur'an by consensus (*ijma'*), so the pronoun in His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ must also refer to it, because they are consecutive pronouns, and so they must refer to one thing.

The second: His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ means: like what We did, We do this threading. Thus this threading is compared to another action that God mentioned before this verse among His own actions. No action of God has been mentioned in the preceding context of this verse except His saying ﴿إنّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا الذِّكْرَ﴾, so this must be joined to it and made like it, and when this is the case, the pronoun in His saying ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ refers to the Reminder. This is the full statement of the people's argument.

The reply: the pronoun in His saying ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ cannot refer to the Reminder, and several things indicate this:

The first: His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ is expressed with the first-person plural *nūn*, and the purpose of it is to show the utmost magnificence and majesty. Such magnificence is appropriately mentioned when the agent performs an act whose effect appears strong and complete, so that the one who opposes and resists it is overcome and subdued. But when He performs an act and no effect of it appears at all, so that the one who opposes and resists it becomes victorious and dominant, then mentioning language that indicates utmost greatness and majesty is unseemly in this context. The matter here is like this, because He threaded the hearing, memorization, and teaching of the Qur'an into the heart of the disbeliever, in order that he might believe in it. Then he paid no attention to it and did not believe in it, so God's act became like wasted loss, and the disbeliever and Satan became like the victorious repeller. When this is so, the mention of the *nūn* that indicates greatness and majesty in His saying ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ is unsuitable for this context. Thus it is established that the interpretation they mentioned is corrupt.

The second: if what they mentioned were intended, it would have been necessary to say: ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ ولا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ [Thus do We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals, and they do not believe in it], meaning: despite this great effort in bringing about their faith, they do not believe. As for why the conjunction *wāw* is not mentioned, we know that His saying ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ is like an explanation and clarification of His saying ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾, and this is only correct if the intended meaning is that We thread disbelief and misguidance into their hearts.

The third: His saying ﴿إنّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنا الذِّكْرَ﴾ is distant, while His saying ﴿يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ is near, and returning a pronoun to the nearest of the mentioned things is what is required. As for their statement that if the pronoun in His saying ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾ referred to mockery, it would also refer to mockery in His saying ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾, and then a contradiction would follow:

We say: the reply to this is from several aspects:

The first: the requirement of the proof is that the pronoun returns to the nearest of the mentioned things. There is no obstacle to applying this principle to the first pronoun, and an obstacle to applying it to the second pronoun arose, so we say that the first pronoun refers to mockery and the second pronoun refers to the Reminder. The separation of consecutive pronouns referring to different things is not rare in the Qur'an. Did not al-Jubba'i, al-Ka'bi, and al-Qadi say about His saying: ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَكم مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ وجَعَلَ مِنها زَوْجَها لِيَسْكُنَ إلَيْها فَلَمّا تَغَشّاها حَمَلَتْ حَمْلًا خَفِيفًا فَمَرَّتْ بِهِ فَلَمّا أثْقَلَتْ دَعَوا اللَّهَ رَبَّهُما لَئِنْ آتَيْتَنا صالِحًا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الشّاكِرِينَ﴾ ﴿فَلَمّا آتاهُما صالِحًا جَعَلا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ فِيما آتاهُما فَتَعالى اللَّهُ عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ [He it is who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate that he might find tranquility in her. And when he covered her, she bore a light burden and continued with it. Then when she became heavy, they both invoked Allah, their Lord, "If You give us a righteous child, we will surely be among the grateful." But when He gave them a righteous child, they attributed to Him partners in what He had given them. Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him] (al-A'raf 7:189–190), that these pronouns from the beginning of the verse up to His saying ﴿جَعَلا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ﴾ [they made for Him partners] refer to Adam and Eve, while in His saying ﴿جَعَلا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ فِيما آتاهُما فَتَعالى اللَّهُ عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ they refer to others? This is what they agreed upon in their exegeses. When this is established, it becomes clear that consecutive pronouns do not necessarily refer to one thing, but the matter depends on the evidence. The same applies here, and God knows best.

The second reply: one of our literary scholars (*udaba'*) among our companions said: His saying ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ﴾ is an explanation of the implicit meaning (*kināya*) in His saying ﴿نَسْلُكُهُ﴾, and the implied sense is: thus do We cause in the hearts of the criminals that they do not believe in it, and the meaning is: We make in their hearts that they do not believe in it.

The third reply: We have demonstrated by compelling rational proofs that the occurrence of faith and disbelief cannot be from the servant. This is because everyone only seeks faith and truthfulness, knowledge and the truth, and no one intends to acquire disbelief, ignorance, or falsehood. Since everyone intends only faith and truth, and yet this does not occur, but rather disbelief and falsehood occur, we know that the occurrence of this disbelief is not from him.

If they say: this disbelief occurred because he thought it was faith, we say: on this assumption, he only consented to acquiring that ignorance because of another ignorance prior to it, and then the discussion is transferred to that prior ignorance. If that was due to another ignorance, it leads to an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), which is impossible. Otherwise, all ignorances must end at a first prior ignorance that occurred in his heart not by his acquiring it but by God's creating it. This is what we have said: the meaning of His saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ نَسْلُكُهُ في قُلُوبِ المُجْرِمِينَ﴾ ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ [Thus do We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals; they do not believe] is: We make in their hearts that they do not believe in it, that is, God creates disbelief and misguidance in them. Furthermore, the early exegetes, such as Ibn 'Abbas and his students, agreed in interpreting this verse as meaning that God creates disbelief and misguidance in them. The interpretation mentioned by the Mu'tazilites is a novel interpretation that none of the earlier scholars held, so it is rejected. Al-Qadi transmitted from 'Ikrima that the meaning is: thus do We cause hardness (*qaswa*) to enter the hearts of the criminals. Then al-Qadi said: hardness only arises from the disbeliever's side, by his persisting in disbelief and being obstinate, so it is not correct to attribute it to God Most High. It is said to al-Qadi: this falls under mere obstinate denial (*mukābara*), because the disbeliever finds in himself a strong aversion to accepting the Messenger's words and a great repulsion from him, to the extent that whenever he sees him, his color changes and his face turns yellow, and perhaps his limbs tremble, and he cannot turn to him or listen to his words. So the occurrence of these states in his heart is a compulsory matter that he cannot repel from himself. How, then, can it be said that they occurred by his act and choice?

If they say: it is possible for him to abandon these states and return to submission and acceptance, we say: this is pure sophistry, because if you mean that, while this strong aversion is in the heart and this great repulsion is in the soul, he can return to submission, acceptance, obedience, and contentment, then this is obstinate denial. If you mean that when these psychological states disappear he can return to acceptance and submission, then this is true, but he cannot remove these motives and obstacles from the heart. For if the human being is the agent of them, then the acquisition of these motives and obstacles would require prior motives, and this would lead to an infinite regress, which is impossible. If God Most High is the agent of them, then it is correct that He is the one who threads these motives and obstacles into the hearts, and this is exactly what we have stated, and God knows best.

As for His saying ﴿وقَدْ خَلَتْ سُنَّةُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ [and the way of the former peoples has already passed], there are two opinions:

The first: it is a threat to the disbelievers of Makkah, saying: the way of God has already passed, of destroying those who denied the messengers in the past generations.

The second, which is the view of al-Zajjaj: the way of God has already passed among the former peoples, by threading disbelief and misguidance into their hearts. This is more fitting to the apparent meaning of the expression.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 14–15:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would surely say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

Know that this statement is the one mentioned in Surat al-An'am in His words: ﴿And even if We had sent down to you a written scroll, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ [al-An'am: 7]. The summary is that when the people asked for the descent of angels who would openly confirm the Messenger, peace be upon him, in his being a messenger from God, Almighty and Exalted, God explained in this verse that, even if this meaning were to be realized, those who disbelieved would say that this is a kind of magic, and that these are things that we are thought to see, while in reality we do not see them.

The summary is that since God, Exalted, knew that there was no benefit in the descent of the angels, for this reason He did not send them down.

If it is asked: How is it possible for a great group of people to come to doubt the existence of what they see with their sound eyes in broad daylight? If doubt about that were permissible, then sophistry (al-sufsata, the art of deceptive argument) would be necessary, and then there would remain no reliance on the senses and observation.

Al-Qadi answered this: He, Exalted, did not describe them as doubting what they perceive; rather, He described them as saying this statement. It is possible for a person to resort to falsehood out of obstinacy and stubborn denial. Then he asked himself and said: Is it valid for a large group to openly express doubt about what is observed? And he answered: It is valid when a sound and recognized purpose unites them upon it, such as collusion to repel an argument or to overcome an opponent. Also, this report concerns only specific people who asked the Messenger ﷺ to send down angels, and this request was made only by the leaders of the people, who were few in number, and it is permissible for a small number to undertake what amounts to obstinacy.

The second issue: His words, ﴿then they kept ascending through it﴾. It is said: "Fulan kept (zalla) doing such-and-such during his day" when he did it during the daytime; the Arabs do not say "zalla yazallu" except for every action done in the daytime, just as they do not say "bata yabitu" except at night. The verbal noun is al-zuluul. His words, ﴿through it they ascend﴾: it is said "'araja ya'ruju ʿurujan," and from it comes al-ma'arij, which are the ascents by which one climbs.

The exegetes have two opinions on this verse:

The first opinion: that His words ﴿then they kept ascending through it﴾ describe the polytheists. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: If the polytheists kept climbing in those ascents and looked at the kingdom of God, His power, His sovereignty, and the worship of the angels who are fearful of Him, they would doubt that vision and would persist in their disbelief and ignorance, just as they denied the other miracles, such as the splitting of the moon and the Qur'an, which was particularly given to the Prophet ﷺ, the miraculous Qur'an, the like of which neither jinn nor humans are able to produce.

The second opinion: that this ascent belongs to the angels. The meaning is that if God had placed these disbelievers in a position where they saw gates of the heaven open, from which the angels ascend and descend, they would have turned that away from its real meaning and would have said: "The sorcerers have bewitched us and made us see these falsehoods which have no reality."

As for His words, ﴿they would surely say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled"﴾, there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir read (sukkirat) with the light form (takhfif), while the others read it with the doubled kaf (tashdid). Al-Wahidi said: sukkirat means "were covered" and "were blocked by magic." This is the statement of the lexicographers. They said: its origin is from al-sakr, which is blocking a crack so that water does not gush out. So these eyes were prevented from seeing, just as the dam prevents water from flowing. The doubling (tashdid) indicates intensity and repetition. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla' said: it is derived from the intoxication of wine, meaning that the eyes became confused and suffered a corruption of vision similar to what happens to an intoxicated man in the change of his reason. If this is the meaning of the light form, then the doubled form (sukkirat) is intended to indicate that this matter occurred again and again. Abu ʿUbayda said: ﴿Our eyes have been dazzled﴾ means: our eyes were covered, so they became still and inoperative. On this view the origin is from stillness; it is said "sakarat al-rih sukran" when the wind became calm, "sakar al-harr yaskur" when the heat subsided, and "laylatun sakira" for a night in which there is no wind. Aws said:

"I rejoiced over a sleepless night, which was neither open nor still."

It is also said: "sukkirat ʿaynuhu sukran" when his eye became bewildered and ceased to look. On this view the meaning of ﴿sukkirat absarunā﴾ is: our eyes ceased to look. This is the view preferred by al-Zajjaj. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: sukkirat means it became such that its light does not penetrate and it does not perceive things as they truly are. The meaning of sakr is cutting a thing off from its flowing course; from this comes taskir of water, which is turning it back from its path of flowing. Sukr in wine is that a person is cut off from the sharpness he had in sobriety, so that his judgment does not penetrate as it does when he is sober. These are four opinions on the interpretation of ﴿sukkirat﴾, and they are in reality close to one another. And God knows best.

The second issue: al-Jubba'i said: Whoever permits the power of sorcerers to seize people's eyes, so that they show them a thing contrary to what it is, cannot have a valid faith in the prophets and messengers. This is because, if they permit that, perhaps the one whom they see as Muhammad son of ʿAbdullah is not that man but a devil, and perhaps these miracles that we witness have no realities, but are rather among the false appearances produced by that sorcerer. And once this possibility is admitted, everything is invalidated. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 15, verses 16–18:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have placed in the sky great stars (burooj), and We have adorned it for the beholders﴾ ﴿And We have guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ ﴿except one who steals a hearing, and he is pursued by a clear flaming fire﴾.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, answered the doubt of those who deny prophethood, and it had been established that belief in prophethood is a branch of belief in tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed it with the proofs of tawhid. Since the proofs of tawhid are partly celestial and partly terrestrial, He began with the celestial proofs, saying: ﴿And We have placed in the sky great stars (burooj) and We have adorned it for the beholders﴾.

Al-Layth said: *al-burj* is one of the constellations (burooj) of the celestial sphere (*falak*), and *burooj* is its plural; they are twelve constellations. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [Al-Furqan: 61], and He said: ﴿By the sky containing constellations﴾ [Al-Buruj: 1].

The way in which these constellations indicate the existence of the Creator who chooses is that the natures of these constellations differ, as is agreed among the practitioners of astrological judgments (*arbab al-ahkam*). If this is so, then the celestial sphere is composed of these parts that differ in essence and in their components that differ in reality. Every composite requires a composer who assembles those parts and components according to choice and wisdom. Thus it is established that the sky's being composed of constellations points to the existence of a chooser who acts, and that is what was to be proven.

As for His saying: ﴿And We have adorned it﴾ ﴿and We have guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ ﴿except one who steals a hearing, and he is pursued by a clear flaming fire﴾, we have thoroughly discussed it in Surah Al-Mulk, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the lowest sky with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [Al-Mulk: 5]. So we will not repeat here except what is necessary. His saying ﴿And We have adorned it﴾ means: with the sun, the moon and the stars. ﴿For the beholders﴾ means: for those who take lessons from them and who use them as evidence for the oneness of their Creator.

His saying: ﴿And We have guarded it from every accursed devil﴾.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of "and We have guarded it from every accursed devil," since the devil has no power to demolish the sky, so what need is there to guard the sky from him?

We say: when He prevented him from approaching it, He guarded the sky from the devil's proximity, so God guarded the sky from them, just as one may guard our dwellings from a spy from whom corruption is feared.

Then we say: the meaning of *rajm* (stoning) in the language is throwing stones. Then the term was applied to a person who was killed, *ruji'a*, as a comparison to being stoned with stones. *Rajm* also means cursing and insulting, because one is "pelted" with an ugly word. From this is His saying: ﴿Surely I will stone you﴾ [Maryam: 46], meaning: I will surely curse you. *Rajm* is also a name for everything that is thrown, and from this is His saying: ﴿And We have made them missiles against the devils﴾ [Al-Mulk: 5], meaning: targets for them. *Rajm* also means speaking by conjecture, and from this is His saying: ﴿Conjecture about the unseen﴾ [Al-Kahf: 22], because one "throws" at it with that conjecture. *Rajm* also means cursing and expelling. His saying "the accursed devil" has been interpreted by them in all these senses.

Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: The devils used not to be barred from the heavens. They would enter them and hear news of the unseen from the angels, and then they would convey it to the soothsayers (*kahana*). When Jesus, peace be upon him, was born, they were prevented from three heavens. When the Messenger of God ﷺ was born, they were prevented from all the heavens. So whenever any one of them wished to steal a hearing, he would be pelted with a flame.

His saying: ﴿except one who steals a hearing﴾ — the particle *illa* (except) cannot be taken here as an exception, because their attempt to steal a hearing does not take the sky out of being guarded from them, since they are prevented from entering it; they only try to approach it. Therefore it cannot be a true exception, so its meaning must be: "but whoever steals a hearing." Al-Zajjaj said: the position of *man* (whoever) is in the accusative case under this interpretation. He said: it is also permissible that it be in the genitive position, and the meaning would be: "except from among those who."

Ibn Abbas said, regarding His saying: ﴿except one who steals a hearing﴾, he means the brief snatching. That is because the rebellious devil ascends and is pelted with a flame, which burns him but does not kill him; and among them is one who is transformed and becomes a *ghul* (a ghoul), which misleads people in the deserts.

His saying: ﴿and he is pursued﴾ — we mentioned its meaning in Surah Al-A'raf in the story of Bal'am ibn Ba'ura, in His saying: ﴿then Satan pursued him﴾ [Al-A'raf: 175]. Its meaning is: he overtook him. *Shihab* is a bright flame of fire. Then the star is called a *shihab*, and the spear-head is called a *shihab*, because both of them, on account of the glitter in them, resemble fire.

Know that at this point there are subtle investigations, which we have mentioned in Surah Al-Mulk and in Surah Al-Jinn. Here we will mention one difficulty. Someone may say: if you permit in general that the devil ascends to the heavens, mingles with the angels, and hears news of the unseen from them, and then they (the angels) descend and convey those unseen matters to the soothsayers, then according to this assumption it follows that reporting about unseen things [p. 135] should cease to be a miracle, because every unseen matter that the Messenger ﷺ reports about carries this possibility, and then it ceases to be a miracle and a proof of truthfulness.
