Then a circular argument (*dawr*) follows, which is false and impossible.

It may be answered: we establish that Muhammad ﷺ is a Messenger through his other miracles. Then, after knowing his prophethood, we are certain that God made the devils incapable of snatching the unseen in this way. Know that when He, may He be exalted, answered the doubt of those who deny prophethood, and it had been established that belief in prophethood is a branch of belief in tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed it with the proofs of tawhid. Since the proofs of tawhid are partly celestial and partly terrestrial, He began with the celestial proofs, saying: ﴿And We have placed in the sky great stars (burooj) and We have adorned it for the beholders﴾.

Al-Layth said: *al-burj* is one of the constellations (burooj) of the celestial sphere (*falak*), and *burooj* is its plural; they are twelve constellations. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations﴾ [Al-Furqan: 61], and He said: ﴿By the sky containing constellations﴾ [Al-Buruj: 1].

The way in which these constellations indicate the existence of the Creator who chooses is that the natures of these constellations differ, as is agreed among the practitioners of astrological judgments (*arbab al-ahkam*). If this is so, then the celestial sphere is composed of these parts that differ in essence and in their components that differ in reality. Every composite requires a composer who assembles those parts and components according to choice and wisdom. Thus it is established that the sky's being composed of constellations points to the existence of a chooser who acts, and that is what was to be proven.

As for His saying: ﴿And We have adorned it﴾ ﴿and We have guarded it from every accursed devil﴾ ﴿except one who steals a hearing, and he is pursued by a clear flaming fire﴾, we have thoroughly discussed it in Surah Al-Mulk, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the lowest sky with lamps and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [Al-Mulk: 5]. So we will not repeat here except what is necessary. His saying ﴿And We have adorned it﴾ means: with the sun, the moon and the stars. ﴿For the beholders﴾ means: for those who take lessons from them and who use them as evidence for the oneness of their Creator.

His saying: ﴿And We have guarded it from every accursed devil﴾.

If it is asked: what is the meaning of "and We have guarded it from every accursed devil," since the devil has no power to demolish the sky, so what need is there to guard the sky from him?

We say: when He prevented him from approaching it, He guarded the sky from the devil's proximity, so God guarded the sky from them, just as one may guard our dwellings from a spy from whom corruption is feared.

Then we say: the meaning of *rajm* (stoning) in the language is throwing stones. Then the term was applied to a person who was killed, *ruji'a*, as a comparison to being stoned with stones. *Rajm* also means cursing and insulting, because one is "pelted" with an ugly word. His saying "the accursed devil" has been interpreted by them in all these senses.

They would enter them and hear news of the unseen from the angels, and then they would convey it to the soothsayers (*kahana*). He said: it is also permissible that it be in the genitive position, and the meaning would be: "except from among those who."

That is because the rebellious devil ascends and is pelted with a flame, which burns him but does not kill him; and among them is one who is transformed and becomes a *ghul* (a ghoul), which misleads people in the deserts.

His saying: ﴿and he is pursued﴾ — we mentioned its meaning in Surah Al-A'raf in the story of Bal'am ibn Ba'ura, in His saying: ﴿then Satan pursued him﴾ [Al-A'raf: 175]. Its meaning is: he overtook him. *Shihab* is a bright flame of fire. Because we say: this incapacity cannot be established except after certainty that Muhammad is a Messenger and that the Qur'an is true, and that certainty cannot be achieved except through a miracle; and the fact that reporting about the unseen is a miracle is not established except after eliminating this possibility. Then a circular argument (*dawr*) follows, which is false and impossible.

It may be answered: we establish that Muhammad ﷺ is a Messenger through his other miracles. Then, after knowing his prophethood, we are certain that God made the devils incapable of snatching the unseen in this way. At that point, reporting about unseen things becomes a miracle, and by this way the circular argument is avoided. And God knows best.

**[Commentary of al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, on Surah 15, verse 19]**

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the earth — We spread it out, and placed in it firm mountains, and caused to grow in it of every thing a measured amount.﴾ ﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood, and [also for] those whom you do not provide for.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, explained the heavenly signs in establishing *tawhid* (the oneness of God), He followed them with mention of the earthly signs, which are of several kinds.

**The first kind:** Allah's words ﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "We spread it out upon the surface of the water." There is another possibility as well. The earth is a body (*jism*), and a body is that which is extended in the three dimensions: length, breadth and thickness. Since this is so, the extension of the body of the earth in these three dimensions is restricted to a specific measure, because it has been established that every body must be finite. Given this, the extension of the earth's body is restricted to a specific measure, although greater or lesser extension is conceivable. Since the restriction of that extension to that particular determined quantity, while a greater or lesser one is possible, is a restriction by a permissible matter, it must be due to the specification of a specifier and the determination of a determiner, namely Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

If it is asked: Does Allah's words ﴿And the earth — We spread it out﴾ indicate that it is flat?

We answer: Yes. For if the earth is assumed to be a sphere, it is a sphere of immense greatness, and when a small piece of a great sphere is looked at, it appears like a level surface. Since this is so, the difficulty that they raised is removed. The proof for this is Allah's words ﴿And the mountains as pegs﴾ [al-Naba': 7]. He called them pegs, although upon them there may be vast level surfaces. So it is likewise here.

**The second kind** of the earthly signs mentioned in this verse is Allah's words ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾. These are the stable mountains; the singular is *rasi*, the plural *rasiyah*, and the plural of the plural is *rawasi*. It is like His words ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains, lest it shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl: 15]. Regarding its interpretation there are two views:

*The first view:* Ibn ʿAbbas said: When Allah spread the earth upon the water, it inclined with its inhabitants like a ship, so Allah anchored it with the heavy mountains, so that it would not tilt with its people.

If it is asked: Do you say that Allah created the earth without the mountains, so that it tilted with its inhabitants, and then He created the mountains in it afterward? Or do you say that Allah created the earth and the mountains together?

We answer: Both views are possible.

*The second view:* Regarding the interpretation of His words ﴿And We placed in it firm mountains﴾, it is possible that what is meant is that He created them so that they would serve as signs for people regarding the roads of the earth and its directions, for they are like landmarks, so that people do not deviate from the straight path and do not fall into error. This view is quite plausible.

**The third kind** of the earthly signs mentioned in this verse is Allah's words ﴿And We caused to grow in it of every thing a measured amount﴾. Concerning it there are two discussions.

*The first discussion:* The pronoun in His words ﴿And caused to grow in it﴾ may refer to the earth, or it may refer to the firm mountains. However, its reference to the earth is preferable, because the kinds of plants that are beneficial are generated in cultivable lands, whereas the fruits of the mountains are of little benefit. Some have said that the reference of that pronoun to the mountains is preferable, because minerals are generated in mountains, and "things measured" (*mawzunat*) in common usage and custom are minerals, not plants.

*The second discussion:* They differed about what is meant by *mawzun* (measured), and there are several views:

*The first view:* That what is meant is that it is proportioned to the measure of need. Al-Qadi said: "This view is closer to the truth, because He, the Exalted, knows the quantity that people need and benefit from, so He causes to grow in the earth that quantity. For this reason He followed it with His words ﴿And We made for you therein means of livelihood﴾, because that provision which appears through plants is a means of livelihood for them in two respects: first, by way of eating and benefiting from it directly; and second, that they may profit by trading in it." Those who hold this view said: Weighing is only intended to know the quantity, so the use of the word "weighing" to mean knowing the quantity is an instance of naming the cause by the effect (*ism al-sabab ʿala al-musabbab*). They said: This is further confirmed by His words ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8], and His words ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21].

*The second view* regarding the interpretation of this term: This world is the world of causes, and Allah creates minerals, plants and animals only through the combination of the natures of this world. Therefore there must come from the earth a specific quantity, and likewise from water and air, and from the influence of the sun and the stars in heat and cold, a specific measure. If we assume that there were an increase beyond that specific measure, or a decrease below it, minerals, plants and animals would not be generated. So Allah, glorified and exalted be He, determined them in a specific manner by His power, knowledge and wisdom. Thus it is as though He weighed them by the balance of wisdom, until these kinds came into being.

*The third view* regarding the interpretation of this term: People of common usage say, "So-and-so's movements are measured" (*mawzun al-harakat*), meaning that his movements are proportionate, good, and consistent with wisdom. Likewise, "this speech is measured" (*kalam mawzun*) when it is proportionate, good, and far from idle talk and frivolity. So what is meant is that it is measured by the balance of wisdom and reason. In sum, they have made the word *mawzun* a metaphor for goodness and proportion. Thus His words ﴿And We caused to grow in it of every thing a measured amount﴾ mean: proportioned, judged by sound minds to be good, delicate, and in accord with the benefit.

*The fourth view* regarding the interpretation of this term: The things that grow from the earth are of two kinds: minerals and plants. As for minerals, they are all measured, namely the seven metals, the stones, the salts, the vitriols, and others. As for plants, their ultimate outcome returns to weighing, because grains are weighed, and likewise fruits for the most part. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 20:

The Exalted's words: ﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood﴾ contain two issues.

The first issue: We have discussed the matter of "ma'ayish" (means of livelihood) in Surat al-A'raf. As for His words: ﴿and those for whom you are not providers﴾, there are two opinions concerning it.

The first opinion: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the place (mahall) of "lakum" (for you), and the sense is: "We have made for you therein means of livelihood, and [for] those for whom you are not providers."

The second opinion: it is conjoined to His words ﴿ma'ayish﴾, and the sense is: "We have made for you means of livelihood, and [for] those for whom you are not providers." On this opinion there are three possibilities:

The first possibility: the word "man" (whoever) is specific to rational beings, so it must be that what is meant by His words ﴿and those for whom you are not providers﴾ is rational beings, namely dependents, servants, attendants and slaves. The explanation of the matter is that people, for the most part, think that they are the ones who provide for dependents, servants and slaves, and that is an error, for God is the Provider; He provides for the servant and the served, the owned and the owner. For were it not that God Most High created the foods and drinks, and bestowed the nourishing and digestive power, no one would obtain any provision.

The second possibility: this is the view of al-Kalbi, who said: what is meant by His words ﴿and those for whom you are not providers﴾ is the wild beasts and the birds.

If it is said: how can this interpretation be valid when the form "man" is specific to those who have reason?

We say: the answer to this is from two aspects:

The first: the form "man" has indeed been used for non-rational beings, and the proof of this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And God created every moving creature from water. Of them are some that move on their bellies, and of them are some that walk on two legs, and of them are some that walk on four﴾ [al-Nur: 45].

The second: He Most High affirmed for all animals a provision upon God, when He said: ﴿And there is no creature on earth but that upon God is its provision, and He knows its place of dwelling and its place of storage﴾ [Hud: 6]. So they, in time of need, seek their provisions from their Creator, and thus they resemble rational beings in this respect; hence it is not far-fetched to mention them with the form of rational beings. Do you not see that He said: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18], mentioning them with the plural form of rational beings, and said of the idols: ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 77], and said: ﴿each in an orbit they glide﴾ [al-Anbiya: 33]. So likewise here, it is not far-fetched to apply to the wild beasts and birds a word specific to rational beings, because they resemble rational beings in this respect. I have heard in the midst of the reports that water became scarce in the valleys and mountains, and the heat intensified in one of the years; it is related from one of them that he saw some of the wild beasts raising their heads toward the sky at the intensity of their thirst. He said: "I saw the clouds approach and rain down, such that the valleys were filled from it."

The third possibility: we take His words ﴿and those for whom you are not providers﴾ to refer to the female slaves and the male slaves, and to the wild beasts and birds; and the form "man" was applied to them only by giving precedence to the side of rational beings over others.

The second issue: His words ﴿and those for whom you are not providers﴾ cannot be genitive (majrur) as a conjunction to the genitive pronoun in "lakum" (for you), because one does not conjoin to a genitive pronoun except by repeating the governing particle, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7]. One does not say: "I took from you and Zayd" except with the repetition of the particle.

Know that this meaning is permissible according to the reading of the one who reads "tasa'alun bihi wal-arham" (by whom you ask one another, and the wombs) with the genitive, and we have discussed this matter there. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 21–22:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We send it down only in a known measure.﴾ ﴿And We send the winds fertilizing, then We send down water from the sky and give you drink from it, and you are not its keepers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that He caused every balanced thing to grow in the earth and placed in it means of livelihood, He followed this with mention of what is like the cause of that, saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries.﴾

This is the fourth of the proofs mentioned in this surah for establishing monotheism (tawhid). In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: "Al-khaza'in" is the plural of "al-khizanah," which is the name of the place where a thing is stored, i.e., kept safe. "Al-khizanah" also means the act of the keeper (al-khazin). It is said: "He stored the thing (khazana al-shay'a), yakhzunuhu, when he secured it in a storehouse (khizanah)." Most exegetes hold that what is meant by His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ is the rain, because it is the cause of provision and the livelihood of the children of Adam and of others, such as birds and wild animals. So when He mentioned that He gives them their livelihoods, He explained that the treasuries of the rain, which is the cause of livelihoods, are with Him, that is, in His command, His judgment and His management. As for His saying ﴿and We send it down only in a known measure﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: it means the measure of sufficiency. Al-Hakam said: No year has more rain than another year, but some people are rained upon and others are deprived, and perhaps it falls in the sea. The meaning is that God, exalted is He, sends down rain every year in a known measure, except that He directs it to whom He wills, where He wills, as He wills.

It may be objected: the wording of the verse does not indicate this meaning, for His saying ﴿and We send it down only in a known measure﴾ does not indicate that He sends it down in the same amount in every year. If that is so, then interpreting the verse in this sense is arbitrary, without evidence. I also say: restricting His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ to rain is pure arbitrariness, because His saying ﴿And there is not a thing﴾ encompasses all things except what the evidence excludes, namely the existent, eternal, necessarily existent Being. And His saying ﴿but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ is an indication that those things are within His power. The gist of the matter is that what is meant is that all possible things are within His power and under His dominion; He brings them from non-existence into existence as He wills. However, although His capabilities are unlimited, that which He brings out of them into existence must be finite, because the entry of what has no end into existence is impossible. So His saying ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾ is an indication that His capabilities are unlimited, and His saying ﴿and We send it down only in a known measure﴾ is an indication that everything that enters existence from them is finite. And whenever what comes out of them into existence is finite, it is necessarily specified in its coming into being to a determined time, while its occurrence before or after that time is possible in its place; and it is specified to a determined location, while its occurrence in other locations is possible in place of that location; and it is specified with determined attributes, while it was possible in reason for other attributes to occur in place of those attributes. Since this is so, the specification of those finite things to that determined time, that determined location, and those determined attributes, in place of their opposites, must be by the act of a specifier and the decree of a decreer. This is what is meant by His saying ﴿and We send it down only in a known measure﴾. The meaning is: were it not for the Capable, Choosing One who specified those things with those permissible states, it would be impossible for them to be specified with those permissible attributes. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 23–25:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritors.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly known those who go before you [in death] among you, and We have certainly known those who remain behind.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise, All-Knowing.﴾

Know that this is the sixth type of the proofs of tawhid (divine oneness), and it is the argument from the occurrence of giving life and causing death to these animals, as evidence for the existence of the Creator-God, the Capable, the Choosing.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

Some of them interpreted it as the common quality between the giving of life to plants and to animals.

Others say: describing plants as "alive" is metaphorical, so it is necessary to restrict it to the giving of life to animals.

Since it has been established by rational proofs that no one has the power to create life except the Truth, glorified is He, the occurrence of life in animals is a conclusive proof of the existence of the God who acts by choice. His saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾ conveys restriction, meaning: there is no power to give life or to cause death except for Us. His saying ﴿and We are the Inheritors﴾ means: when all creation dies, then the dominion of every individual ceases at his death, and God alone remains, the Enduring Truth, the sole Owner of all owned things. So this resembles inheritance, and in this respect He is the Inheritor.

As for His saying: ﴿And We have certainly known those who go before you [in death] among you, and We have certainly known those who remain behind﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in the narration of 'Ata', said: "those who go before" refers to the people of obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and "those who remain behind" refers to those who lag behind in obedience to Allah.

The second: By "those who go before" is meant the first row of those who pray, and by "those who remain behind" the last row. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) encouraged the first row in prayer, so the people crowded toward it, and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The meaning: We will reward them according to the measure of their intentions.

The third: al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: it means in the description of fighting.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Abu al-Jawza', said: there was a beautiful woman who prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and some people would move forward to the first row so as not to see her, while others would hang back and lag behind so as to see her, and when they bowed they would hold their arms away from their bodies so they could look from beneath their armpits. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

The fifth: It has been said that "those who go before" are the dead and "those who remain behind" are the living. It has also been said: "those who go before" are the earlier nations, and "those who remain behind" are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). 'Ikrimah said: "those who go before" are those who have been created, and "those who remain behind" are those who have not yet been created.

Know that this is the sixth type of the proofs of tawhid (divine oneness), and it is the argument from the occurrence of giving life and causing death to these animals, as evidence for the existence of the Creator-God, the Capable, the Choosing.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

Some of them interpreted it as the common quality between the giving of life to plants and to animals.

Others say: describing plants as "alive" is metaphorical, so it is necessary to restrict it to the giving of life to animals.

Since it has been established by rational proofs that no one has the power to create life except the Truth, glorified is He, the occurrence of life in animals is a conclusive proof of the existence of the God who acts by choice. His saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾ conveys restriction, meaning: there is no power to give life or to cause death except for Us. His saying ﴿and We are the Inheritors﴾ means: when all creation dies, then the dominion of every individual ceases at his death, and God alone remains, the Enduring Truth, the sole Owner of all owned things. So this resembles inheritance, and in this respect He is the Inheritor.

As for His saying: ﴿And We have certainly known those who go before you [in death] among you, and We have certainly known those who remain behind﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in the narration of 'Ata', said: "those who go before" refers to the people of obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and "those who remain behind" refers to those who lag behind in obedience to Allah.

The second: By "those who go before" is meant the first row of those who pray, and by "those who remain behind" the last row. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) encouraged the first row in prayer, so the people crowded toward it, and Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. The meaning: We will reward them according to the measure of their intentions.

The third: al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: it means in the description of fighting.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Abu al-Jawza', said: there was a beautiful woman who prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and some people would move forward to the first row so as not to see her, while others would hang back and lag behind so as to see her, and when they bowed they would hold their arms away from their bodies so they could look from beneath their armpits. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

The fifth: It has been said that "those who go before" are the dead and "those who remain behind" are the living. It has also been said: "those who go before" are the earlier nations, and "those who remain behind" are the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). 'Ikrimah said: "those who go before" are those who have been created, and "those who remain behind" are those who have not yet been created.

Know that when He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, it is We who give life and cause death﴾, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And We have certainly known those who go before you [in death] among you, and We have certainly known those who remain behind﴾, as an alert that nothing of their circumstances is hidden from Allah. This includes His knowledge of their precedence and their lagging behind in coming into existence and in being, and of their precedence and lagging behind in the various kinds of acts of obedience and good. It is not fitting to restrict the verse to one state rather than another.

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them﴾, its purpose is to alert that gathering, resurrection, raising up and the Last Day are an obligatory matter.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Wise, All-Knowing﴾ means: wisdom requires the obligation of gathering and resurrection, as we have established by the many proofs at the beginning of Surah Yunus, peace be upon him.

**The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And We created man from clay, from black mud molded into shape.﴾ ﴿And the jinn We had created before from the fire of scorching wind.﴾**

**On this verse there are several issues:**

**The first issue:** Know that this is the seventh type of the proofs of *tawhid* (the oneness of God). When He, the Exalted, argued for the soundness of *tawhid* in the previous verse by the creation of animals, He followed it with an argument from the creation of man for the same purpose.

**The second issue:** Conclusive proofs have established that it is impossible to hold that there exist events without a first beginning. Once this is established, it becomes necessary that events end at a first event, which is the first of all events. If this is so, then people must end at a first human being, who is the first of all people. And if this is so, then that first human was not created from two parents, and so he must necessarily have been created by the power of Allah, the Exalted.

So His words, ﴿And We created man﴾, refer to that first human. The exegetes are unanimous that what is meant is Adam, peace be upon him. It is reported in the books of the Shi'a, on the authority of Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir, peace be upon him, that he said: "There passed before Adam, who is our father, a thousand thousand Adams or more." I say: this does not undermine the createdness of the world, but rather is a matter of however it was. There must be an ending at a first human who is the first of humankind. As for whether that human is our father Adam, there is no way to establish it except through revelation (*sam'*).

Know that a body is originated (*muhdath*), so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that Adam, peace be upon him, and other bodies were created from pure nonexistence. Also, the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59], indicate that Adam was created from dust. Another verse indicates that he was created from clay, namely His words: ﴿Indeed, I am going to create a human from clay﴾ [Sad: 71]. In this verse it comes that Adam, peace be upon him, was created from *salsal* (dry clay that rings) from *hama'* (black mud) *masnun* (molded). The closest view is that He first created him from dust, then from clay, then from *hama' masnun*, then from *salsal* like pottery. There is no doubt that He, the Exalted, is able to create him from whatever kind of bodies there are. Rather, He is able to create him from the beginning. He created him in this manner either purely by His will, or for what it contains of indicating the angels, serving their benefit and the benefit of the jinn; because the creation of man from these substances is more wondrous than creating a thing from its own form and kind.

**The third issue:** Regarding *al-salsal* there are two views. It is said: *al-salsal* is dry clay that rings (*yusalsil*), and it is unfired; when it is fired, it becomes pottery (*fakhkhar*). They said: if you imagine in its sound a prolongation, it is *salil*; if you imagine in it a vibration, it is *salsalah*. The exegetes said: Allah, the Exalted, created Adam, peace be upon him, from clay, shaped him, and left him in the sun for forty years, so he became *salsal* like earthenware. No one knows what is meant by it, and they did not see any image resembling him until He breathed the spirit into him.

The reality of the matter is that He, the Exalted, created Adam from clay in the form of a human, and it dried out. Whenever the wind passed through it, a ringing sound was heard from it, and for this reason Allah, the Exalted, named him *salsal*.

The second view: *al-salsal* is the foul-smelling, from their saying *salla al-lahm* and *asalla* when meat became putrid and changed. This view, in my opinion, is weak. Because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿from *salsal* from *hama'* *masnun*﴾, and that it is *hama' masnun* indicates putridity and change. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that this *salsal* was produced only from the *hama' masnun*, so it must be that its being *salsal* is different from its being *hama' masnun*. If its being *salsal* were an expression for putridity and change, there would remain no difference between its being *salsal* and its being *hama' masnun*.

As for *al-hama'*: Al-Laith said: *al-hamʼah* is on the pattern *fa'lah*, and its plural is *al-hama'*, and it is black, foul-smelling mud. Abu 'Ubaydah and most (scholars) said: *hama'ah* on the pattern of *kama'ah*.

As for His words ﴿*masnun*﴾, there are several views:

The first: Ibn al-Sikkit said: I heard Abu 'Umar say regarding His words ﴿*masnun*﴾ that it means changed. Abu al-Haytham said: it is said *sanna al-ma'*, and it is *masnun*, meaning it changed. The evidence for this is His words, ﴿it has not changed﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 259], meaning it has not changed.

The second: *al-masnun* is the scraped, derived from *sananta al-hajar* when you rub a stone upon it, and what comes out between them is called *al-sunun*, and the whetstone (*masass*) was called *masass* because iron is sharpened on it.

The third: Al-Zajjaj said: this word is derived from anything placed on the path of a road (*sunan al-tariq*), because whenever it is so, it has changed.

The fourth: Abu 'Ubaydah said: *al-masnun* is the poured, and *al-sann* is pouring; it is said: *sanna al-ma'a 'ala wajhihi sannan*.

The fifth: Sibawayh said: *al-masnun* is that which is formed into an image and a pattern, from *sunnat al-wajh*, which is its form.

The sixth: It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: *al-masnun* is moist clay. This returns to the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, because when it is moist it flows and spreads over the earth, so it is *masnun* in the sense that it is poured.

As for His words, the Exalted, ﴿And the jinn We created﴾: they differ about who the jinn is. 'Ata', on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, said: it means Iblis. This is the view of al-Hasan, Muqatil and Qatadah. Ibn 'Abbas said in another narration: the jinn is the father of the jinn, and this is the view of most (scholars). It is called *jann* because of its concealment from the eyes, just as the fetus (*janin*) is called *janin* for this reason, since the fetus is hidden in its mother's womb. The meaning of *jann* linguistically is the concealer, from your saying *janna al-shay'* when he covered it. So the *jann* mentioned here may be so named because it conceals itself from the eyes of the children of Adam, or it may be of the category of the active participle used to mean the passive, as is said of *laban* and *tamir*, and *ma' dafiq* and *'isha radiyah*.

They differed about the jinn. Some of them said: they are a kind distinct from the devils. The sounder view is that the devils are a category of the jinn. So whoever among them is a believer is not called a devil, and whoever among them is a disbeliever is called by this name. The evidence for the correctness of this is that the word *jinn* is derived from concealment, so whoever is in that state is of the jinn.

As for His words, ﴿We created it before﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: it means before the creation of Adam. As for His words ﴿from the fire of *al-samum*﴾: the meaning of *al-samum* linguistically is the hot wind which occurs in the daytime and may also occur at night. On this basis, the hot wind contains fire, and has a scorching blast and intense heat, as is reported in the tradition that it is a blast of Hell. It is said: it was called *samum* because by its subtlety it enters the pores of the body, which are the hidden openings in the skin of a human through which his sweat and the vapor of his interior emerge. Ibn Mas'ud said: this *samum* is a part of seventy parts of the *samum* with which Allah created the jinn, and he recited this verse.

**If it is said:** how is it conceivable that the jinn was created from fire?

**We say:** according to our doctrine this is clear, because physical structure (*bunyah*) is not, in our view, a condition for the possibility of the occurrence of life. Allah, the Exalted, is able to create life and knowledge in an atom (*jawhar fard*), and likewise He is able to create life and intellect in a hot body. Some of them argued that life cannot occur in the stars, saying: because the sun is at the utmost of heat, and whatever is like that, life is impossible in it. We refute this by His words, the Exalted: ﴿And the jinn We created from before, from the fire of *al-samum*﴾. Rather, what is relied upon in negating life from the stars is consensus (*ijma'*).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 15, verses 28–35:**

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وإذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إنِّي خالِقٌ بَشَرًا مِن صَلْصالٍ مِن حَمَإٍ مَسْنُونٍ﴾ ﴿فَإذا سَوَّيْتُهُ ونَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِن رُوحِي فَقَعُوا لَهُ ساجِدِينَ﴾ ﴿فَسَجَدَ المَلائِكَةُ كُلُّهم أجْمَعُونَ﴾ ﴿إلّا إبْلِيسَ أبى أنْ يَكُونَ مَعَ السّاجِدِينَ﴾ ﴿قالَ ياإبْلِيسُ ما لَكَ ألّا تَكُونَ مَعَ السّاجِدِينَ﴾ ﴿قالَ لَمْ أكُنْ لِأسْجُدَ لِبَشَرٍ خَلَقْتَهُ مِن صَلْصالٍ مِن حَمَإٍ مَسْنُونٍ﴾ ﴿قالَ فاخْرُجْ مِنها فَإنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ ﴿وإنَّ عَلَيْكَ اللَّعْنَةَ إلى يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾

Know that when Almighty God mentioned the creation of the first human and used it as evidence for the existence of the All-Powerful, Chooser God, He then mentioned the incident that followed: He commanded the angels to prostrate to him, and they obeyed, except Iblis, who refused and rebelled. In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue:** What is meant by his being "a human" (basharan)? It means that he is a dense body that comes into contact and makes contact. The angels and the jinn do not make contact with human bodies because their bodies are too subtle. The *basharah* is the outer surface of the skin of any living creature. As for his being "of clay, from black mud, moulded," this has already been mentioned.

As for His saying ﴿فَإذا سَوَّيْتُهُ﴾ (When I have fashioned him), there are two opinions:

The first: When I have shaped his form with the human image and the human creation.

The second: When I have balanced the parts of his body with the moderation of the temperaments and the harmony of the mixed elements, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿إنّا خَلَقْنا الإنْسانَ مِن نُطْفَةٍ أمْشاجٍ﴾ (Indeed, We created man from a drop of mingled fluid) [al-Insan: 2].

As for His saying ﴿ونَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِن رُوحِي﴾ (and I breathed into him of My spirit), there are several discussions:

**The first:** Blowing (*nafkh*) is the moving of air within the cavities of another body. The apparent meaning of this word suggests that the spirit (*ruh*) is wind; otherwise it would not be correct to describe it as being blown. However, the complete discussion of the reality of the spirit will come in His saying: ﴿قُلِ الرُّوحُ مِن أمْرِ رَبِّي﴾ (Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord) [al-Isra: 85]. God, glorified is He, attributed the spirit of Adam to Himself only to honour and dignify him.

As for His saying ﴿فَقَعُوا لَهُ ساجِدِينَ﴾ (then fall down to him in prostration) [Sad: 72], there are several discussions:

**One:** Was that prostration truly to Adam, or was Adam like a *qiblah* (direction of prayer) for that prostration? This discussion has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

**Two:** The ones commanded to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, were either all the angels of the heavens, or some of them, or the angels of the earth. Some people hold that it is not permissible to say that the chief angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him. The evidence for this is His saying at the end of Surat al-A'raf, describing the angels: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ لا يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبادَتِهِ ويُسَبِّحُونَهُ ولَهُ يَسْجُدُونَ﴾ (Indeed, those who are near your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate) [al-A'raf: 206]. His saying ﴿ولَهُ يَسْجُدُونَ﴾ (and to Him they prostrate) implies restriction (*hasr*), and this indicates that they prostrate only to God, Exalted is He. This contradicts their being prostrators to Adam, or to anyone other than God, Exalted is He. At most, it could be said that His saying ﴿فَقَعُوا لَهُ ساجِدِينَ﴾ (then fall down to him in prostration) implies generality, but the specific takes precedence over the general.

**Three:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that, just as God breathed the spirit into Adam, peace be upon him, the angels became obliged to prostrate to him. This is because His saying ﴿فَإذا سَوَّيْتُهُ ونَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِن رُوحِي فَقَعُوا لَهُ ساجِدِينَ﴾ (When I have fashioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration) is connected by the particle *fa'* of consequence (*ta'qib*), which precludes delay. As for His saying ﴿فَسَجَدَ المَلائِكَةُ كُلُّهم أجْمَعُونَ﴾ (So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely), al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: His saying ﴿كُلُّهم أجْمَعُونَ﴾ (all of them entirely) is emphasis upon emphasis (*tawkid ba'd tawkid*). Al-Mubarrad was asked about this verse and said: If it had said "the angels prostrated," it would have been possible that only some of them prostrated. When it said ﴿كُلُّهم﴾ (all of them), that possibility was removed, and it became clear that they had all prostrated. Then another possibility remained: that they prostrated all at once, or that each one prostrated at a different time. When it said ﴿أجْمَعُونَ﴾ (entirely), it became clear that all of them prostrated at once. However, this is weak, because Iblis replied: ﴿لَمْ أكُنْ لِأسْجُدَ لِبَشَرٍ خَلَقْتَهُ مِن صَلْصالٍ﴾ (I would not prostrate to a human whom You created from clay). His saying ﴿خَلَقْتَهُ﴾ (You created him) is a second-person address of presence, not of absence, and its apparent meaning requires that God, Exalted is He, spoke with Iblis without an intermediary, and that Iblis spoke with God, Exalted is He, without an intermediary. How can this be conceived, when speaking with God, Exalted is He, without an intermediary is among the greatest of ranks and the most noble of stations? How can it be conceived that it was granted to the head of the disbelievers and their chief? Perhaps the answer is that God's speaking is a lofty rank only when it is by way of honour and exaltation; but when it is by way of humiliation and abasement, it is not.

As for His saying ﴿لَمْ أكُنْ لِأسْجُدَ لِبَشَرٍ خَلَقْتَهُ مِن صَلْصالٍ مِن حَمَإٍ مَسْنُونٍ﴾ (I would not prostrate to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud, moulded), there are two discussions in it:

**The first discussion:** The *lam* in His saying ﴿لِأسْجُدَ﴾ (to prostrate) is for emphasizing the negation. Its meaning is: it is not valid for me to prostrate to a human.

**The second discussion:** The meaning of this statement is that his being a human implies that he is a dense body, whereas Iblis was a subtle spiritual being. Thus there is a difference between them in their present state from this aspect. It is as if he said: The human is a corporeal, dense being that has a skin, while I am a spiritual, subtle being. The corporeal dense being is lower in status than the spiritual subtle being, and how can the lower be prostrated to by the higher? Also, Adam was created from clay that came into being from black mud moulded, and this origin is extremely base, whereas the origin of Iblis is fire, which is the noblest of the elements. Therefore the origin of Iblis is nobler than the origin of Adam, and so Iblis must be nobler than Adam. And it is improper for the noble to be commanded to prostrate to the lower.

Thus the first statement points to the difference arising from humanity and spirituality, which is a difference existing in the present state, while the second statement points to the difference arising from the element and origin. This is the sum of Iblis's doubt.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿قالَ فاخْرُجْ مِنها فَإنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ (He said: "Then get out of it, for indeed you are outcast"), this is not an explicit answer to that doubt, but it is an answer to it by way of alerting. Its explanation is that what God, Exalted is He, said is a text (*nass*), and what Iblis said is analogy (*qiyas*), and whoever opposes a text with analogy is outcast and cursed. The full discussion of this meaning we have presented in detail in Surat al-A'raf.

As for His saying ﴿فاخْرُجْ مِنها﴾ (get out of it), it has been said: the intended meaning is the Garden of Eden; it has been said: from the heavens; it has been said: from the company of the angels. The full discussion of this, together with the explanation of *rajim* (outcast), has already been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf.

As for His saying ﴿وإنَّ عَلَيْكَ اللَّعْنَةَ إلى يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾ (and indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgement), Ibn Abbas said: He means the Day of Recompense, when God recompenses His servants for their deeds, like His saying: ﴿مالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾ (Master of the Day of Judgement) [al-Fatihah: 4].

If it is objected: the word *ila* (until) indicates the termination of a limit, so this implies that the curse will only occur until the Day of Resurrection, and when the Resurrection comes, the curse will cease.

They answered this from several aspects:

**The first:** What is meant by it is perpetuity. The mention of the Resurrection is the furthest limit people mention in their speech, like their saying: ﴿ما دامَتِ السَّماواتُ والأرْضُ﴾ (as long as the heavens and the earth endure) [Hud: 107], meaning perpetuity.

**The second:** You are blamed and invoked against with the curse in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Judgement, without being punished. But when that Day comes, you will be punished with a punishment through which the curse will be forgotten, so the curse at that time becomes as if it has passed away, because the severity of the punishment will distract from it.

**One:** Was that prostration truly to Adam, or was Adam like a *qiblah* (direction of prayer) for that prostration? This discussion has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 36–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved"﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all"﴾ ﴿except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a path [leading] to Me, straight."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿then reprieve me﴾ is connected to what precedes, and the implied meaning is: "Since You have made me accursed and expelled until the Day of Judgment, then reprieve me." So he sought to be kept alive by God, may He be exalted, when he despaired of the Hereafter, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. For His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ means the Day of Resurrection and Rising, which is the Day of Judgment. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, know that Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection and the Judgment, and his purpose in it was that he would not die, because if he does not die before the Day of Judgment, its apparent meaning is that after the establishment of the Judgment no one dies either, and thus it would follow that he would never die at all. Then God, may He be exalted, refused him this request and said: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ The scholars differed about what is meant by it, in several ways:

The first: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the time of the first blast, when all creatures die. This time was called "the Appointed Time" because it is known that all creatures will die in it. It was also said: God named it by this name because the One who knows that time is God alone, as He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34].

The second: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the one that Iblis mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾. God named it "the Day of the Appointed Time" because when Iblis specified it and pointed to it precisely, it became as though known.

If it is said: When God granted him his request, it follows that he would not die until the time of the establishment of the Hour, and after the establishment of the Resurrection he would also not die, so it would follow that death would be entirely removed from him.

We say: His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is to be understood as referring to what is close to it. The time in which all the responsible beings die is close to the Day of Resurrection, and on this view the outcome of this statement returns to the first view.

The third: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is a day that no one knows except God, and it is not the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: It is not permissible for the responsible person to know when he will die, because that would be an incitement to sins, and that is not permissible for God, may He be exalted.

It is answered: This objection applies only if the time of the establishment of the Resurrection were known to the responsible person. As for when it is known that He has granted him respite until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, but He did not inform him of the time in which the Resurrection will be established, then no incitement to sins follows from it.

And this answer is countered: Even if he did not know the time in which the Resurrection will be established precisely, he did know in general that from the time of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection there is a long period, so it is as though he knew that he would not die during that long period.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The "bi" in ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ is for oath, and "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., "by Your leading me astray"), and the answer to the oath is ﴿la-uzayyinanna﴾ (I will surely make attractive). The meaning is: "I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely make [evil] attractive to them." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], except that in that place he swore by the might of God, which is one of the attributes of the Essence, whereas in His saying ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ he swore by God's leading him astray, which is one of the attributes of the Actions. The jurists said: swearing by the attributes of the Essence is valid; as for swearing by the attributes of the Actions, they differed about it. Al-Wahidi reported from another group that they said: the "ba" here means causation, i.e., "because of my being led astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive," like the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so swore by his disobedience that he will surely enter the Fire, and by his obedience that he will surely enter Paradise."

The second discussion: Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse that God may will the creation of disbelief in the disbeliever, and turn him away from the religion, and lead him astray from the truth, in several ways:

The first: Iblis asked for a respite and requested to remain until the Establishment of the Resurrection, although he explicitly stated that he sought this reprieve and continuance only to mislead and misguide the children of Adam, and God reprieved him and granted him this request. Had God been looking after the interests of the responsible persons in religion, He would not have reprieved him for this long time, nor would He have empowered him to lead astray, mislead, and whisper.

The second: The great Prophets and saints are diligent and striving in guiding creation to the true religion, and Iblis and his band and his partisans are diligent and striving in misguidance and leading astray. So if God's purpose were guidance and direction, it would have been obligatory to preserve the guides and the realized ones and to destroy the misleaders and the seducers; and since He did the opposite, we know that He intended for them abandonment and disbelief.

The third: When God informed him that he would die upon disbelief and that he was accursed until the Day of Judgment, this was an incitement to him toward disbelief and ugliness, because he despaired of forgiveness and of winning Paradise, and so he would then become bold in all kinds of sins and disbelief.

The fourth: When he asked God for this long life, although God knew that he would gain from this long life only an increase in disbelief and disobedience, and because of that increase his deserving of various severe punishments would increase, this reprieve became a cause of greater punishment for him, and this indicates that God intended by it that his punishment and retribution should increase.

The fifth: He explicitly stated that God led him astray, saying: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an explicit statement that God led him astray. It cannot be said: this is the speech of Iblis, and it is not a proof. Moreover, it is contradicted by Iblis's saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], where he attributed the misleading to himself. For we say:

As for the answer to the first: when he mentioned this statement, God did not deny it upon him, and this indicates that he was truthful in what he said.

As for the answer to the second: he said in this verse: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾, so what is meant here by His saying ﴿I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾ is what is meant by His saying in that verse ﴿and will mislead them all﴾, except that in this verse he made clear that he was only able to make falsehoods attractive to them because God had led him astray before that. On this assumption the contradiction disappears, and this is reinforced by what God mentioned, relating about the devils in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿These are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63].

The sixth question: He said: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an acknowledgment that God led him astray. So we say: either it is said that he knew that God had led him astray, or he did not know that. If he knew that God had led him astray, it is impossible for him to be misguided; for he knows that God led him astray only if he knows that what he is upon is ignorance and falsehood, and whoever knows that is prevented from remaining in ignorance and error. But if we say that he did not know that God had led him astray, then how was it possible for him to say: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾? This is the entirety of the questions raised in this verse.

As for the first problem: the Mu'tazilah have two approaches to it:

The first approach, that of al-Jubba'i: God only reprieved Iblis for that long period because He knew that the conditions of people would not differ because of his whispering; so if neither Iblis nor his whispering existed, that disbeliever and sinner would still commit that disbelief and disobedience. Since the matter was thus, He reprieved him for this period.

The second approach, that of Abu Hashim: it is not far-fetched to say that God knew that groups would fall into disbelief and disobedience because of his whispering, but his whispering was not the cause that necessitated that disbelief and disobedience; rather the disbeliever and the sinner, by their own choice, chose that disbelief and that disobedience. At most one can say: avoiding ugliness when there is no whispering is easier than when it exists; yet on this assumption his whispering becomes a cause of increased hardship in performing acts of obedience, and that does not prevent the Wise from doing it, just as the sending down of hardships and of ambiguous verses became a cause of additional doubts, and yet their doing was not prevented; so likewise here. These two approaches are themselves the answer to the second question.

As for the third question: that his being informed that he would die upon disbelief would drive him to boldness in sins and to multiplying them, its answer is that this follows only if Iblis's knowledge of his death upon disbelief would drive him to increase in sins. But if God knows from his condition that this does not necessitate any difference at all, then the question is removed, and this very thing is the answer to the fourth question.

As for the fifth question: that Iblis explicitly stated that God led him astray and misguided him from the religion, they have answered it by saying that this is not what is meant; rather there are other meanings in it:

The first: what is meant by "because You have deprived me of Your mercy" is: I will surely deprive them by calling them to Your disobedience.

The second: what is meant is: just as You led me astray from the path of Paradise, I too will lead them astray from it by calling them to disobedience.

The third: that the first "leading astray" means deprivation, and the second means misguidance.

The fourth: that what is meant by God's leading him astray is that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, and this led to his error, meaning: that this error came about after it through Iblis's own choice. As for saying that this command became by its very nature the necessitating cause of that error, it is known that the matter is not so. This is the sum of the speech of these people on this topic, and all of it is weak. As for his saying that the condition does not differ because of Iblis's whispering, we say: this is false, and the Qur'an and proof indicate it. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], attributing that slip to Satan, and His saying: ﴿so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be made wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], attributing the expulsion to him, and Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]; all of this indicates that the work of Satan has an effect in those deeds. As for proof, the first principles of reason testify that the condition of one who is afflicted with the company of a person who constantly encourages him toward ugliness and deters him from good is not the same as the condition of one whose situation is the opposite of that, and knowledge of this difference is necessary.

وأما قوله إنَّ وُجُودَهُ يَصِيرُ سَبَبًا لِزِيادَةِ المَشَقَّةِ في الطّاعَةِ فَنَقُولُ: تَأْثِيرُ زِيادَةِ المَشَقَّةِ إنَّما هو في كَثْرَةِ الثَّوابِ عَلى أحَدِ التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ، وفي الإلْقاءِ في العَذابِ الشَّدِيدِ عَلى التَّقْدِيرِ الثّانِي وهو التَّقْدِيرُ الأكْثَرُ الأغْلَبُ، وكُلُّ مَن يُراعِي المَصالِحَ، فَإنَّ رِعايَةَ هَذا التَّقْدِيرِ الثّانِي أوْلى عِنْدَهُ مِن رِعايَةِ التَّقْدِيرِ الأوَّلِ؛ لِأنَّ دَفْعَ الضَّرَرِ العَظِيمِ أوْلى مِنَ السَّعْيِ في طَلَبِ النَّفْعِ الزّائِدِ الَّذِي لا حاجَةَ إلى حُصُولِهِ أصْلًا، ولَمّا انْدَفَعَ هَذانِ الجَوابانِ عَنْ هَذا السُّؤالِ قَوِيَتْ سائِرُ الوُجُوهِ المَذْكُورَةِ. وأما قوله: المُرادُ مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿رَبِّ بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ الخَيْبَةُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ أوِ الإضْلالِ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ فَنَقُولُ: كُلُّ هَذا بَعِيدٌ؛ لِأنَّهُ هو الَّذِي خَيَّبَ نَفْسَهُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ وهو الَّذِي أضَلَّ نَفْسَهُ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ؛ لِأنَّهُ لَمّا أقْدَمَ عَلى الكُفْرِ بِاخْتِيارِهِ فَقَدْ خَيَّبَ نَفْسَهُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ، وأضَلَّ نَفْسَهُ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ فَكَيْفَ يَحْسُنُ إضافَتُهُ إلى اللَّهِ تَعالى فَثَبَتَ أنَّ الإشْكالاتِ لازِمَةٌ وأنَّ أجْوِبَتَهم ضَعِيفَةٌ. واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

Wa-amma qawluhu: ﴿illā ʿibādaka minhumu l-mukhlaṣīn﴾ (Except Your sincere servants among them), fa-fīhi masāʾil:

The first issue: Know that Iblis made an exception for the sincere (al-mukhlaṣīn), because he knew that his scheme would not take effect on them and they would not accept from him. I mentioned in a session of admonition that what led Iblis to mention this exception was that he would not become a liar in his claim. So when Iblis guarded himself against lying, we know that lying is at the extreme of baseness.

The second issue: Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr read al-mukhliṣīn with a kasra on the lām in the whole Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatḥa on the lām. The reasoning of the first reading (qirāʾah, recitation) is that they are those who made their religion and worship sincere, free of every impurity that contradicts faith and monotheism,

and whoever reads with a fatḥa on the lām, its meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere through guidance, faith, success and protection; and this reading indicates that sincerity and faith are only from Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: Ikhlāṣ (sincerity) is making a thing pure, free of admixture with others. So we say: every one who performs an act either performs it for Allah alone, or for other than Allah alone, or for a combination of both. On this third assumption, either seeking the pleasure of Allah is predominant, or subordinate, or equal. The fourth assumption is that he performs it with no purpose at all, and this is impossible, because an act without a motive is impossible.

As for the first: it is sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted, because what moves him to that act is seeking the pleasure of Allah, and he did not make this motive mixed with another motive, but it remained pure, free of admixtures of others. This is sincerity.

As for the second: which is sincerity with regard to other than Allah, it is clear that this is not sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted.

As for the third: which is that it includes both aspects, but the side of Allah is predominant, this is hoped to be among the sincere, because an equal portion is matched by an equal portion, and the remaining excess remains pure of impurity.

As for the fourth and fifth: it is clear that he is not among the sincere with regard to Allah the Exalted. The conclusion is that the first category is definitely sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted. The second category: it is hoped that by the grace of Allah He will make it from the category of sincerity. As for the rest of the categories, they are definitely outside of sincerity. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for the statement of the Exalted: ﴿Qāla hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿalayya mustaqīm﴾ (He said: This is a path leading to Me, straight), there are several aspects:

The first: When Iblis said ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, the word mukhlaṣ indicates sincerity, so his statement here refers back to sincerity, and the meaning is: sincerity is a path ʿalayya and ilayya, that is, it leads to My honor and My reward. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: this is a straight path to Me. Others said: this is the path of one who passes by it, as if he passed by Me and My pleasure and My honor, and it is like saying: your path is ʿalayya.

The second: that sincerity is the path of servitude, so His statement ﴿This is a path ʿalayya, straight﴾ means: this path of servitude is a straight path leading to Me.

The third: Some of them said: When Iblis mentioned that he would lead the children of Adam astray except those whom Allah protects by His success, this statement included the entrusting of matters to Allah the Exalted and to His will, so the Exalted said: ﴿This is a path ʿalayya﴾, that is: entrusting matters to My will and My decree is a straight path leading to Me.

The fourth: its meaning: this is a path ʿalayya, its establishment and confirmation, and it is straight, true and truthful. Yaʿqūb read ṣirāṭun ʿalīyun with a ḍamma and tanwīn, considering it an attribute of ṣirāṭ (path), meaning: it is ʿalī, in the sense that it is elevated, straight, with no crookedness in it. Al-Wāḥidī said: its meaning is that the path of entrusting to Allah the Exalted and believing in the decree of Allah is an elevated, straight path.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 36–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved"﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all"﴾ ﴿except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a path [leading] to Me, straight."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿then reprieve me﴾ is connected to what precedes, and the implied meaning is: "Since You have made me accursed and expelled until the Day of Judgment, then reprieve me." So he sought to be kept alive by God, may He be exalted, when he despaired of the Hereafter, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. For His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ means the Day of Resurrection and Rising, which is the Day of Judgment. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, know that Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection and the Judgment, and his purpose in it was that he would not die, because if he does not die before the Day of Judgment, its apparent meaning is that after the establishment of the Judgment no one dies either, and thus it would follow that he would never die at all. Then God, may He be exalted, refused him this request and said: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ The scholars differed about what is meant by it, in several ways:

The first: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the time of the first blast, when all creatures die. This time was called "the Appointed Time" because it is known that all creatures will die in it. It was also said: God named it by this name because the One who knows that time is God alone, as He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34].

The second: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the one that Iblis mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾. God named it "the Day of the Appointed Time" because when Iblis specified it and pointed to it precisely, it became as though known.

If it is said: When God granted him his request, it follows that he would not die until the time of the establishment of the Hour, and after the establishment of the Resurrection he would also not die, so it would follow that death would be entirely removed from him.

We say: His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is to be understood as referring to what is close to it. The time in which all the responsible beings die is close to the Day of Resurrection, and on this view the outcome of this statement returns to the first view.

The third: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is a day that no one knows except God, and it is not the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: It is not permissible for the responsible person to know when he will die, because that would be an incitement to sins, and that is not permissible for God, may He be exalted.

It is answered: This objection applies only if the time of the establishment of the Resurrection were known to the responsible person. As for when it is known that He has granted him respite until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, but He did not inform him of the time in which the Resurrection will be established, then no incitement to sins follows from it.

And this answer is countered: Even if he did not know the time in which the Resurrection will be established precisely, he did know in general that from the time of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection there is a long period, so it is as though he knew that he would not die during that long period.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The "bi" in ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ is for oath, and "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., "by Your leading me astray"), and the answer to the oath is ﴿la-uzayyinanna﴾ (I will surely make attractive). The meaning is: "I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely make [evil] attractive to them." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], except that in that place he swore by the might of God, which is one of the attributes of the Essence, whereas in His saying ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ he swore by God's leading him astray, which is one of the attributes of the Actions. The jurists said: swearing by the attributes of the Essence is valid; as for swearing by the attributes of the Actions, they differed about it. Al-Wahidi reported from another group that they said: the "ba" here means causation, i.e., "because of my being led astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive," like the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so swore by his disobedience that he will surely enter the Fire, and by his obedience that he will surely enter Paradise."

The second discussion: Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse that God may will the creation of disbelief in the disbeliever, and turn him away from the religion, and lead him astray from the truth, in several ways:

The first: Iblis asked for a respite and requested to remain until the Establishment of the Resurrection, although he explicitly stated that he sought this reprieve and continuance only to mislead and misguide the children of Adam, and God reprieved him and granted him this request. Had God been looking after the interests of the responsible persons in religion, He would not have reprieved him for this long time, nor would He have empowered him to lead astray, mislead, and whisper.

The second: The great Prophets and saints are diligent and striving in guiding creation to the true religion, and Iblis and his band and his partisans are diligent and striving in misguidance and leading astray. So if God's purpose were guidance and direction, it would have been obligatory to preserve the guides and the realized ones and to destroy the misleaders and the seducers; and since He did the opposite, we know that He intended for them abandonment and disbelief.

The third: When God informed him that he would die upon disbelief and that he was accursed until the Day of Judgment, this was an incitement to him toward disbelief and ugliness, because he despaired of forgiveness and of winning Paradise, and so he would then become bold in all kinds of sins and disbelief.

The fourth: When he asked God for this long life, although God knew that he would gain from this long life only an increase in disbelief and disobedience, and because of that increase his deserving of various severe punishments would increase, this reprieve became a cause of greater punishment for him, and this indicates that God intended by it that his punishment and retribution should increase.

The fifth: He explicitly stated that God led him astray, saying: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an explicit statement that God led him astray. It cannot be said: this is the speech of Iblis, and it is not a proof. Moreover, it is contradicted by Iblis's saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], where he attributed the misleading to himself. For we say:

As for the answer to the first: when he mentioned this statement, God did not deny it upon him, and this indicates that he was truthful in what he said.

As for the answer to the second: he said in this verse: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾, so what is meant here by His saying ﴿I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾ is what is meant by His saying in that verse ﴿and will mislead them all﴾, except that in this verse he made clear that he was only able to make falsehoods attractive to them because God had led him astray before that. On this assumption the contradiction disappears, and this is reinforced by what God mentioned, relating about the devils in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿These are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63].

The sixth question: He said: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an acknowledgment that God led him astray. So we say: either it is said that he knew that God had led him astray, or he did not know that. If he knew that God had led him astray, it is impossible for him to be misguided; for he knows that God led him astray only if he knows that what he is upon is ignorance and falsehood, and whoever knows that is prevented from remaining in ignorance and error. But if we say that he did not know that God had led him astray, then how was it possible for him to say: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾? This is the entirety of the questions raised in this verse.

As for the first problem: the Mu'tazilah have two approaches to it:

The first approach, that of al-Jubba'i: God only reprieved Iblis for that long period because He knew that the conditions of people would not differ because of his whispering; so if neither Iblis nor his whispering existed, that disbeliever and sinner would still commit that disbelief and disobedience. Since the matter was thus, He reprieved him for this period.

The second approach, that of Abu Hashim: it is not far-fetched to say that God knew that groups would fall into disbelief and disobedience because of his whispering, but his whispering was not the cause that necessitated that disbelief and disobedience; rather the disbeliever and the sinner, by their own choice, chose that disbelief and that disobedience. At most one can say: avoiding ugliness when there is no whispering is easier than when it exists; yet on this assumption his whispering becomes a cause of increased hardship in performing acts of obedience, and that does not prevent the Wise from doing it, just as the sending down of hardships and of ambiguous verses became a cause of additional doubts, and yet their doing was not prevented; so likewise here. These two approaches are themselves the answer to the second question.

As for the third question: that his being informed that he would die upon disbelief would drive him to boldness in sins and to multiplying them, its answer is that this follows only if Iblis's knowledge of his death upon disbelief would drive him to increase in sins. But if God knows from his condition that this does not necessitate any difference at all, then the question is removed, and this very thing is the answer to the fourth question.

As for the fifth question: that Iblis explicitly stated that God led him astray and misguided him from the religion, they have answered it by saying that this is not what is meant; rather there are other meanings in it:

The first: what is meant by "because You have deprived me of Your mercy" is: I will surely deprive them by calling them to Your disobedience.

The second: what is meant is: just as You led me astray from the path of Paradise, I too will lead them astray from it by calling them to disobedience.

The third: that the first "leading astray" means deprivation, and the second means misguidance.

The fourth: that what is meant by God's leading him astray is that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, and this led to his error, meaning: that this error came about after it through Iblis's own choice. As for saying that this command became by its very nature the necessitating cause of that error, it is known that the matter is not so. This is the sum of the speech of these people on this topic, and all of it is weak. As for his saying that the condition does not differ because of Iblis's whispering, we say: this is false, and the Qur'an and proof indicate it. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], attributing that slip to Satan, and His saying: ﴿so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be made wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], attributing the expulsion to him, and Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]; all of this indicates that the work of Satan has an effect in those deeds. As for proof, the first principles of reason testify that the condition of one who is afflicted with the company of a person who constantly encourages him toward ugliness and deters him from good is not the same as the condition of one whose situation is the opposite of that, and knowledge of this difference is necessary.
