As for the fourth and fifth: it is clear that he is not among the sincere with regard to Allah the Exalted. The conclusion is that the first category is definitely sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted. The second category: it is hoped that by the grace of Allah He will make it from the category of sincerity. As for the rest of the categories, they are definitely outside of sincerity. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for the statement of the Exalted: ﴿Qāla hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿalayya mustaqīm﴾ (He said: This is a path leading to Me, straight), there are several aspects:

The first: When Iblis said ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, the word mukhlaṣ indicates sincerity, so his statement here refers back to sincerity, and the meaning is: sincerity is a path ʿalayya and ilayya, that is, it leads to My honor and My reward. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: this is a straight path to Me. Others said: this is the path of one who passes by it, as if he passed by Me and My pleasure and My honor, and it is like saying: your path is ʿalayya.

The second: that sincerity is the path of servitude, so His statement ﴿This is a path ʿalayya, straight﴾ means: this path of servitude is a straight path leading to Me.

The third: Some of them said: When Iblis mentioned that he would lead the children of Adam astray except those whom Allah protects by His success, this statement included the entrusting of matters to Allah the Exalted and to His will, so the Exalted said: ﴿This is a path ʿalayya﴾, that is: entrusting matters to My will and My decree is a straight path leading to Me.

The fourth: its meaning: this is a path ʿalayya, its establishment and confirmation, and it is straight, true and truthful. Yaʿqūb read ṣirāṭun ʿalīyun with a ḍamma and tanwīn, considering it an attribute of ṣirāṭ (path), meaning: it is ʿalī, in the sense that it is elevated, straight, with no crookedness in it. Al-Wāḥidī said: its meaning is that the path of entrusting to Allah the Exalted and believing in the decree of Allah is an elevated, straight path.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 36–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved"﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all"﴾ ﴿except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a path [leading] to Me, straight."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿then reprieve me﴾ is connected to what precedes, and the implied meaning is: "Since You have made me accursed and expelled until the Day of Judgment, then reprieve me." So he sought to be kept alive by God, may He be exalted, when he despaired of the Hereafter, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. For His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ means the Day of Resurrection and Rising, which is the Day of Judgment. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, know that Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection and the Judgment, and his purpose in it was that he would not die, because if he does not die before the Day of Judgment, its apparent meaning is that after the establishment of the Judgment no one dies either, and thus it would follow that he would never die at all. Then God, may He be exalted, refused him this request and said: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ The scholars differed about what is meant by it, in several ways:

The first: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the time of the first blast, when all creatures die. This time was called "the Appointed Time" because it is known that all creatures will die in it. It was also said: God named it by this name because the One who knows that time is God alone, as He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34].

The second: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the one that Iblis mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾. God named it "the Day of the Appointed Time" because when Iblis specified it and pointed to it precisely, it became as though known.

If it is said: When God granted him his request, it follows that he would not die until the time of the establishment of the Hour, and after the establishment of the Resurrection he would also not die, so it would follow that death would be entirely removed from him.

We say: His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is to be understood as referring to what is close to it. The time in which all the responsible beings die is close to the Day of Resurrection, and on this view the outcome of this statement returns to the first view.

The third: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is a day that no one knows except God, and it is not the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: It is not permissible for the responsible person to know when he will die, because that would be an incitement to sins, and that is not permissible for God, may He be exalted.

It is answered: This objection applies only if the time of the establishment of the Resurrection were known to the responsible person. As for when it is known that He has granted him respite until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, but He did not inform him of the time in which the Resurrection will be established, then no incitement to sins follows from it.

And this answer is countered: Even if he did not know the time in which the Resurrection will be established precisely, he did know in general that from the time of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection there is a long period, so it is as though he knew that he would not die during that long period.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The "bi" in ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ is for oath, and "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., "by Your leading me astray"), and the answer to the oath is ﴿la-uzayyinanna﴾ (I will surely make attractive). The meaning is: "I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely make [evil] attractive to them." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], except that in that place he swore by the might of God, which is one of the attributes of the Essence, whereas in His saying ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ he swore by God's leading him astray, which is one of the attributes of the Actions. The jurists said: swearing by the attributes of the Essence is valid; as for swearing by the attributes of the Actions, they differed about it. Al-Wahidi reported from another group that they said: the "ba" here means causation, i.e., "because of my being led astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive," like the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so swore by his disobedience that he will surely enter the Fire, and by his obedience that he will surely enter Paradise."

The second discussion: Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse that God may will the creation of disbelief in the disbeliever, and turn him away from the religion, and lead him astray from the truth, in several ways:

The first: Iblis asked for a respite and requested to remain until the Establishment of the Resurrection, although he explicitly stated that he sought this reprieve and continuance only to mislead and misguide the children of Adam, and God reprieved him and granted him this request. Had God been looking after the interests of the responsible persons in religion, He would not have reprieved him for this long time, nor would He have empowered him to lead astray, mislead, and whisper.

The second: The great Prophets and saints are diligent and striving in guiding creation to the true religion, and Iblis and his band and his partisans are diligent and striving in misguidance and leading astray. So if God's purpose were guidance and direction, it would have been obligatory to preserve the guides and the realized ones and to destroy the misleaders and the seducers; and since He did the opposite, we know that He intended for them abandonment and disbelief.

The third: When God informed him that he would die upon disbelief and that he was accursed until the Day of Judgment, this was an incitement to him toward disbelief and ugliness, because he despaired of forgiveness and of winning Paradise, and so he would then become bold in all kinds of sins and disbelief.

The fourth: When he asked God for this long life, although God knew that he would gain from this long life only an increase in disbelief and disobedience, and because of that increase his deserving of various severe punishments would increase, this reprieve became a cause of greater punishment for him, and this indicates that God intended by it that his punishment and retribution should increase.

The fifth: He explicitly stated that God led him astray, saying: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an explicit statement that God led him astray. It cannot be said: this is the speech of Iblis, and it is not a proof. Moreover, it is contradicted by Iblis's saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], where he attributed the misleading to himself. For we say:

As for the answer to the first: when he mentioned this statement, God did not deny it upon him, and this indicates that he was truthful in what he said.

As for the answer to the second: he said in this verse: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾, so what is meant here by His saying ﴿I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾ is what is meant by His saying in that verse ﴿and will mislead them all﴾, except that in this verse he made clear that he was only able to make falsehoods attractive to them because God had led him astray before that. On this assumption the contradiction disappears, and this is reinforced by what God mentioned, relating about the devils in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿These are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63].

The sixth question: He said: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an acknowledgment that God led him astray. So we say: either it is said that he knew that God had led him astray, or he did not know that. If he knew that God had led him astray, it is impossible for him to be misguided; for he knows that God led him astray only if he knows that what he is upon is ignorance and falsehood, and whoever knows that is prevented from remaining in ignorance and error. But if we say that he did not know that God had led him astray, then how was it possible for him to say: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾? This is the entirety of the questions raised in this verse.

As for the first problem: the Mu'tazilah have two approaches to it:

The first approach, that of al-Jubba'i: God only reprieved Iblis for that long period because He knew that the conditions of people would not differ because of his whispering; so if neither Iblis nor his whispering existed, that disbeliever and sinner would still commit that disbelief and disobedience. Since the matter was thus, He reprieved him for this period.

The second approach, that of Abu Hashim: it is not far-fetched to say that God knew that groups would fall into disbelief and disobedience because of his whispering, but his whispering was not the cause that necessitated that disbelief and disobedience; rather the disbeliever and the sinner, by their own choice, chose that disbelief and that disobedience. At most one can say: avoiding ugliness when there is no whispering is easier than when it exists; yet on this assumption his whispering becomes a cause of increased hardship in performing acts of obedience, and that does not prevent the Wise from doing it, just as the sending down of hardships and of ambiguous verses became a cause of additional doubts, and yet their doing was not prevented; so likewise here. These two approaches are themselves the answer to the second question.

As for the third question: that his being informed that he would die upon disbelief would drive him to boldness in sins and to multiplying them, its answer is that this follows only if Iblis's knowledge of his death upon disbelief would drive him to increase in sins. But if God knows from his condition that this does not necessitate any difference at all, then the question is removed, and this very thing is the answer to the fourth question.

As for the fifth question: that Iblis explicitly stated that God led him astray and misguided him from the religion, they have answered it by saying that this is not what is meant; rather there are other meanings in it:

The first: what is meant by "because You have deprived me of Your mercy" is: I will surely deprive them by calling them to Your disobedience.

The second: what is meant is: just as You led me astray from the path of Paradise, I too will lead them astray from it by calling them to disobedience.

The third: that the first "leading astray" means deprivation, and the second means misguidance.

The fourth: that what is meant by God's leading him astray is that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, and this led to his error, meaning: that this error came about after it through Iblis's own choice. As for saying that this command became by its very nature the necessitating cause of that error, it is known that the matter is not so. This is the sum of the speech of these people on this topic, and all of it is weak. As for his saying that the condition does not differ because of Iblis's whispering, we say: this is false, and the Qur'an and proof indicate it. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], attributing that slip to Satan, and His saying: ﴿so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be made wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], attributing the expulsion to him, and Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]; all of this indicates that the work of Satan has an effect in those deeds. As for proof, the first principles of reason testify that the condition of one who is afflicted with the company of a person who constantly encourages him toward ugliness and deters him from good is not the same as the condition of one whose situation is the opposite of that, and knowledge of this difference is necessary.

وأما قوله إنَّ وُجُودَهُ يَصِيرُ سَبَبًا لِزِيادَةِ المَشَقَّةِ في الطّاعَةِ فَنَقُولُ: تَأْثِيرُ زِيادَةِ المَشَقَّةِ إنَّما هو في كَثْرَةِ الثَّوابِ عَلى أحَدِ التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ، وفي الإلْقاءِ في العَذابِ الشَّدِيدِ عَلى التَّقْدِيرِ الثّانِي وهو التَّقْدِيرُ الأكْثَرُ الأغْلَبُ، وكُلُّ مَن يُراعِي المَصالِحَ، فَإنَّ رِعايَةَ هَذا التَّقْدِيرِ الثّانِي أوْلى عِنْدَهُ مِن رِعايَةِ التَّقْدِيرِ الأوَّلِ؛ لِأنَّ دَفْعَ الضَّرَرِ العَظِيمِ أوْلى مِنَ السَّعْيِ في طَلَبِ النَّفْعِ الزّائِدِ الَّذِي لا حاجَةَ إلى حُصُولِهِ أصْلًا، ولَمّا انْدَفَعَ هَذانِ الجَوابانِ عَنْ هَذا السُّؤالِ قَوِيَتْ سائِرُ الوُجُوهِ المَذْكُورَةِ. وأما قوله: المُرادُ مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿رَبِّ بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ الخَيْبَةُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ أوِ الإضْلالِ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ فَنَقُولُ: كُلُّ هَذا بَعِيدٌ؛ لِأنَّهُ هو الَّذِي خَيَّبَ نَفْسَهُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ وهو الَّذِي أضَلَّ نَفْسَهُ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ؛ لِأنَّهُ لَمّا أقْدَمَ عَلى الكُفْرِ بِاخْتِيارِهِ فَقَدْ خَيَّبَ نَفْسَهُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ، وأضَلَّ نَفْسَهُ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ فَكَيْفَ يَحْسُنُ إضافَتُهُ إلى اللَّهِ تَعالى فَثَبَتَ أنَّ الإشْكالاتِ لازِمَةٌ وأنَّ أجْوِبَتَهم ضَعِيفَةٌ. واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

* * *

Wa-amma qawluhu: ﴿illā ʿibādaka minhumu l-mukhlaṣīn﴾ (Except Your sincere servants among them), fa-fīhi masāʾil:

The first issue: Know that Iblis made an exception for the sincere (al-mukhlaṣīn), because he knew that his scheme would not take effect on them and they would not accept from him. I mentioned in a session of admonition that what led Iblis to mention this exception was that he would not become a liar in his claim. So when Iblis guarded himself against lying, we know that lying is at the extreme of baseness.

The second issue: Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr read al-mukhliṣīn with a kasra on the lām in the whole Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatḥa on the lām. The reasoning of the first reading (qirāʾah, recitation) is that they are those who made their religion and worship sincere, free of every impurity that contradicts faith and monotheism,
Page 150
and whoever reads with a fatḥa on the lām, its meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere through guidance, faith, success and protection; and this reading indicates that sincerity and faith are only from Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: Ikhlāṣ (sincerity) is making a thing pure, free of admixture with others. So we say: every one who performs an act either performs it for Allah alone, or for other than Allah alone, or for a combination of both. On this third assumption, either seeking the pleasure of Allah is predominant, or subordinate, or equal. The fourth assumption is that he performs it with no purpose at all, and this is impossible, because an act without a motive is impossible.

As for the first: it is sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted, because what moves him to that act is seeking the pleasure of Allah, and he did not make this motive mixed with another motive, but it remained pure, free of admixtures of others. This is sincerity.

As for the second: which is sincerity with regard to other than Allah, it is clear that this is not sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted.

As for the third: which is that it includes both aspects, but the side of Allah is predominant, this is hoped to be among the sincere, because an equal portion is matched by an equal portion, and the remaining excess remains pure of impurity.

As for the fourth and fifth: it is clear that he is not among the sincere with regard to Allah the Exalted. The conclusion is that the first category is definitely sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted. The second category: it is hoped that by the grace of Allah He will make it from the category of sincerity. As for the rest of the categories, they are definitely outside of sincerity. So if God's purpose were guidance and direction, it would have been obligatory to preserve the guides and the realized ones and to destroy the misleaders and the seducers; and since He did the opposite, we know that He intended for them abandonment and disbelief.

The fourth: When he asked God for this long life, although God knew that he would gain from this long life only an increase in disbelief and disobedience, and because of that increase his deserving of various severe punishments would increase, this reprieve became a cause of greater punishment for him, and this indicates that God intended by it that his punishment and retribution should increase.

The fifth: He explicitly stated that God led him astray, saying: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an explicit statement that God led him astray. It cannot be said: this is the speech of Iblis, and it is not a proof. Moreover, it is contradicted by Iblis's saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], where he attributed the misleading to himself. For we say:

As for the answer to the first: when he mentioned this statement, God did not deny it upon him, and this indicates that he was truthful in what he said.

As for the answer to the second: he said in this verse: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾, so what is meant here by His saying ﴿I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾ is what is meant by His saying in that verse ﴿and will mislead them all﴾, except that in this verse he made clear that he was only able to make falsehoods attractive to them because God had led him astray before that. On this assumption the contradiction disappears, and this is reinforced by what God mentioned, relating about the devils in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿These are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63].

The sixth question: He said: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an acknowledgment that God led him astray. So we say: either it is said that he knew that God had led him astray, or he did not know that. If he knew that God had led him astray, it is impossible for him to be misguided; for he knows that God led him astray only if he knows that what he is upon is ignorance and falsehood, and whoever knows that is prevented from remaining in ignorance and error. But if we say that he did not know that God had led him astray, then how was it possible for him to say: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾? This is the entirety of the questions raised in this verse.

As for the first problem: the Mu'tazilah have two approaches to it:

The first approach, that of al-Jubba'i: God only reprieved Iblis for that long period because He knew that the conditions of people would not differ because of his whispering; so if neither Iblis nor his whispering existed, that disbeliever and sinner would still commit that disbelief and disobedience. Since the matter was thus, He reprieved him for this period.

The second approach, that of Abu Hashim: it is not far-fetched to say that God knew that groups would fall into disbelief and disobedience because of his whispering, but his whispering was not the cause that necessitated that disbelief and disobedience; rather the disbeliever and the sinner, by their own choice, chose that disbelief and that disobedience. At most one can say: avoiding ugliness when there is no whispering is easier than when it exists; yet on this assumption his whispering becomes a cause of increased hardship in performing acts of obedience, and that does not prevent the Wise from doing it, just as the sending down of hardships and of ambiguous verses became a cause of additional doubts, and yet their doing was not prevented; so likewise here. These two approaches are themselves the answer to the second question.

As for the third question: that his being informed that he would die upon disbelief would drive him to boldness in sins and to multiplying them, its answer is that this follows only if Iblis's knowledge of his death upon disbelief would drive him to increase in sins. But if God knows from his condition that this does not necessitate any difference at all, then the question is removed, and this very thing is the answer to the fourth question.

As for the fifth question: that Iblis explicitly stated that God led him astray and misguided him from the religion, they have answered it by saying that this is not what is meant; rather there are other meanings in it:

The first: what is meant by "because You have deprived me of Your mercy" is: I will surely deprive them by calling them to Your disobedience.

The second: what is meant is: just as You led me astray from the path of Paradise, I too will lead them astray from it by calling them to disobedience.

The third: that the first "leading astray" means deprivation, and the second means misguidance.

The fourth: that what is meant by God's leading him astray is that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, and this led to his error, meaning: that this error came about after it through Iblis's own choice. As for saying that this command became by its very nature the necessitating cause of that error, it is known that the matter is not so. This is the sum of the speech of these people on this topic, and all of it is weak. As for his saying that the condition does not differ because of Iblis's whispering, we say: this is false, and the Qur'an and proof indicate it. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], attributing that slip to Satan, and His saying: ﴿so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be made wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], attributing the expulsion to him, and Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]; all of this indicates that the work of Satan has an effect in those deeds. As for proof, the first principles of reason testify that the condition of one who is afflicted with the company of a person who constantly encourages him toward ugliness and deters him from good is not the same as the condition of one whose situation is the opposite of that, and knowledge of this difference is necessary.

وأما قوله إنَّ وُجُودَهُ يَصِيرُ سَبَبًا لِزِيادَةِ المَشَقَّةِ في الطّاعَةِ فَنَقُولُ: تَأْثِيرُ زِيادَةِ المَشَقَّةِ إنَّما هو في كَثْرَةِ الثَّوابِ عَلى أحَدِ التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ، وفي الإلْقاءِ في العَذابِ الشَّدِيدِ عَلى التَّقْدِيرِ الثّانِي وهو التَّقْدِيرُ الأكْثَرُ الأغْلَبُ، وكُلُّ مَن يُراعِي المَصالِحَ، فَإنَّ رِعايَةَ هَذا التَّقْدِيرِ الثّانِي أوْلى عِنْدَهُ مِن رِعايَةِ التَّقْدِيرِ الأوَّلِ؛ لِأنَّ دَفْعَ الضَّرَرِ العَظِيمِ أوْلى مِنَ السَّعْيِ في طَلَبِ النَّفْعِ الزّائِدِ الَّذِي لا حاجَةَ إلى حُصُولِهِ أصْلًا، ولَمّا انْدَفَعَ هَذانِ الجَوابانِ عَنْ هَذا السُّؤالِ قَوِيَتْ سائِرُ الوُجُوهِ المَذْكُورَةِ. وأما قوله: المُرادُ مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿رَبِّ بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ الخَيْبَةُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ أوِ الإضْلالِ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ فَنَقُولُ: كُلُّ هَذا بَعِيدٌ؛ لِأنَّهُ هو الَّذِي خَيَّبَ نَفْسَهُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ وهو الَّذِي أضَلَّ نَفْسَهُ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ؛ لِأنَّهُ لَمّا أقْدَمَ عَلى الكُفْرِ بِاخْتِيارِهِ فَقَدْ خَيَّبَ نَفْسَهُ عَنِ الرَّحْمَةِ، وأضَلَّ نَفْسَهُ عَنْ طَرِيقِ الجَنَّةِ فَكَيْفَ يَحْسُنُ إضافَتُهُ إلى اللَّهِ تَعالى فَثَبَتَ أنَّ الإشْكالاتِ لازِمَةٌ وأنَّ أجْوِبَتَهم ضَعِيفَةٌ. واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

* * *

Wa-amma qawluhu: ﴿illā ʿibādaka minhumu l-mukhlaṣīn﴾ (Except Your sincere servants among them), fa-fīhi masāʾil:

The first issue: Know that Iblis made an exception for the sincere (al-mukhlaṣīn), because he knew that his scheme would not take effect on them and they would not accept from him. I mentioned in a session of admonition that what led Iblis to mention this exception was that he would not become a liar in his claim. So when Iblis guarded himself against lying, we know that lying is at the extreme of baseness.

The second issue: Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr read al-mukhliṣīn with a kasra on the lām in the whole Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatḥa on the lām. The reasoning of the first reading (qirāʾah, recitation) is that they are those who made their religion and worship sincere, free of every impurity that contradicts faith and monotheism,
Page 150
and whoever reads with a fatḥa on the lām, its meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere through guidance, faith, success and protection; and this reading indicates that sincerity and faith are only from Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: Ikhlāṣ (sincerity) is making a thing pure, free of admixture with others. So we say: every one who performs an act either performs it for Allah alone, or for other than Allah alone, or for a combination of both. On this third assumption, either seeking the pleasure of Allah is predominant, or subordinate, or equal. The fourth assumption is that he performs it with no purpose at all, and this is impossible, because an act without a motive is impossible.

As for the first: it is sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted, because what moves him to that act is seeking the pleasure of Allah, and he did not make this motive mixed with another motive, but it remained pure, free of admixtures of others. This is sincerity.

As for the second: which is sincerity with regard to other than Allah, it is clear that this is not sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted.

As for the third: which is that it includes both aspects, but the side of Allah is predominant, this is hoped to be among the sincere, because an equal portion is matched by an equal portion, and the remaining excess remains pure of impurity.

As for the fourth and fifth: it is clear that he is not among the sincere with regard to Allah the Exalted. The conclusion is that the first category is definitely sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted. The second category: it is hoped that by the grace of Allah He will make it from the category of sincerity. As for the rest of the categories, they are definitely outside of sincerity. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for the statement of the Exalted: ﴿Qāla hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿalayya mustaqīm﴾ (He said: This is a path leading to Me, straight), there are several aspects:

The first: When Iblis said ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, the word mukhlaṣ indicates sincerity, so his statement here refers back to sincerity, and the meaning is: sincerity is a path ʿalayya and ilayya, that is, it leads to My honor and My reward. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: this is a straight path to Me. Others said: this is the path of one who passes by it, as if he passed by Me and My pleasure and My honor, and it is like saying: your path is ʿalayya.

The second: that sincerity is the path of servitude, so His statement ﴿This is a path ʿalayya, straight﴾ means: this path of servitude is a straight path leading to Me.

The third: Some of them said: When Iblis mentioned that he would lead the children of Adam astray except those whom Allah protects by His success, this statement included the entrusting of matters to Allah the Exalted and to His will, so the Exalted said: ﴿This is a path ʿalayya﴾, that is: entrusting matters to My will and My decree is a straight path leading to Me.

The fourth: its meaning: this is a path ʿalayya, its establishment and confirmation, and it is straight, true and truthful. Yaʿqūb read ṣirāṭun ʿalīyun with a ḍamma and tanwīn, considering it an attribute of ṣirāṭ (path), meaning: it is ʿalī, in the sense that it is elevated, straight, with no crookedness in it. Al-Wāḥidī said: its meaning is that the path of entrusting to Allah the Exalted and believing in the decree of Allah is an elevated, straight path.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 36–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved"﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all"﴾ ﴿except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a path [leading] to Me, straight."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿then reprieve me﴾ is connected to what precedes, and the implied meaning is: "Since You have made me accursed and expelled until the Day of Judgment, then reprieve me." So he sought to be kept alive by God, may He be exalted, when he despaired of the Hereafter, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. For His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ means the Day of Resurrection and Rising, which is the Day of Judgment. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, know that Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection and the Judgment, and his purpose in it was that he would not die, because if he does not die before the Day of Judgment, its apparent meaning is that after the establishment of the Judgment no one dies either, and thus it would follow that he would never die at all. Then God, may He be exalted, refused him this request and said: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ The scholars differed about what is meant by it, in several ways:

The first: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the time of the first blast, when all creatures die. This time was called "the Appointed Time" because it is known that all creatures will die in it. It was also said: God named it by this name because the One who knows that time is God alone, as He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34].

The second: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the one that Iblis mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾. God named it "the Day of the Appointed Time" because when Iblis specified it and pointed to it precisely, it became as though known.

If it is said: When God granted him his request, it follows that he would not die until the time of the establishment of the Hour, and after the establishment of the Resurrection he would also not die, so it would follow that death would be entirely removed from him.

We say: His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is to be understood as referring to what is close to it. The time in which all the responsible beings die is close to the Day of Resurrection, and on this view the outcome of this statement returns to the first view.

The third: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is a day that no one knows except God, and it is not the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: It is not permissible for the responsible person to know when he will die, because that would be an incitement to sins, and that is not permissible for God, may He be exalted.

It is answered: This objection applies only if the time of the establishment of the Resurrection were known to the responsible person. As for when it is known that He has granted him respite until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, but He did not inform him of the time in which the Resurrection will be established, then no incitement to sins follows from it.

And this answer is countered: Even if he did not know the time in which the Resurrection will be established precisely, he did know in general that from the time of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection there is a long period, so it is as though he knew that he would not die during that long period.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The "bi" in ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ is for oath, and "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., "by Your leading me astray"), and the answer to the oath is ﴿la-uzayyinanna﴾ (I will surely make attractive). The meaning is: "I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely make [evil] attractive to them." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], except that in that place he swore by the might of God, which is one of the attributes of the Essence, whereas in His saying ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ he swore by God's leading him astray, which is one of the attributes of the Actions. The jurists said: swearing by the attributes of the Essence is valid; as for swearing by the attributes of the Actions, they differed about it. Al-Wahidi reported from another group that they said: the "ba" here means causation, i.e., "because of my being led astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive," like the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so swore by his disobedience that he will surely enter the Fire, and by his obedience that he will surely enter Paradise."

The second discussion: Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse that God may will the creation of disbelief in the disbeliever, and turn him away from the religion, and lead him astray from the truth, in several ways:

The first: Iblis asked for a respite and requested to remain until the Establishment of the Resurrection, although he explicitly stated that he sought this reprieve and continuance only to mislead and misguide the children of Adam, and God reprieved him and granted him this request. Had God been looking after the interests of the responsible persons in religion, He would not have reprieved him for this long time, nor would He have empowered him to lead astray, mislead, and whisper.

The second: The great Prophets and saints are diligent and striving in guiding creation to the true religion, and Iblis and his band and his partisans are diligent and striving in misguidance and leading astray. So if God's purpose were guidance and direction, it would have been obligatory to preserve the guides and the realized ones and to destroy the misleaders and the seducers; and since He did the opposite, we know that He intended for them abandonment and disbelief.

The third: When God informed him that he would die upon disbelief and that he was accursed until the Day of Judgment, this was an incitement to him toward disbelief and ugliness, because he despaired of forgiveness and of winning Paradise, and so he would then become bold in all kinds of sins and disbelief.

Wa-amma qawluhu: ﴿illā ʿibādaka minhumu l-mukhlaṣīn﴾ (Except Your sincere servants among them), fa-fīhi masāʾil:

The first issue: Know that Iblis made an exception for the sincere (al-mukhlaṣīn), because he knew that his scheme would not take effect on them and they would not accept from him. I mentioned in a session of admonition that what led Iblis to mention this exception was that he would not become a liar in his claim. So when Iblis guarded himself against lying, we know that lying is at the extreme of baseness.

The second issue: Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū ʿAmr read al-mukhliṣīn with a kasra on the lām in the whole Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatḥa on the lām. The reasoning of the first reading (qirāʾah, recitation) is that they are those who made their religion and worship sincere, free of every impurity that contradicts faith and monotheism,

and whoever reads with a fatḥa on the lām, its meaning is: those whom Allah has made sincere through guidance, faith, success and protection; and this reading indicates that sincerity and faith are only from Allah the Exalted.

The third issue: Ikhlāṣ (sincerity) is making a thing pure, free of admixture with others. So we say: every one who performs an act either performs it for Allah alone, or for other than Allah alone, or for a combination of both. On this third assumption, either seeking the pleasure of Allah is predominant, or subordinate, or equal. The fourth assumption is that he performs it with no purpose at all, and this is impossible, because an act without a motive is impossible.

As for the first: it is sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted, because what moves him to that act is seeking the pleasure of Allah, and he did not make this motive mixed with another motive, but it remained pure, free of admixtures of others. This is sincerity.

As for the second: which is sincerity with regard to other than Allah, it is clear that this is not sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted.

As for the third: which is that it includes both aspects, but the side of Allah is predominant, this is hoped to be among the sincere, because an equal portion is matched by an equal portion, and the remaining excess remains pure of impurity.

As for the fourth and fifth: it is clear that he is not among the sincere with regard to Allah the Exalted. The conclusion is that the first category is definitely sincerity with regard to Allah the Exalted. The second category: it is hoped that by the grace of Allah He will make it from the category of sincerity. As for the rest of the categories, they are definitely outside of sincerity. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for the statement of the Exalted: ﴿Qāla hādhā ṣirāṭun ʿalayya mustaqīm﴾ (He said: This is a path leading to Me, straight), there are several aspects:

The first: When Iblis said ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, the word mukhlaṣ indicates sincerity, so his statement here refers back to sincerity, and the meaning is: sincerity is a path ʿalayya and ilayya, that is, it leads to My honor and My reward. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: this is a straight path to Me. Others said: this is the path of one who passes by it, as if he passed by Me and My pleasure and My honor, and it is like saying: your path is ʿalayya.

The second: that sincerity is the path of servitude, so His statement ﴿This is a path ʿalayya, straight﴾ means: this path of servitude is a straight path leading to Me.

The third: Some of them said: When Iblis mentioned that he would lead the children of Adam astray except those whom Allah protects by His success, this statement included the entrusting of matters to Allah the Exalted and to His will, so the Exalted said: ﴿This is a path ʿalayya﴾, that is: entrusting matters to My will and My decree is a straight path leading to Me.

The fourth: its meaning: this is a path ʿalayya, its establishment and confirmation, and it is straight, true and truthful. Yaʿqūb read ṣirāṭun ʿalīyun with a ḍamma and tanwīn, considering it an attribute of ṣirāṭ (path), meaning: it is ʿalī, in the sense that it is elevated, straight, with no crookedness in it. Al-Wāḥidī said: its meaning is that the path of entrusting to Allah the Exalted and believing in the decree of Allah is an elevated, straight path.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 36–41 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved"﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all"﴾ ﴿except among them Your chosen servants.﴾ ﴿He said, "This is a path [leading] to Me, straight."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿then reprieve me﴾ is connected to what precedes, and the implied meaning is: "Since You have made me accursed and expelled until the Day of Judgment, then reprieve me." So he sought to be kept alive by God, may He be exalted, when he despaired of the Hereafter, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection. For His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ means the Day of Resurrection and Rising, which is the Day of Judgment. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, know that Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection and the Judgment, and his purpose in it was that he would not die, because if he does not die before the Day of Judgment, its apparent meaning is that after the establishment of the Judgment no one dies either, and thus it would follow that he would never die at all. Then God, may He be exalted, refused him this request and said: ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾ ﴿until the Day of the Appointed Time.﴾ The scholars differed about what is meant by it, in several ways:

The first: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the time of the first blast, when all creatures die. This time was called "the Appointed Time" because it is known that all creatures will die in it. It was also said: God named it by this name because the One who knows that time is God alone, as He said: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and He said: ﴿Indeed, with Allah is the knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34].

The second: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is the one that Iblis mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾. God named it "the Day of the Appointed Time" because when Iblis specified it and pointed to it precisely, it became as though known.

If it is said: When God granted him his request, it follows that he would not die until the time of the establishment of the Hour, and after the establishment of the Resurrection he would also not die, so it would follow that death would be entirely removed from him.

We say: His saying ﴿until the Day they are resurrected﴾ is to be understood as referring to what is close to it. The time in which all the responsible beings die is close to the Day of Resurrection, and on this view the outcome of this statement returns to the first view.

The third: What is meant by "the Day of the Appointed Time" is a day that no one knows except God, and it is not the Day of Resurrection.

If it is said: It is not permissible for the responsible person to know when he will die, because that would be an incitement to sins, and that is not permissible for God, may He be exalted.

It is answered: This objection applies only if the time of the establishment of the Resurrection were known to the responsible person. As for when it is known that He has granted him respite until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection, but He did not inform him of the time in which the Resurrection will be established, then no incitement to sins follows from it.

And this answer is countered: Even if he did not know the time in which the Resurrection will be established precisely, he did know in general that from the time of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, until the time of the establishment of the Resurrection there is a long period, so it is as though he knew that he would not die during that long period.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will mislead them all﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The "bi" in ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ is for oath, and "ma" is verbal-masdariyyah (i.e., "by Your leading me astray"), and the answer to the oath is ﴿la-uzayyinanna﴾ (I will surely make attractive). The meaning is: "I swear by Your leading me astray that I will surely make [evil] attractive to them." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], except that in that place he swore by the might of God, which is one of the attributes of the Essence, whereas in His saying ﴿bima aghwaytani﴾ he swore by God's leading him astray, which is one of the attributes of the Actions. The jurists said: swearing by the attributes of the Essence is valid; as for swearing by the attributes of the Actions, they differed about it. Al-Wahidi reported from another group that they said: the "ba" here means causation, i.e., "because of my being led astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive," like the saying of a speaker: "So-and-so swore by his disobedience that he will surely enter the Fire, and by his obedience that he will surely enter Paradise."

The second discussion: Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) have argued with this verse that God may will the creation of disbelief in the disbeliever, and turn him away from the religion, and lead him astray from the truth, in several ways:

The first: Iblis asked for a respite and requested to remain until the Establishment of the Resurrection, although he explicitly stated that he sought this reprieve and continuance only to mislead and misguide the children of Adam, and God reprieved him and granted him this request. Had God been looking after the interests of the responsible persons in religion, He would not have reprieved him for this long time, nor would He have empowered him to lead astray, mislead, and whisper.

The second: The great Prophets and saints are diligent and striving in guiding creation to the true religion, and Iblis and his band and his partisans are diligent and striving in misguidance and leading astray. So if God's purpose were guidance and direction, it would have been obligatory to preserve the guides and the realized ones and to destroy the misleaders and the seducers; and since He did the opposite, we know that He intended for them abandonment and disbelief.

The third: When God informed him that he would die upon disbelief and that he was accursed until the Day of Judgment, this was an incitement to him toward disbelief and ugliness, because he despaired of forgiveness and of winning Paradise, and so he would then become bold in all kinds of sins and disbelief.

The fourth: When he asked God for this long life, although God knew that he would gain from this long life only an increase in disbelief and disobedience, and because of that increase his deserving of various severe punishments would increase, this reprieve became a cause of greater punishment for him, and this indicates that God intended by it that his punishment and retribution should increase.

The fifth: He explicitly stated that God led him astray, saying: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an explicit statement that God led him astray. It cannot be said: this is the speech of Iblis, and it is not a proof. Moreover, it is contradicted by Iblis's saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Sad: 82], where he attributed the misleading to himself. For we say:

As for the answer to the first: when he mentioned this statement, God did not deny it upon him, and this indicates that he was truthful in what he said.

As for the answer to the second: he said in this verse: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾, so what is meant here by His saying ﴿I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾ is what is meant by His saying in that verse ﴿and will mislead them all﴾, except that in this verse he made clear that he was only able to make falsehoods attractive to them because God had led him astray before that. On this assumption the contradiction disappears, and this is reinforced by what God mentioned, relating about the devils in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿These are the ones whom we led astray; we led them astray as we ourselves went astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63].

The sixth question: He said: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, and this is an acknowledgment that God led him astray. So we say: either it is said that he knew that God had led him astray, or he did not know that. If he knew that God had led him astray, it is impossible for him to be misguided; for he knows that God led him astray only if he knows that what he is upon is ignorance and falsehood, and whoever knows that is prevented from remaining in ignorance and error. But if we say that he did not know that God had led him astray, then how was it possible for him to say: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾? This is the entirety of the questions raised in this verse.

As for the first problem: the Mu'tazilah have two approaches to it:

The first approach, that of al-Jubba'i: God only reprieved Iblis for that long period because He knew that the conditions of people would not differ because of his whispering; so if neither Iblis nor his whispering existed, that disbeliever and sinner would still commit that disbelief and disobedience. Since the matter was thus, He reprieved him for this period.

The second approach, that of Abu Hashim: it is not far-fetched to say that God knew that groups would fall into disbelief and disobedience because of his whispering, but his whispering was not the cause that necessitated that disbelief and disobedience; rather the disbeliever and the sinner, by their own choice, chose that disbelief and that disobedience. At most one can say: avoiding ugliness when there is no whispering is easier than when it exists; yet on this assumption his whispering becomes a cause of increased hardship in performing acts of obedience, and that does not prevent the Wise from doing it, just as the sending down of hardships and of ambiguous verses became a cause of additional doubts, and yet their doing was not prevented; so likewise here. These two approaches are themselves the answer to the second question.

As for the third question: that his being informed that he would die upon disbelief would drive him to boldness in sins and to multiplying them, its answer is that this follows only if Iblis's knowledge of his death upon disbelief would drive him to increase in sins. But if God knows from his condition that this does not necessitate any difference at all, then the question is removed, and this very thing is the answer to the fourth question.

As for the fifth question: that Iblis explicitly stated that God led him astray and misguided him from the religion, they have answered it by saying that this is not what is meant; rather there are other meanings in it:

The first: what is meant by "because You have deprived me of Your mercy" is: I will surely deprive them by calling them to Your disobedience.

The second: what is meant is: just as You led me astray from the path of Paradise, I too will lead them astray from it by calling them to disobedience.

The third: that the first "leading astray" means deprivation, and the second means misguidance.

The fourth: that what is meant by God's leading him astray is that He commanded him to prostrate to Adam, and this led to his error, meaning: that this error came about after it through Iblis's own choice. As for saying that this command became by its very nature the necessitating cause of that error, it is known that the matter is not so. This is the sum of the speech of these people on this topic, and all of it is weak. As for his saying that the condition does not differ because of Iblis's whispering, we say: this is false, and the Qur'an and proof indicate it. As for the Qur'an, His saying: ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], attributing that slip to Satan, and His saying: ﴿so let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be made wretched﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], attributing the expulsion to him, and Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿This is from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Qasas: 15]; all of this indicates that the work of Satan has an effect in those deeds. As for proof, the first principles of reason testify that the condition of one who is afflicted with the company of a person who constantly encourages him toward ugliness and deters him from good is not the same as the condition of one whose situation is the opposite of that, and knowledge of this difference is necessary.

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾ ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾ ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾ ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein, nor will they be removed from it﴾.**

Know that when Exalted is He had explained the condition of the people of punishment, He followed it with the description of the people of reward. In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue: concerning His saying, ﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾, there are two opinions.**

**The first opinion:** al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian) and the majority of the Mu'tazila, who hold the doctrine of *al-wa'īd* (the threat of punishment for grave sinners), said: the intended meaning of "the righteous" is those who guarded against all sins. They said: because it is a term of praise, it applies only to one who is like that.

**The second opinion:** this is the view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors, and it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: the intended meaning is those who guarded against *shirk* (associating partners with Allah, Exalted is He) and *kufr* (disbelief) in Him. I say: this view is the true and correct one, and what indicates it is that the *muttaqī* (the one who is righteous/God-conscious) is one who performs *taqwā* (God-consciousness) even once, just as the one who strikes is one who performs a strike even once, and the killer is one who performs a killing even once. Just as it is not a condition for the description to be applicable to someone that he is a striker and a killer that he performs every kind of striking and killing, likewise it is not a condition for the truth of the description "righteous" that he performs every kind of *taqwā*. What strengthens this point is that one who performs a single instance of *taqwā* is one who performs *taqwā*, because every individual of a reality necessarily includes that reality. So one who performs *taqwā* must be righteous. It is thus established that one who performs a single instance of *taqwā* truly qualifies as righteous. On the basis of this verification, the exegetes agreed that the apparent sense of a command does not indicate repetition.

Having established this, we say: the apparent sense of His saying, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾, requires that the gardens and springs belong to everyone who guarded against one thing. However, the community (*ummah*) is unanimous that guarding against disbelief is a condition for this ruling. Also, this verse came after the words of Iblīs: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾, and after the words of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾. For these evidences, we take faith (*īmān*) into account in this ruling, and it is necessary that no other condition be added to it. Since the specification of a general statement (*takhṣīṣ al-ʿāmm*) is contrary to the apparent sense, the less the specification, the more it accords with the requirement of the basic principle and the apparent meaning. Thus it is established that His saying, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾, encompasses all who say "There is no god but Allah, Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah," both in statement and in belief, whether they are among the obedient or among the disobedient. This is a clear demonstration and an evident statement.

**The second issue: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿in gardens and springs﴾.** As for the gardens, they are four, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But for one who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 46], and then He said: ﴿And beneath them are two gardens﴾ [al-Raḥmān: 62]. So the total is four. His saying, ﴿But for one who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾, confirms what we have said, because whoever believes in Allah does not have a heart free of fear of Allah, Exalted is He. And His saying, ﴿for one who fears﴾, is sufficiently true by the occurrence of this fear even once.

As for the springs, it is possible that what is meant by them is what Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿The description of the Garden which the righteous have been promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of purified honey﴾ [Muḥammad: 15]. It is also possible that what is meant by these springs are fountains distinct from those rivers.

[Page 153 continues]

If it is said: Do you claim that each one of the righteous has springs particular to him, or that those springs flow from one to another? It is answered: Neither of the two possibilities is impossible, so it is permissible that each person has a spring of his own, and that everyone who serves him, from among the *ḥūr* (maidens of paradise) and the *wildān* (youths), benefits from it, and that this is according to their need and in accordance with their desires. It is also possible that it flows from some of them to others, because they are purified of resentment and envy.

His saying, ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾, may be understood as meaning that the one who says "Enter them" is Allah, Exalted is He, or that this speaker is one of His angels. There is an objection to this: since Allah, Exalted is He, had already ruled before this verse that they are in gardens and springs, and if they are in them, how is it possible to say to them, ﴿Enter them﴾?

The answer to this is given in two ways:

**First:** Perhaps what is meant is that it was said to them before they entered them: ﴿Enter them in peace﴾.

**Second:** Perhaps what is meant is that when they possess many gardens, then whenever they wish to move from one garden to another, it is said to them: "Enter them." His saying, ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾, means: enter the Garden with safety from all calamities at present, and with certainty that this safety will endure, and with security from its cessation.

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾. *Ghill* is the hatred lodged in the heart, and it is derived from their saying *aghalla fī jawfihi wa-taghalghala*, meaning it penetrated and spread deep within. That is, if any of them had resentment against another in this world, Allah removes that from their hearts and purifies their souls.

It is reported from ʿAlī, peace be upon him, that he said: "I hope that I, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr will be among them." It is related that al-Ḥārith ibn al-Aʿwar was sitting with ʿAlī, peace be upon him, when Zakariyyā ibn Ṭalḥa entered, and ʿAlī said to him: "Welcome, nephew. By Allah, I hope that I and your father will be among those about whom Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾." Al-Ḥārith said: "Nay, rather Allah is too just to place you and Ṭalḥa in one place." ʿAlī, peace be upon him, said: "Then to whom does this verse refer? May you have no mother, one-eyed man!"

It is also reported that the believers will be held back at the gate of the Garden, and retribution will be exacted among them for some against others, and then they will be ordered into the Garden. Allah has purified their hearts of *ghill* (resentment), *ghishsh* (deceit), *ḥiqd* (rancor) and *ḥasad* (envy).

His saying, ﴿as brothers (*ikhwānan*)﴾, is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). The intended meaning is not brotherhood by lineage, but brotherhood of affection and sincere friendship, as He said: ﴿The close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

His saying, ﴿upon couches facing one another﴾: *sarīr* is well known, and its plurals are *asiррah* and *surur*. Abū ʿUbayda said: it is said *surur* and *surar* with a *fatḥah* on the *rāʾ*, and likewise every *faʿīl* of the doubled-letter type, its plural being *fuʿul* and *fuʿal*, such as *surur* and *surar*, and *judud* and *judad*. Al-Mufaḍḍal said: some of Tamīm and Kalb pronounce it with a *fatḥah*, because they find it heavy to have two consecutive *ḍammahs* on two letters of the same kind. Some scholars of meanings said: the *sarīr* is an elevated seat prepared for joy, and it is derived from that, because it is a seat of joy.

Al-Layth said: the "*sarīr* of life" is its place of rest in which one is at ease during one's time of happiness and joy. Ibn ʿAbbās said: he means upon couches of gold, adorned with emerald, pearls and rubies, and the *sarīr* is like the distance between Ṣanʿāʾ and al-Jābiya.

His saying, ﴿facing one another (*mutaqābilīn*)﴾: *taqābul* means facing one another, and it is the opposite of *tadābur* (turning away from one another). There is no doubt that facing one another is the most honourable of states.

His saying, ﴿No fatigue (*naṣab*) will touch them therein﴾: *naṣab* means exhaustion and weariness, that is, no weariness will reach them therein. ﴿Nor will they be removed from it﴾: the intended meaning is that it is eternal without cessation, lasting without end, complete without deficiency, and success without deprivation.

[Page 154 begins]

Know that reward has four conditions: that it be benefits, combined with honour, free of impurities, and lasting.

As for the first condition, that it is a benefit, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in gardens and springs﴾.

As for the second condition, that it is combined with honour, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿Enter them in peace, secure﴾, because when Allah, glorified is He, says this speech to His servants, it implies the utmost honour and the highest exaltation.

As for the third condition, that those benefits are free of harmful impurities: know that harms are either spiritual or physical. As for spiritual harms, they are rancor, envy, resentment and anger; and as for physical harms, they are like exhaustion and weariness. So His saying: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾ is an indication of the negation of spiritual harms, and His saying: ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein﴾ is an indication of the negation of physical harms.

As for the fourth condition, that those benefits are lasting and secure from cessation, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿Nor will they be removed from it﴾. This is a good and reasonable arrangement based on the four conditions that are considered in the reality of reward.

The philosophers of Islam have also spoken on this verse. They said: the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾, is an indication that the holy, rational souls are pure and purified from the attachments of the appetitive and irascible faculties, and free from the occurrences of illusion and imagination. And His saying, ﴿as brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾ means that those souls, when they became clear of the turbidity of the world of bodies and the impulses of imagination and illusions, and the lights of the world of greatness and majesty fell upon them, shone with those divine lights and gleamed with those eternal illuminations. So every light that overflowed upon one of them was reflected from it upon the other, like facing, opposite mirrors. Because they are in this state, the expression of them was given by His saying: ﴿as brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 49–50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾

In the verse there are two issues.

The first issue: The silent hamza (hamzah sakinah) in (nabbi') is written out in full, whereas it was not written out in His saying ﴿warmth﴾ [al-Nahl: 5]. This is because when the letter before it is silent, it is often elided, and its vowel is transferred to the silent letter before it. So (nabbi') in the script follows the realization of the hamza, and there is no silent letter before the hamza of (nabbi'), so they wrote it according to the analogy of the original form.

The second issue: Know that the servants of God are of two kinds: among them are those who are god-fearing (muttaqi), and among them are those who are not so. When God, exalted is He, mentioned the states of the god-fearing in the previous verse, He mentioned the states of those who are not god-fearing in this verse, so He said: ﴿Inform My servants﴾.

Know also that it is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the placing of a ruling upon a fitting attribute (wasf munasib) indicates that this attribute is the effective cause ('illah) of that ruling. Here He described them by being His servants, then, immediately after mentioning this attribute, He established the ruling of His being Forgiving and Merciful. This indicates that whoever acknowledges servitude, the fact of God being Forgiving and Merciful manifests with respect to him, and whoever denies that deserves the painful punishment. In the verse there are subtle points:

The first: He attributed the servants to Himself by saying ﴿My servants﴾, and this is a great honor. Do you not see that when He wished to honor Muhammad ﷺ on the night of the Ascension (mi'raj), He did not go beyond saying ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

The second: When He mentioned mercy and forgiveness, He emphasized them with three expressions:

The first: His saying ﴿innee﴾ (indeed I).

The second: His saying ﴿anaa﴾ (I).

The third: the inclusion of the definite article in His saying ﴿the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. When He mentioned punishment, He did not say "indeed I am the Punisher," nor did He describe Himself by that; rather He said: ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾

The third: He commanded His Messenger to convey this meaning to them, as if He made His Messenger a witness against Himself to His commitment to forgiveness and mercy.

The fourth: When He said ﴿Inform My servants﴾, its meaning is: inform everyone who acknowledges My servitude. Just as the obedient believer is included in this, so too the disobedient believer is included, and all of this indicates the predominance of the side of mercy from God, exalted is He. It is reported from Qatadah who said: "It has reached us from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: 'If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from what is forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy himself.'" That is, he would kill it. And it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he passed by a group of his companions who were laughing, and he said: "Are you laughing while the Fire is before you?" Then there was revealed His saying: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 51–56:**

**His saying, may He be exalted:** ﴿And inform them about the guests of Ibrahim﴾ ﴿when they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me? Then of what do you give good tidings?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have given you good tidings in truth, so do not be of those who despair."﴾ ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that when He, may He be exalted, had elaborated on the matter of prophethood (nubuwwah), then followed it with mention of the evidences of divine unity (tawhid), and then mentioned after it the conditions of the Resurrection and the description of the wretched and the blessed, He followed this with mention of the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, so that hearing them would encourage obedience, which brings about attaining the ranks of the prophets, and would warn against disobedience, which merits the levels of the wretched. He began first with the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The pronoun in His saying ﴿and inform them﴾ refers to His saying ﴿My servants﴾, and the meaning is: "Inform My servants about the guests of Ibrahim." It is said: "anba'tu al-qawma inba'an" and "nabba'tuhum tanbi'atan" when you inform them. He, may He be exalted, mentioned in the verse that the guests of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, gave him good tidings of a son after old age, and of the deliverance of the believers from the punishment of the people of Lut, and they also informed him that He, may He be exalted, would punish the disbelievers among the people of Lut with a punishment of annihilation. All of this strengthens what He mentioned, that He is Forgiving and Merciful to the believers, and that His punishment is a painful punishment for the disbelievers.

**The second issue:** The word *dayf* (guest) is originally a verbal noun of "dhāfa yadīfu," when one comes to a person seeking hospitality, and then it was applied to the guests. For this reason the singular form is used in the wording, although they are a group.

If it is said: How did he call them guests, given that they refused to eat?

We say: When Ibrahim thought that they had only entered upon him seeking hospitality, it was permissible to call them that. It has also been said: whoever enters a person's house and seeks refuge with him is called a guest, even if he does not eat. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿when they entered upon him and said, "Peace"﴾ means: we greet you with peace, or: I greet you with peace. Then Ibrahim said, ﴿Indeed, we are fearful of you﴾, meaning: fearful. His fear was due to their refusal to eat. It has also been said: it was because they entered upon him without permission and at an improper time. Al-Hasan recited "*lā tūjal*" with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'*, from "awjalahu yūjiluhu," meaning when he frightened him. It has also been recited as "*lā ta'jal*" and "*lā tuwājal*," from "wājalahu," in the sense of "awjalahu." This story has already been mentioned in detail in Surat Hud. His saying: ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy."﴾ contains discussions:

**The first discussion:** Hamzah recited "*innā nabshuruka*" with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and a light *bā'*, while the rest read ﴿nubashshiruka﴾ with a doubled *shīn*.

**The second discussion:** His saying ﴿Indeed, we give you good tidings﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) in the sense of giving a reason for the prohibition of fear. The meaning is: you are in the position of one who is secure and receives good tidings, so do not fear.

**The third discussion:** His saying ﴿Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy﴾: they gave him good tidings of two matters. One of them is that the child is a male, and the other is that he will become knowing. They differed over the interpretation of "knowing" (*'alīm*). It was said: they gave him good tidings of his prophethood after him. It was also said: they gave him good tidings that he would be knowing of the religion. Then Allah, may He be exalted, related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me? Then of what do you give good tidings?﴾ So the meaning of "*'alā*" here is for circumstance, that is, the state of old age. His saying ﴿Then of what do you give good tidings?﴾ contains two issues:

**The first issue:** The word *mā* here is an interrogative in the sense of amazement, as if he said: "By what wonder do you give me good tidings?"

If it is said: there are two difficulties in the verse:

The first: How could he regard Allah's power to create a child from him in old age as improbable, when denying Allah's power in this context is disbelief?

The second: How could he say ﴿Then of what do you give good tidings?﴾ when they had already stated what they gave him good tidings of, and what is the benefit of this question? The judge (al-Qadi) said: The best of what has been said in answer to this is that he wanted to know whether He, may He be exalted, would give him a child while keeping him in the state of old age, or would turn him into a youth and then give him a child. The reason for this question is that the custom is that a child does not come about in the state of complete old age, but only in the state of youth.

If it is said: if the meaning of the speech is as you have mentioned, then why did they say: ﴿We have given you good tidings in truth, so do not be of those who despair﴾?

We say: They clarified that Allah, may He be exalted, gave him good tidings of a child while keeping him in the state of old age. His saying ﴿so do not be of those who despair﴾ does not indicate that he was in that state, as evidenced by the fact that in their answer to him they stated explicitly what indicates he was not in that state, when he said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾ There is another answer too: when a person has a very great desire for something, and the time in which he strongly expects that thing to be realized has passed, then when he is given good tidings of its realization after that, his joy and happiness become great, and that strong joy becomes overwhelming to him and removes the strength of his understanding and intelligence. So perhaps he speaks disjointed words in that joy at that time. It has also been said: he savored that good news, so he may repeat the question to hear that good news once more, twice, and more, seeking enjoyment in hearing that good news, and seeking increased reassurance and certainty, like His saying: ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. It has also been said: he asked, "Are you giving me good tidings by the command of Allah, or from your own selves and your own effort?"

**The second issue:** Nafi' recited ﴿tubashshirūnanī﴾ with a *kasra* on the *nūn* and a light pronunciation throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir recited it with a *kasra* on the *nūn* and a doubled *nūn*. The rest recited it with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and a light pronunciation. As for the *kasra* with doubling, its underlying form is *tubashshirūnanī*, with the *nūn* of the plural assimilated into the *nūn* of the first person pronoun. As for the *kasra* with lightening, it is based on deleting the *nūn* of the plural because of the dislike of two similar letters together and seeking lightness. Abu Hatim said: Nafi' deleted the *yā'* along with the *nūn*. He said: The deletion of two letters is not permissible. It was answered: he deleted only one letter, which is the *nūn* that marks the nominative case. And also because the deletion of two letters is permissible; Allah, may He be exalted, said in one place ﴿and do not be﴾ (wa lā taku) and in another place ﴿and do not be﴾ (wa lā takun). As for the *fatḥa* on the *nūn*, it is for a case other than the first-person suffix, and the *nūn* is the sign of the nominative, which is always pronounced with a *fatḥa*. His saying ﴿We have given you good tidings in truth﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: he means by what Allah has decreed. The meaning is that Allah, may He be exalted, decreed that He would bring forth Ishaq, peace be upon him, from the loins of Ibrahim, and would bring forth from the loins of Ishaq the like of what He brought forth from the loins of Adam, for He, may He be exalted, gave good tidings that He would bring forth from the loins of Ishaq most of the prophets. So His saying ﴿in truth﴾ is an indication of this meaning. His saying ﴿so do not be of those who despair﴾ is a prohibition to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from despair. We have mentioned many times that a prohibition of a person from something does not indicate that the one prohibited is doing that which is prohibited, as in His saying: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1]. Then Allah, may He be exalted, related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾ In this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** This statement is true, because despair of the mercy of Allah, may He be exalted, does not arise except from ignorance of three matters:

First: that one ignores that He is capable of it.

Second: that one ignores that He knows the servant's need for it.

Third: that one ignores that He is exempt from stinginess, need, and ignorance. All these matters are causes of straying. For this reason He said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾

**The second issue:** Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿yaqnit﴾ with a *kasra* on the *nūn*, and likewise ﴿lā taqnitū﴾. The rest recited it with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn*. Both are dialects: "qanaṭa yaqnitu," like "ḍaraba yaḍribu," and "qaniṭa yaqnaṭu," like "'alima ya'lamu." Abu 'Ubaydah related: "qanaṭa yaqnuṭu" with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*. This is indicated by their agreement on His saying: ﴿after they had despaired﴾ [al-Shura: 28]. The report of Abu 'Ubaydah also indicates that "qanaṭa" with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* is more common, because the present tense of *fa'ala* comes as *yaf'ilu* and *yaf'alu*, like "fasaqa yafsiqu" and "yafsaqu," and the present tense of *fa'ala* does not come as *yaf'ulu*. And Allah knows best.
