It is said: "anba'tu al-qawma inba'an" and "nabba'tuhum tanbi'atan" when you inform them. He, may He be exalted, mentioned in the verse that the guests of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, gave him good tidings of a son after old age, and of the deliverance of the believers from the punishment of the people of Lut, and they also informed him that He, may He be exalted, would punish the disbelievers among the people of Lut with a punishment of annihilation. All of this strengthens what He mentioned, that He is Forgiving and Merciful to the believers, and that His punishment is a painful punishment for the disbelievers.

**The second issue:** The word *dayf* (guest) is originally a verbal noun of "dhāfa yadīfu," when one comes to a person seeking hospitality, and then it was applied to the guests. For this reason the singular form is used in the wording, although they are a group.

If it is said: How did he call them guests, given that they refused to eat?

We say: When Ibrahim thought that they had only entered upon him seeking hospitality, it was permissible to call them that. It has also been said: whoever enters a person's house and seeks refuge with him is called a guest, even if he does not eat. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿when they entered upon him and said, "Peace"﴾ means: we greet you with peace, or: I greet you with peace. Then Ibrahim said, ﴿Indeed, we are fearful of you﴾, meaning: fearful. His fear was due to their refusal to eat. It has also been said: it was because they entered upon him without permission and at an improper time. Al-Hasan recited "*lā tūjal*" with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'*, from "awjalahu yūjiluhu," meaning when he frightened him. It has also been recited as "*lā ta'jal*" and "*lā tuwājal*," from "wājalahu," in the sense of "awjalahu." This story has already been mentioned in detail in Surat Hud. His saying: ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy."﴾ contains discussions:

**The first discussion:** Hamzah recited "*innā nabshuruka*" with a *fatḥa* on the *nūn* and a light *bā'*, while the rest read ﴿nubashshiruka﴾ with a doubled *shīn*.

**The second discussion:** His saying ﴿Indeed, we give you good tidings﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) in the sense of giving a reason for the prohibition of fear. The meaning is: you are in the position of one who is secure and receives good tidings, so do not fear.

**The third discussion:** His saying ﴿Indeed, we give you good tidings of a knowing boy﴾: they gave him good tidings of two matters. One of them is that the child is a male, and the other is that he will become knowing. They differed over the interpretation of "knowing" (*'alīm*). It was said: they gave him good tidings of his prophethood after him. It was also said: they gave him good tidings that he would be knowing of the religion. Then Allah, may He be exalted, related about Ibrahim, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me? Then of what do you give good tidings?﴾ So the meaning of "*'alā*" here is for circumstance, that is, the state of old age. His saying ﴿Then of what do you give good tidings?﴾ contains two issues:

**The first issue:** The word *mā* here is an interrogative in the sense of amazement, as if he said: "By what wonder do you give me good tidings?"

If it is said: there are two difficulties in the verse:

The first: How could he regard Allah's power to create a child from him in old age as improbable, when denying Allah's power in this context is disbelief?

The second: How could he say ﴿Then of what do you give good tidings?﴾ when they had already stated what they gave him good tidings of, and what is the benefit of this question? The judge (al-Qadi) said: The best of what has been said in answer to this is that he wanted to know whether He, may He be exalted, would give him a child while keeping him in the state of old age, or would turn him into a youth and then give him a child. The reason for this question is that the custom is that a child does not come about in the state of complete old age, but only in the state of youth.

If it is said: if the meaning of the speech is as you have mentioned, then why did they say: ﴿We have given you good tidings in truth, so do not be of those who despair﴾?

We say: They clarified that Allah, may He be exalted, gave him good tidings of a child while keeping him in the state of old age. His saying ﴿so do not be of those who despair﴾ does not indicate that he was in that state, as evidenced by the fact that in their answer to him they stated explicitly what indicates he was not in that state, when he said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾ There is another answer too: when a person has a very great desire for something, and the time in which he strongly expects that thing to be realized has passed, then when he is given good tidings of its realization after that, his joy and happiness become great, and that strong joy becomes overwhelming to him and removes the strength of his understanding and intelligence. So perhaps he speaks disjointed words in that joy at that time. It has also been said: he savored that good news, so he may repeat the question to hear that good news once more, twice, and more, seeking enjoyment in hearing that good news, and seeking increased reassurance and certainty, like His saying: ﴿but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. It has also been said: he asked, "Are you giving me good tidings by the command of Allah, or from your own selves and your own effort?"

As for the *kasra* with doubling, its underlying form is *tubashshirūnanī*, with the *nūn* of the plural assimilated into the *nūn* of the first person pronoun. As for the *kasra* with lightening, it is based on deleting the *nūn* of the plural because of the dislike of two similar letters together and seeking lightness. Abu Hatim said: Nafi' deleted the *yā'* along with the *nūn*. He said: The deletion of two letters is not permissible. It was answered: he deleted only one letter, which is the *nūn* that marks the nominative case. And also because the deletion of two letters is permissible; Allah, may He be exalted, said in one place ﴿and do not be﴾ (wa lā taku) and in another place ﴿and do not be﴾ (wa lā takun). First: that one ignores that He is capable of it.

Second: that one ignores that He knows the servant's need for it.

Third: that one ignores that He is exempt from stinginess, need, and ignorance. All these matters are causes of straying. For this reason He said: ﴿And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?﴾

This is indicated by their agreement on His saying: ﴿after they had despaired﴾ [al-Shura: 28]. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 57–61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals,"﴾ ﴿except the family of Lut; indeed, we will surely save them all,﴾ ﴿except his wife. We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind.﴾

In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿What is your business?﴾ is a question about the purpose for which Allah sent them. Al-khatb (business), al-sha'n (affair) and al-amr (matter) are synonymous, except that the word khatb is more indicative of the gravity of the situation.

If it is said: when the angels gave him the good news of a learned boy, how then did he say to them afterwards, ﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾

We say: there are several answers to this:

The first: al-Asamm said: its meaning is, "What is the matter toward which you have directed yourselves, other than the glad tidings?"

The second: al-Qadi said: he knew that if the complete purpose were the delivery of the glad tidings, one angel would have been sufficient. When he saw a group of angels, he knew that they had another aim beyond delivering the glad tidings, so he rightly said: ﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾

The third: It may be said that they said: "We give you the good news of a learned boy," in the context of removing fear and apprehension. Do you not see that when Abraham, upon him be peace, became afraid, they said to him: "Do not fear; we give you the good news of a learned boy"? Had the complete purpose of their coming been the mention of that glad tiding, they would have mentioned it at the very first moment they entered upon him. Since the matter was not so, Abraham, upon him be peace, knew by this means that their coming was not merely for this glad tiding but for another purpose, so he rightly asked them about that purpose, saying: ﴿What is your business, O messengers?﴾

Then Allah relates of the angels that they said: ﴿Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals﴾. They confined themselves to this much because Abraham, upon him be peace, knew that when angels are sent to criminals, it is for their destruction and eradication. Also, their saying: ﴿except the family of Lut; indeed, we will surely save them all﴾ indicates that the purpose of that sending was the destruction of the people.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except the family of Lut﴾, what is meant by the family of Lut is his followers who were upon his religion.

If it is said: is His saying ﴿except the family of Lut﴾ an exceptive that is disjunctive (munqati') or connected (muttasil)?

We say: the author of al-Kashshaf said: if this exception is an exception from (people), it is disjunctive, because the people are described as being criminals, and the family of Lut were not criminals, so the two kinds differ, and therefore the exception must be disjunctive. If it is an exception from the pronoun in (criminals), it is connected, as if it were said: "to a people who have all committed crime except the family of Lut alone," as He said: ﴿We found in it no house except one of the submitters﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 36]. Then the author of al-Kashshaf said: the meaning differs according to the difference of these two readings, because the family of Lut, in the disjunctive reading, are excluded from the ruling of being sent, since on this assumption the angels were sent to the criminal people specifically and were not sent to the family of Lut at all; whereas in the connected reading the angels were sent to them all, to destroy these and to save those. As for His saying: ﴿indeed, we will surely save them all﴾, know that Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "munjuhum" with a light (unshaddened) jim, while the rest read it shaddened, and both are two dialects.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except his wife﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: this is an exception from the pronoun in the phrase ﴿to save them﴾, and it is not of the type of an exception from an exception, because an exception from an exception occurs only where the ruling is one and the same, as if it were said: "We destroyed them except the family of Lut except his wife," or as when a divorcer says to his wife: "You are divorced three times except two except one," or as when one who acknowledges a debt to a person says: "ten dirhams except three except one dirham." But in this verse the two rulings differ, because His saying ﴿except the family of Lut﴾ is linked to His saying ﴿we were sent﴾ or to His saying ﴿criminals﴾, while His saying ﴿except his wife﴾ is linked to His saying ﴿to save them﴾; so how can this be an exception from an exception?

As for His saying: ﴿We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: know that the meaning of taqdir (decreeing) in the language is making a thing equal to the measure of another. It is said: "Measure this thing by this," i.e., make it according to its measure; and Allah decreed the sustenance, i.e., made it according to the measure of sufficiency. Then taqdir is interpreted as qada' (decree), so it is said: "Allah decreed such-and-such upon him," and "He measured it upon him," i.e., made it according to the measure that suffices in good and evil. It was said that the meaning of ﴿qaddarna﴾ is "we wrote," az-Zajjaj said: "we arranged," and it was said: "we decided," and all of these are close in meaning.

The second issue: Abu Bakr, from Asim, read "qadarna" with a light dal here and in an-Naml, while the rest read both with shadda. al-Wahidi said: it is said qaddartu ash-shay' and qadartu, and from it is the reading of Ibn Kathir: (We have decreed death among you) [al-Waqi'ah: 60] lightly, and the reading of al-Kisa'i: (and He who decreed and then guided) [al-A'la: 3]. Then he said: the shaddened form in this meaning is more common in usage, due to His saying: ﴿and He decreed therein its sustenance﴾ [Fussilat: 10] and His saying: ﴿and He created everything and decreed for it a decree﴾ [al-Furqan: 2].

The third issue: One may ask: why did the angels attribute the act of decreeing to themselves, when it belongs to Allah, exalted is He? Why did they not say, "Allah, exalted is He, decreed"?

The answer: they mentioned this expression because of the nearness and special relation they have with Allah, exalted is He, just as the close companions of a king say, "We have arranged such-and-such, and we have commanded such-and-such," while the one who arranges and commands is the king, not they. They intend by mentioning this speech only to show the special relation they have with that king. So it is likewise here; and Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿that she is among those who remain behind﴾ is in the position of an object. The meaning is: "We decreed that she would be left behind, remaining with those who remain until they perish as they perish, and that she would not be among those who remain with Lut and thus reach salvation." And Allah knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 62–64:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed you are a people unknown to me."﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to doubt."﴾ ﴿And we have come to you with the truth, and indeed we are truthful.﴾

Know that when the angels gave Ibrahim (Abraham) the good news of a son and informed him that they had been sent to punish a criminal people, they then went after that to Lut (Lot) and his family. Lut and his people did not know that they were angels of Allah, and so he said to them: ﴿Indeed you are a people unknown to me.﴾ Regarding its interpretation there are several views:

The first: he described them as "unknown" only because he (peace be upon him) did not recognise them. When they rushed upon him, he disapproved of this and feared that they had entered upon him for an evil purpose they intended to carry out against him, so he said this statement.

The second: they were young men, beardless and of handsome faces, and he feared that his people would rush upon him because of their demand (for them), so he said this statement.

The third: the word *nakirah* (unknown) is the opposite of *ma'rifah* (known). So his saying ﴿Indeed you are a people unknown to me﴾ means: I do not know you, nor do I know which peoples you are from, nor for what purpose you have entered upon me. At this statement the angels said: ﴿Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to doubt﴾, meaning: the punishment which they used to doubt would descend. Then they confirmed what they had mentioned with their saying: ﴿And we have come to you with the truth﴾. Al-Kalbi said: "with the punishment." It was also said: "with certainty and a settled matter about which there is no doubt, which is the punishment of those peoples." Then they emphasised this emphasis with their saying: ﴿and indeed we are truthful.﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verse 65–71:

Page 160
﴿And We decreed to him this matter: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning.﴾

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So set out with your family in the last part of the night, and follow behind them, and let none of you look back, and proceed to where you are commanded.﴾ ﴿And We decreed to him this matter: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning.﴾

It was recited "fa-asri" (فَأسْرِ) with a cut hamza and with a connected hamza, from asra and sara. The author of al-Kashshaf related from the author of al-Iqlid "fasir" (فَسِرْ), from al-sayr (travel). Al-qit' (القِطْع) is the last part of the night. The poet said:

Open the door and look at the stars, how much of the dark night remains upon us.

His statement ﴿and follow behind them﴾ means: follow the traces of your daughters and your family.

His statement ﴿and let none of you look back﴾ has several benefits:

First: so that none of you lags behind and is struck by the punishment.

Second: so that he does not see the great calamity that will descend upon them.

Third: its meaning is haste and abandoning concern for what was left behind, as you say: "Go about your business and do not turn aside for anything."

Fourth: if any property of his remained in that place, he should never return on its account at all.

His statement ﴿and proceed to where you are commanded﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means Syria. al-Mufaddal said: to where Gabriel tells you, because Gabriel, peace be upon him, commanded them to proceed to a specific town whose people had not done the like of the deed of the people of Lot.

His statement ﴿And We decreed to him﴾: he made qadaynā (قَضَيْنا) transitive with ilā (إلى) because it was taken to imply awhā-nā (أوْحَيْنا, "We revealed"), as if it were said: "And We revealed it to him as a decree, final and settled." A parallel is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Isra: 4] and His statement: ﴿Then carry out your decision against me﴾ [Yunus: 71]. Then after that he explained the final decree with His statement: ﴿that the last remnant of these would be cut off﴾. In its being vague at first and then explained second there is an exaltation and magnification of the matter.

al-Aʿmash recited "inna" (إنَّ) with a kasra, as a fresh sentence, as if a speaker had said: "Inform us about that matter," and it was answered: "Indeed the last remnant of these..." In the recitation of Ibn Masʿud: "wa-qulna: 'anna dabira ha'ula'" (وقُلْنا: أنَّ دابِرَ هَؤُلاءِ). Dabir means the last of them, meaning they will be uprooted down to the last of them, until none of them remains. His statement ﴿muṣbiḥīn﴾ means: at the time of the appearance of dawn.

[Page 161]

Know that by "the people of the city" is meant the people of Lot. The verse gives no indication of the place they came to, but the story indicates that they came to Lot's house. It has been said that when the angels were at the height of beauty, their news spread until it reached the people of Lot. It has also been said that Lot's wife informed them of this. In sum, the people said: "Three beardless youths have stayed with Lot, and we have never seen faces more radiant or forms more handsome than theirs." So they went to Lot's house seeking those beardless youths. Al-istibshar (rejoicing) means showing joy.

When they approached his guests, Lot spoke two statements.

The first statement: he said, ﴿Indeed these are my guests, so do not disgrace me.﴾ One says fadahahu, yafdahuhu, fadhan and fadihah, meaning he revealed something about him that brings shame upon him. The meaning is that a guest must be honored, so if you target them with evil, that is an insult to me. Then he reinforced this by saying, ﴿And fear Allah and do not humiliate me.﴾ They answered him, ﴿Did we not forbid you from [taking on] the people of the worlds?﴾ The meaning is: Did we not forbid you from speaking to us on behalf of anyone among the people whom we intend to approach for indecency?

The second statement, from what Lot said, is his words: ﴿These are my daughters, if you are going to act.﴾ It has been said that by "my daughters" he meant his own daughters. It has also been said that he meant the women of his people, because the messenger of a community is like a father to them. This is like the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. It is also in the recitation of Ubayy: "and he is a father to them." The discussion of these matters has already been treated exhaustively in Surat Hud, peace be upon him.

As for His words: ﴿By your life, indeed they were, in their intoxication, wandering blindly﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: al-'amr and al-'umr are the same word. A man was named 'Umar as an omen that he would survive. From this is the saying of Ibn Ahmar:

"Youth has gone, and life has worn out."

One says 'ammara al-rajul, yu'ammiru, 'amran and 'umran. When they swear by it, they say la'amruka and 'amruka, pronouncing the 'ayn with a fatha only. Al-Zajjaj said: this is because the fatha is lighter for them, and since they frequently swear with la'amri and la'amruka, they adopted the lighter form.

The second issue: concerning His words ﴿By your life, indeed they were, in their intoxication, wandering blindly﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: the meaning is that the angels said to Lot, peace be upon him: ﴿By your life, indeed they were, in their intoxication, wandering blindly﴾, that is, in their misguidance they are bewildered. How, then, would they accept your words or heed your advice?

The second: the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted swore by his life, and He swore by no one else's life. This indicates that he is the most noble of creation before Allah the Exalted. The grammarians said: the word ﴿la'amruka﴾ is in the nominative as a mubtada' (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is omitted. The meaning is: "By your life is my oath." The predicate is omitted because the sentence itself indicates it. In the case of oaths, the verb is omitted, as in: "By Allah, I will do it," meaning "I swear by Allah," and it is omitted because the addressee knows that you are swearing.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So the Shout seized them﴾, that is, the shout of Jibril, peace be upon him. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the verse does not indicate that this shout was the shout of Jibril, peace be upon him. If that is established by strong evidence, it may be affirmed; otherwise the verse only indicates that a great, destructive shout came upon them.

As for His words ﴿at sunrise﴾, one says sharraqa al-sharriq, yusharriqu, shuruqan, for everything that rises from the east. From this is the expression ma dharra sharriq, meaning "no riser has risen." So ﴿mushriqin﴾ means entering into sunrise. One says ashraqa al-rajul when he enters the time of sunrise, which is the rising of the sun.

Know that the verse indicates that Allah the Exalted punished them with three kinds of punishment:

The first: the terrible, horrifying shout.

The second: He made its highest part its lowest.

The third: He rained upon them stones of baked clay (sijjil).

All these circumstances have already been explained in Surat Hud.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ One says tawassamtu fi fulanin khayran, meaning I saw in him a trace of it and I perceived it in him. The exegetes (mufassirin) differed in their expressions regarding the meaning of al-mutawassimin (those who discern). It has been said: those who perceive, those who look, those who reflect, those who take lessons, and those who see clearly. Al-Zajjaj said: the true meaning of al-mutawassimin in the language is those who are firm in their looking until they recognize the mark of a thing, its description, and its sign. The mutawassim is the one who looks at the distinguishing mark that indicates something. You say: "I discerned such-and-such in so-and-so," meaning I recognized the mark of that and its characteristic in him.

Then He said: ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains.﴾ The pronoun in His words ﴿and indeed it﴾ refers to the city of the people of Lot, which was already mentioned in His words: ﴿And the people of the city came﴾ [al-Hijr: 67]. His words ﴿on a road that remains﴾ mean that these towns and the traces of Allah's wrath and anger that appeared in them are on a road that remains, firm, not effaced and not concealed. Those who travel from the Hijaz to Syria see them.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾ That is, everyone who believes in Allah and affirms the prophets and messengers knows that this happened only because Allah the Exalted took vengeance for His prophets upon those ignorant people. As for those who do not believe in Allah, they attribute it to the events and occurrences of the world, and to the occurrence of planetary conjunctions and celestial alignments. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 78–84:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿So We took retribution from them. And indeed, they both are on an evident highway.﴾

Know that this is the third of the stories mentioned in this surah.

The first of them is the story of Adam and Iblis.

The second is the story of Ibrahim and Lut.

The third is this story.

The companions of the thicket (Ashab al-Aykah) are the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. They were people of thickets, and they denied Shu'ayb, so Allah the Exalted destroyed them with the punishment of the Day of the Canopy (Yawm al-Zullah). Allah the Exalted mentioned their story in Surah al-Shu'ara'. Al-Aykah means dense-growing trees. It is said: aykah and ayk, like shajarah and shajar. Ibn Abbas said: al-Ayk is the thorn-tree of the muql (muql tree). Al-Kalbi said: al-Aykah is a thicket. Al-Zajjaj said: they were the people of a place that had trees. Al-Wahidi said: the meaning of "in" and the "lam" is for emphasis (tawkid), and "in" here is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah). His saying, ﴿So We took retribution from them﴾: the exegetes said: the heat intensified upon them for days, then the place blazed with fire over them, and they all perished to the last one. His saying, ﴿And indeed, they both﴾, concerning it there are two opinions:

The first opinion: what is meant is the towns of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, and the Aykah.

The second opinion: the pronoun refers to the Aykah and Madyan, because Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent to both of them. When he mentioned the Aykah, mention of it indicated Madyan, so he used the dual pronoun for both of them. His saying, ﴿on an evident highway﴾ means: on a clear path. Al-imam is the name of that which is followed. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the path was only called imam because it is traveled and followed. Ibn Qutaybah said: because the traveler follows it until he reaches the place he intends. His saying, ﴿evident﴾ may mean that it is evident in itself, and it may mean that it is evident to others, because the path guides to the destination.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, the companions of the thicket were wrongdoers﴾ ﴿So We took retribution from them. And indeed, they both are on an evident highway.﴾

The second is the story of Ibrahim and Lut.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 85–86:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they turned away from them﴾ ﴿And they used to hew out houses from the mountains, secure﴾ ﴿So the Shout seized them at morning time﴾ ﴿So what they had earned did not avail them﴾.

This is the fourth story, and it is the story of Salih. The exegetes said: al-Hijr is the name of a valley in which Thamud used to dwell. And His saying, ﴿the messengers﴾, is meant to refer to Salih alone. Perhaps the people were Brahmins who denied all the messengers. His saying, ﴿We gave them Our signs﴾, means the she-camel. There were many signs in the she-camel, such as her emergence from the rock, the greatness of her body, the appearance of her offspring at the time of her emergence, and the abundance of her milk. He attributed the giving to them, although the she-camel was a sign for Salih, because she was the sign of their messenger. His saying, ﴿but they turned away from them﴾, indicates that reflection and reasoning are obligatory, and that blind imitation (taqlid) is blameworthy. His saying, ﴿and they used to hew out from the mountains﴾: we have already mentioned the manner of that hewing in Surat al-A'raf. His saying, ﴿secure﴾, means secure from the punishment of God. Al-Farra' said: ﴿secure﴾ means secure from their roof falling upon them. His saying, ﴿So what they had earned did not avail them﴾, means: what they did of hewing those mountains and gathering those possessions did not repel from them harm and affliction. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed, the Hour is coming. So forgive with gracious forgiveness﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the Knowing﴾.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He destroyed the disbelievers, it is as if it were said: how does destruction and punishment befit the Merciful, the Generous? He answered this by saying: I only created creation so that they would be occupied with worship and obedience. So when they abandon it and turn away from it, it is required by wisdom that they be destroyed and the face of the earth be purified of them. This arrangement is good, but it only holds according to the view of the Mu'tazilah. Al-Jubba'i said: the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth, and by the fact that the truth is not falsehood, because everything done in falsehood, and whose act is intended to be falsehood, is not truth and is not created in truth. In this is the refutation of the doctrine of the Jabriyyah, who claim that most of what God, exalted is He, created between the heavens and the earth, such as disbelief and sins, is falsehood.

Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) said: this verse indicates that He, glorified is He, is the Creator of all the actions of the servants, because it indicates that He, glorified is He, is the Creator of the heavens and the earth and of everything between them. There is no doubt that the actions of the servants are between them, so it is necessary that their Creator be God, glorified is He. There is another aspect in the arrangement of the verse, namely that the purpose of mentioning these stories is to make God, exalted is He, strengthen Muhammad (ﷺ) in patience against the folly of his people. For when he hears that earlier nations treated the prophets of God, exalted is He, with such corrupt treatment, it becomes easier for Muhammad (ﷺ) to bear those follies. Then, when He, exalted is He, explained that He sent punishment upon the earlier nations, at this point He said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And indeed, the Hour is coming﴾, and that God will avenge you against your enemies therein and will recompense you and them for your good deeds and their evil deeds. For He did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth, justice and equity, so how does it befit His wisdom to neglect your affair? Then, when He, exalted is He, had made him patient under the harm of his people, He encouraged him after that to pardon their evil deeds, saying: ﴿So forgive with gracious forgiveness﴾, that is: turn away from them, and bear what you encounter from them with a gracious turning away, with forbearance and overlooking.

It was said: it is abrogated by the verse of the sword, but this is far-fetched, because the purpose of that is to show good character, pardon and forgiveness, so how could it become abrogated?

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the Knowing﴾. Its meaning: He created creation with the difference of their natures and the variation of their conditions, while knowing that they are so. And if that is the case, then He created them with this variation and with knowledge of that variation. As for the view of the People of the Sunnah, it is due to pure will and volition. As for the view of the Mu'tazilah, it is for the sake of benefit and wisdom. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 87–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [al-mathani] and the Great Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Do not strain your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to of them, [as] pairs, nor grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had made him patient over the harm of his people, and commanded him to forgive with gracious forgiveness, He followed that with mention of the great blessings with which God, exalted is He, singled out Muhammad (ﷺ), because when a person remembers the abundance of God's blessings upon him, forgiving and overlooking becomes easy for him. In the verse there are issues:

The first issue: Know that His saying ﴿seven [sab'an]﴾ may mean seven of the verses, or seven of the surahs, or seven of the benefits. The wording contains nothing that specifies one of these. As for al-mathani, it is a plural form whose singular is mathnah, and the mathnah is everything that is doubled (yuthna), meaning made into two. It derives from your saying: "I doubled [thanaytu] the thing" when you bent it or joined another to it. From this comes the saying that the two knees and the two elbows of a beast are mathani, because they are bent with the thigh and the upper arm, and the mathani of a valley are its bends.

Having understood this, we say: "seven of the mathani" means seven things of the kind that are doubled. There is no doubt that this quantity is general (mujmal), and there is no way to specify it except by a separate proof. People have various views on it:

The first, which is the view of most exegetes: it is the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah). This is the view of 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Fatihah and said: "It is the seven mathani." Abu Hurayrah narrated it. The reason this name applies to the Fatihah is that it consists of seven verses. As for the reason it is called al-mathani, there are several explanations:

The first: it is doubled in every prayer, in the sense that it is recited in every rak'ah.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: it is called mathani because what is recited with it is doubled after it.

The third: the verses of the Fatihah are called mathani because it is divided into two halves. The evidence for this is what is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God, exalted is He, says: I have divided the prayer between Me and My servant into two halves," and the hadith is well known.

The fourth: it is called mathani because it has two parts, praise (thana') and supplication (du'a'). Also, its first half is the right of lordship (rububiyyah), which is praise, and its second half is the right of servitude ('ubudiyyah), which is supplication.

The fifth: the Fatihah was called al-mathani because it was revealed twice: once in Makkah, at the beginning of what was revealed of the Qur'an, and once in Madinah.

The sixth: it was called al-mathani because its words are doubled, such as: "the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," "You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help," "Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour," and in the reading of 'Umar: "not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray."

[Page 165]

The seventh: al-Zajjaj said: the Fatihah was called al-mathani because it includes praise of God, exalted is He, which is the praising of God, His unity and His dominion.

* * *

Know that if we take His saying ﴿seven of the mathani﴾ to refer to the surah of al-Fatihah, then there are rulings here:

(The first ruling)
Al-Qadi narrated from Abu Bakr al-Asamm that he said: Ibn Mas'ud used to write the Opening of the Book in his codex, but he considered that it was not part of the Qur'an. I say: perhaps his argument in this is that since it has been established that the seven mathani is the Fatihah, and God, exalted is He, has then joined the seven mathani to the Qur'an by conjunction, and what is conjoined must be different from what it is conjoined to, it follows that the seven mathani must be other than the Qur'an. However, this is problematic in light of His saying: ﴿And [mention] when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 7], and likewise His saying: ﴿His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. The opponent may answer that it is not far-fetched to mention the whole and then to conjoin to it the mention of some of its parts and divisions, because it is the most noble of its divisions. But when one thing is mentioned and then another thing is conjoined to it, the first mentioned must be different from the second mentioned. Here He mentioned the seven mathani and then conjoined to it the Great Qur'an, so difference must exist. The correct answer is: part of a thing is different from its whole, so why would this degree of difference not suffice for the goodness of the conjunction? And God knows best.

(The second ruling)
Since the meaning of His saying ﴿seven of the mathani﴾ is the Fatihah, this indicates that this surah is the most excellent of the surahs of the Qur'an, for two reasons:

One: that singling it out for mention, although it is a part of the parts of the Qur'an, must be because of its being specially distinguished by greater nobility and virtue.

The second: that when God, exalted is He, revealed it twice, this indicates an increase in its excellence and nobility.

Given this, we say: since we have seen that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) persisted in reciting it in all the prayers throughout his life, and never substituted another surah for it in any of the prayers, this indicates that it is obligatory for the responsible person to recite it in his prayer, and not to substitute the rest of the verses of the Qur'an in its place, and to beware of this substitution, for in it there is a great danger. And God knows best.

The second explanation of His saying ﴿seven of the mathani﴾: they are the seven long surahs (al-tiwal). This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr in some narrations, and Mujahid. They are: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal and al-Tawbah together. They said: these surahs were called mathani because the obligations, the limits, the parables and the lessons are repeated in them. Al-Rabi' rejected this view and said: this verse is Meccan, and most of these seven surahs are Madinan, and nothing of them was revealed in Makkah, so how is it possible to apply this verse to them?

Some people answered this objection by saying: God revealed the entire Qur'an to the lowest heaven, then He revealed it to His Prophet from there in installments. So when He sent it down to the lowest heaven, and decreed its being sent down to him, it is among what He gave him, even if it had not yet been revealed to him.

One may say: God said ﴿We have certainly given you seven of the mathani﴾, and this statement is only true if that thing reached Muhammad (ﷺ). As for what was sent down to the lowest heaven and had not yet reached Muhammad (peace be upon him), this statement is not true of it. The second: that when God, exalted is He, revealed it twice, this indicates an increase in its excellence and nobility.

Given this, we say: since we have seen that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) persisted in reciting it in all the prayers throughout his life, and never substituted another surah for it in any of the prayers, this indicates that it is obligatory for the responsible person to recite it in his prayer, and not to substitute the rest of the verses of the Qur'an in its place, and to beware of this substitution, for in it there is a great danger. And God knows best.

The second explanation of His saying ﴿seven of the mathani﴾: they are the seven long surahs (al-tiwal). This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, Sa'id ibn Jubayr in some narrations, and Mujahid. They are: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal and al-Tawbah together. They said: these surahs were called mathani because the obligations, the limits, the parables and the lessons are repeated in them. Al-Rabi' rejected this view and said: this verse is Meccan, and most of these seven surahs are Madinan, and nothing of them was revealed in Makkah, so how is it possible to apply this verse to them?

Some people answered this objection by saying: God revealed the entire Qur'an to the lowest heaven, then He revealed it to His Prophet from there in installments. So when He sent it down to the lowest heaven, and decreed its being sent down to him, it is among what He gave him, even if it had not yet been revealed to him.

One may say: God said ﴿We have certainly given you seven of the mathani﴾, and this statement is only true if that thing reached Muhammad (ﷺ). As for what was sent down to the lowest heaven and had not yet reached Muhammad (peace be upon him), this statement is not true of it. As for their saying that when God decreed its being sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), this was treated as if it had been revealed to him, this too is weak, because treating what was not revealed to him as if it were revealed to him is contrary to the apparent meaning.

The third explanation of the seven mathani: they are the surahs that are shorter than the long ones and the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses), but longer than the mufassal (the short surahs at the end of the Qur'an). Some people chose this view and argued for it with what Thawban narrated: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God gave me the seven long surahs in place of the Torah, and He gave me the mi'in in place of the Gospel, and He gave me the mathani in place of the Psalms, and my Lord favoured me with the mufassal." Al-Wahidi said: the explanation for calling these surahs mathani is like the explanation for calling the long ones mathani.

I say: if this explanation is sound from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then there is no objection to it. If it is not sound, then this view is problematic, because we have shown that what is named the seven mathani must be more excellent than the rest of the surahs, and they have agreed that these surahs which they named mathani are not more excellent than others, so it is impossible to apply the seven mathani to those surahs.

The fourth view: the seven mathani is the entire Qur'an. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas in some narrations and from the view of Tawus. They said: the proof for this view is His saying: ﴿A Book similar [in its verses], oft-repeated [mutashabihan mathani]﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], so He described the whole Qur'an as mathani. Then those who held this view differed over what is meant by "seven" and what is meant by "mathani." As for "seven," they gave several explanations:

One: the Qur'an is seven sevenths.

Two: the Qur'an includes seven types of knowledge: tawhid, prophethood, the afterlife (ma'ad), divine decree (qada'), predestination (qadar), the conditions of the world, narratives, and obligations.

Three: it includes command and prohibition, information and inquiry, address, oath, and parables. As for describing the whole Qur'an as mathani, it is because it repeats within it the proofs of tawhid, prophethood and obligations. This view is also weak, because if the seven mathani meant the Qur'an, then His saying ﴿and the Great Qur'an﴾ would be the conjoining of a thing to itself, and that is not permissible.

It was answered: it is good to introduce the conjunction particle here because the two expressions differ, like the saying of the poet:

To the sovereign king of the herd, and the son of the lofty one, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd.

Know that although this is permissible because of its occurrence in this verse, the scholars have agreed that the original rule is otherwise.

The fifth view: it is permissible that "seven" means the Fatihah, because it consists of seven verses, and "mathani" means the entire Qur'an, and the meaning would be: "We have certainly given you seven verses, which are the Fatihah, and which are part of the mathani that is the Qur'an." This view is the same as the first, and the difference is only slight. And God knows best.

* * *

The second issue: the particle "min" in His saying ﴿seven of the mathani﴾. Al-Zajjaj said that it has two possibilities:

One: that it is partitive (lil-tab'id) of the Qur'an, meaning: "We have certainly given you seven verses from among the verses by which God, exalted is He, is praised, and We have given you the Great Qur'an." He said: it is also permissible that it be explanatory (silah), and the meaning would be: "We have given you seven [verses] which are the mathani," just as He said ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], meaning: avoid the idols, not that some of them are an abomination. And God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not strain your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to of them, [as] pairs﴾, know that when He made His Messenger aware of the greatness of His blessings upon him in matters related to religion, namely that He gave him seven of the mathani and the Great Qur'an, He forbade him from desiring the world, and prohibited him from straining his eyes toward it out of desire for it. Regarding straining the eyes there are several views:

The first view: it is as if it was said to him: "You have been given the Great Qur'an, so do not occupy your inner self and your thoughts by turning toward the world." From this is the hadith: "He is not of us who does not chant the Qur'an beautifully." Abu Bakr said: whoever has been given the Qur'an and then thinks that someone has been given more of this world's goods than what he has been given has belittled something great and magnified something small. It was also said: seven caravans came from some regions to the Jews of Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, containing kinds of silk, perfume, jewels and all sorts of goods. The Muslims said: "If these possessions were ours, we would be strengthened by them, and we would spend them in the way of God, exalted is He." So God, exalted is He, said: "We have given you seven verses which are better than these seven caravans."

The second view: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not strain your eyes" means: do not wish for what We have favoured anyone with of the goods of this world. Al-Wahidi confirmed this meaning and said: a person only strains his eyes toward a thing when he continues to look at it, and continuing to look at a thing indicates approval of it and longing for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not look at what was admirable among the goods of this world. It is narrated that he looked at the camels of Banu al-Mustaliq, which had become dirty with their urine and dung, so he covered himself with his garment and recited this verse. His saying "had become dirty [ 'abasat] with their urine and dung" means that their urine and dung dried on their thighs when they were left from work during the spring days, so their fat and flesh increased, and they were at their best.

The third view: some said: "Do not strain your eyes" means: do not envy anyone for what he has been given of this world. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this is far-fetched, because envy is repugnant from anyone, since it is a desire for the removal of another's blessings from him, and this is akin to an objection to God, exalted is He, and a condemnation of His judgment and decree, which is repugnant from anyone. So how could it be fitting to single out the Messenger (ﷺ) with it?

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 87–89 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿azwājan minhum﴾ (﴿kinds of them﴾). Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, categories of the disbelievers, and the zawj (pair, kind) in the language means the ṣinf (category). Then He said: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, meaning, if they do not believe, so that Islam may grow strong by their position and the believers may be revived by them. The summary is that His saying: ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given to pairs of them as enjoyment﴾ is a prohibition to him from turning toward their wealth, and His saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ is a prohibition to him from turning toward them, and from allowing them to acquire in his heart any measure or weight.

Then He said: ﴿And lower your wing for the believers﴾. Al-khafḍ (lowering) in the language means the opposite of raising (rafʿ), and from it is His saying, Exalted is He, describing the Resurrection: ﴿abasing, exalting﴾ [al-Wāqiʿah: 3], that is, it abases the people of sins and exalts the people of obedience. So al-khafḍ means placing down. The wing (janāḥ) of a person is his hand. Al-Layth said: the two hands of a person are his two wings. From it is His saying: ﴿And draw your arm close to your side from fear﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 32]. Lowering the wing is a metaphor for gentleness, kindness and humility. The intended meaning is that when He, Exalted is He, forbade him from turning toward those wealthy disbelievers, He commanded him to be humble toward the poor among the Muslims. A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 54], and He said, describing the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): ﴿hard against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fatḥ: 29].

The Exalted said: ﴿And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner,"﴾ ﴿as We sent down upon the dividers,﴾ ﴿those who made the Qur'an into fragments.﴾

Know that when the Exalted commanded His Messenger to renounce the world and to lower his wing to the believers, He commanded him to say to the people: ﴿Indeed, I﴾

﴿am the clear warner,﴾ so within his being a warner is included his being a conveyor of all the obligations, because whatever is obligatory incurs punishment for its abandonment, and whatever is forbidden incurs punishment for its commission. Thus the announcement of the occurrence of this punishment falls under the term "warner." Also included is his being an explainer of the degrees of reward and punishment, and of Paradise and Hell. Then He followed it with his being "clear" (mubīn), meaning that he comes in all of that with conclusive clarifications and complete proofs. Then He said after it: ﴿as We sent down upon the dividers,﴾ and concerning this there are two discussions.

The first discussion: they differed about who the "dividers" (al-muqtasimīn) are, and there are opinions on this.

The first opinion: Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are those who divided the roads of Mecca, barring people from believing in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and their number was close to forty. Muqātil ibn Sulaymān said: they were sixteen men whom al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah sent during the season of pilgrimage. They divided the passes and roads of Mecca, saying to whoever traveled them: "Do not be deceived by the one who comes out from among us, claiming prophethood, for he is a madman." They would turn people away from him by saying he is a sorcerer, a soothsayer, or a poet. So Allah sent down disgrace upon them, and they died the worst death. The meaning is: I warn you with the like of what befell the dividers.

The second opinion, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) in some narrations, is that the dividers are the Jews and the Christians. They differed about why Allah named them "dividers." It was said: because they made the Qur'an into fragments, believing in what agreed with the Torah and disbelieving in the rest. ʿIkrimah said: because they divided the Qur'an mockingly, so one of them would say, "Such-and-such a surah is mine," and another would say, "Such-and-such a surah is mine." Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: they divided the Qur'an, so some of them said it is sorcery, some said it is poetry, some said it is falsehood, and some said it is the fables of the ancients.

The third opinion regarding the explanation of "dividers": Ibn Zayd said: they are the people of Ṣāliḥ, who swore to one another, "We will surely attack him and his family by night," and the angels struck them with stones until they killed them. According to this view, "iqtisām" (swearing/dividing) derives from "qasam" (oath), not from "qismah" (division). This is the choice of Ibn Qutaybah.

The third discussion: His saying, ﴿as We sent down upon the dividers,﴾ requires that something be likened to that. So what is that thing?

The answer to this has two aspects.

The first aspect: the estimated sense is: "And We have certainly given you the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an, as We sent down upon the People of the Book, who are the dividers, who made the Qur'an into fragments, when in their obstinacy and ignorance they said: 'Part of it is true, agreeing with the Torah and the Gospel, and part of it is false, contrary to them,' and so they divided it into true and false."

If it is said: On this view, how did His saying, ﴿Do not extend your eyes...﴾ up to its end, come between the compared and the thing compared to?

We say: Since that was a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding their denial and hostility, it intervened with what is the basis of the meaning of consolation, namely the prohibition against turning one's attention to their worldly life and grieving over their disbelief.

The second aspect: that this statement is connected to His saying, ﴿And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner,"﴾.

Know that this aspect is not complete except by one of two matters: either the necessity of an implied elision (iḍmār) or the necessity of an omission (ḥadhf). As for the implied elision, the sense would be: "Indeed, I am the clear warner of a punishment like what We sent down upon the dividers." In this aspect, the object is omitted, and it is the compared, which is indicated by the thing compared to. This is like when you say: "I saw someone like the moon in beauty," meaning, "I saw a person like the moon in

**Page 170**

beauty."

As for the omission, it is that one says: the kāf (like) is an extra omitted particle, and the sense is: "Indeed, I am the clear warner of what We sent down upon the dividers." The addition of the kāf has a parallel in His saying, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shūrā: 11], where the sense is "There is nothing like Him." Some have said: there is no need for either implied elision or omission. The sense is: "Indeed, I am the warner," that is, "I warn the Quraysh with the like of the punishment We sent down upon the dividers."

His saying, ﴿those who made the Qur'an into fragments,﴾ has two discussions.

The first discussion: regarding this word there are two views.

The first: that it is an attribute of "the dividers."

The second: that it is a subject (mubtadaʾ), whose predicate is His saying, ﴿We will surely question them﴾, and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The second discussion: the lexicographers mentioned two views regarding the singular of ʿiḍīn.

The first view: its singular is ʿiḍah, like ʿizzah, birah, and thibah. Its origin is ʿuḍwah, from ʿaḍaytu al-shayʾ, meaning "I divided the thing," and every piece is an ʿiḍah. It is among those words from which a wāw has been dropped, which is the lām of the verb. Al-taʿḍiyah means dividing into parts and separating. It is said: "ʿaḍḍaytu al-jazūr and al-shāh taʿḍiyah," when you make them into limbs and divide them. In a hadith: "There is no taʿḍiyah in inheritance except in what admits division." That is: there is no partitioning in what does not admit division, such as a jewel or a sword. So His saying, ﴿made the Qur'an ʿiḍīn﴾ means: they divided it into parts, saying: sorcery, poetry, the fables of the ancients, and fabrication.

The second view: its singular is ʿiḍah, and its origin is ʿiḍahah. They found the joining of two hāʾs burdensome, so they said ʿiḍah, as they said shifah, while the original is shifahah, as evidenced by their saying: shāfahtu mushāfahah, and sanah, whose origin in some opinions is sanhah. It is derived from ʿiḍah in the sense of slander, and from it the hadith: "Beware of ʿiḍah." Ibn al-Sikkīt said: ʿiḍah is when a person slanders another and says about him what is not in him. This is the view of al-Khalīl as transmitted by al-Layth from him. According to this view, the meaning of His saying, ﴿made the Qur'an ʿiḍīn﴾ is: they made it fabricated. The word ʿiḍah was pluralized as a masculine rational plural (ʿiḍīn), because of the deletion that affected it, so the sound plural with wāw and nūn was made a substitute for the deletion that affected it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 15, verses 92–96:**

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾ ﴿So declare what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾ ﴿who set up with Allah another god. But they will come to know﴾.

On this verse there are several issues.

**First issue:** His statement, ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾, may refer to the dividers (al-muqtasimin) who made the Qur'an into fragments (ʿidin), because returning the pronoun to the nearest antecedent is preferable. The meaning would then be that He, the Exalted, swore by Himself that He would question these dividers about what they used to say concerning the division of the Qur'an, and about all their other sins. It may also refer to all the responsible (mukallafin), because their mention preceded in His statement, ﴿Say: "I am the clear warner"﴾, meaning to all creation. The mention of believers and the mention of disbelievers has also preceded, so His statement, ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾, returns to all of them. There is no sense in the view of those who say that questioning is only about disbelief or only about belief. Rather, questioning applies to both and to all deeds, because the wording is general and encompasses all.

If it is asked: how is His statement, ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them﴾, reconciled with His statement, ﴿So on that Day, no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ (al-Rahman: 39)? The scholars answered this in several ways.

**The first way:** Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they will not be asked a question of inquiry (suʾal al-istifham), because He, the Exalted, has full knowledge of all their deeds. Rather, they will be asked a question of reproach (suʾal al-taqriʿ), and it will be said to them: "Why did you do such-and-such?"

It may be said: this answer is weak, because if the intended meaning of His statement, ﴿So on that Day, no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾, were a question of inquiry, then specifying this negation with the words "on that Day" would have no benefit, since such a question directed at Allah, the Exalted, is impossible at all times.

**The second way** of answering is to direct the negation to some times and the affirmation to another time, because the Day of Resurrection is a long day.

It may be said: His statement, ﴿So on that Day, no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾, is an explicit declaration that questioning does not take place on that Day. So if questioning took place in any part of that Day, a contradiction would result.

**The third way:** We say that His statement, ﴿So on that Day, no man or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ (al-Rahman: 39), conveys general negation, while His statement, ﴿By your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾, returns to the dividers, and this is specific. There is no doubt that the specific takes precedence over the general.

As for His statement, ﴿So declare what you are commanded﴾, know that the meaning of al-sadʿ (declaring/splitting) in the language is cleaving and separating. Ibn al-Sikkit recited the verse of Jarir:

*"This is the caliph, so be content with what he has decided for you in truth, which separates (yasdaʿu) whatever in it is injustice."*

He said: yasdaʿu means "separates." Tasadda'a al-qawm means the people scattered. From this is His statement, ﴿That Day they will scatter (yassaddaʿun)﴾. Al-Farra' said: they will disperse. Al-sadʿ in a glass vessel means a clear break. I say: perhaps the pain in the head was called ṣudaʿ (headache) because at that pain the skull seems to be splitting. It is said: "ṣadaʿa bil-ḥujjah" when one speaks with it openly, like your saying ṣarrraḥa bihā (he stated it clearly). In reality this also returns to the meaning of splitting and separating.

As for His statement, ﴿what you are commanded﴾, there are two views:

**The first:** that *ma* is in the sense of *alladhi* (that which), meaning: what you are commanded with of the laws (sharaʾiʿ). The preposition has been omitted, as in the verse:

*"I commanded you the good, so do what you were commanded with."*

**The second:** that *ma* is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), meaning: declare your command and your affair.

They said: the Prophet ﷺ remained hidden until this verse was revealed.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and turn away from the polytheists﴾, meaning: do not be concerned with them, and do not pay attention to their blaming you for making the call public. Some said: this is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of fighting (al-qital). This view is weak, because the meaning of this turning away is abandoning concern for them, so it is not abrogated.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾. It is said: they were five men from the polytheists: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, ʿAdi ibn Qays, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth. Jibril said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "I have been commanded to suffice you against them." He pointed to the heel of al-Walid, and he passed by an arrow-maker, and an arrow caught on his garment, but he did not bend down out of pride in it, so it struck a vein in his heel and cut it, and he died. He pointed to the sole of al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il's foot, and a thorn entered it, and he said: "I have been bitten! I have been bitten!" His foot swelled until it became like a millstone, and he died. He pointed to the eyes of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he went blind. He pointed to the nose of ʿAdi ibn Qays, and he expelled pus and died. He pointed to al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth while he was sitting under the root of a tree, and he began to strike his head against the tree and to strike his face with thorns, until he died.

Know that the exegetes disagreed about the number of these mockers, about their names, and about the manner of their mockery. There is no need for any of these details. The known matter is that they were a class that had power, strength, and leadership, because such people are the ones who are able to display this kind of foolishness toward a figure such as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, given his high rank and great station. The Qur'an indicates that Allah, the Exalted, annihilated them, destroyed them, and removed their scheming. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 15, verses 97–99:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is distressed by what they say.﴾ ﴿So exalt your Lord with His praise and be among those who prostrate.﴾ ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty (al-yaqin).﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that his people mock him, especially those who divided the Qur'an (al-muqtasimun) and those who ridicule (al-mustahzi'un), He said to him: ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is distressed by what they say.﴾ This is because human nature and the human temperament necessitate that. At this point He said to him: ﴿So exalt your Lord with His praise﴾, commanding him with four things: glorification (tasbih), praise (tahmid), prostration (sujud), and worship (ibadah). People differed over how devotion to these acts became a cause for the removal of constriction of the heart and sorrow. The knowers who verify (al-arifun al-muhaqqiqun) said: When a person occupies himself with these types of worship, the lights of the realm of lordship (alam al-rububiyyah) are revealed to him. Once that unveiling occurs, the world becomes entirely insignificant, and when it becomes insignificant, the loss and the attainment of it weigh lightly on the heart: he does not feel desolate at its loss, nor find rest in its attainment. At that point sorrow and grief depart. The Mu'tazilah said: Whoever believes that God, exalted is He, is free from ugly acts, hardship becomes easy for him to bear, for he knows that He is just, exalted above inflicting hardships upon him without purpose or benefit, and then his heart is at ease. The People of the Sunnah said: When some adversity befalls the servant, he turns to acts of obedience, as if he were saying: "Your worship is obligatory upon me, whether You give me good things or cast me into what is disliked." His saying: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He means death, and death is called "the certainty" because it is a matter that is certain.

If it is said: What is the benefit of this time-limit, given that everyone knows that when he dies the acts of worship fall away from him?

We say: What is meant is: ﴿worship your Lord﴾ during the time of your life, and no moment of life is free from this worship. And God knows best.

The commentary of this surah is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings be upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), his family, and peace.
